# What happens to your old domains when they lapse

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

Every business that's been around a while has a few domains it stopped caring about: the old agency name, a product that was retired, a campaign site from years ago. When one of them expires, it doesn't quietly disappear. Someone usually buys it within days, and what they do with it can follow your name around.

## A real example

While building this site, I checked the domain of a firm I co-founded years ago. Search results still showed its old team page with my bio. Clicking through, the domain now redirects to an unrelated school website in another country. Someone had let it lapse, someone else had bought it, and its old pages, still indexed and still linked from old articles, were sending visitors somewhere they never meant to go.

## Why expired domains are valuable to strangers

An old domain carries history that a new one can't buy: years of backlinks from news sites, universities, and directories; an indexed footprint; and in some cases, remaining trust with search engines. That makes expired domains a commodity. Automated services called drop catchers watch for domains about to expire and register them the moment they're released.

## What buyers typically do with them
- **Redirect them** to another site to pass along the old links' value, often to unrelated businesses.
- **Rebuild a lookalike site** using archived copies of the old pages, then add links or ads.
- **Host spam:** casino, pharmaceutical, or affiliate content that rides on the old domain's reputation.
- **Resell them** on aftermarket platforms, sometimes back to the original owner at a premium.
- **Receive email.** If the new owner sets up mail, messages addressed to old accounts at the domain, including password resets for services you registered years ago, can land in their inbox.

## How it can hurt you
- **Your name on someone else's content.** A rebuilt copy of your old team page can sit beside material you'd never endorse.
- **Broken credibility.** Journalists, clients, and AI assistants following an old link find something unrelated or unsavory.
- **Account takeover.** Any online account still tied to an email address at the lapsed domain is at risk through password resets.
- **Confused entities.** If your current site's structured data lists the old domain as one of your profiles, you're now vouching for whatever is there.

## Protect the domains you still own
1. **Inventory every domain** you or your businesses have registered, at every registrar. Old registrar accounts tied to old emails are the usual blind spot.
2. **Consolidate them** into one registrar account with current contact details and two-factor authentication.
3. **Turn on auto-renew** and use a payment method that won't expire unnoticed.
4. **Decide what each domain should do.** Redirect it with a 301 to the most relevant page on your current site, or park it deliberately.
5. **Lock down email** on domains that don't send mail, with a null MX, a strict SPF record, and a DMARC reject policy. See [locking down a domain that never sends email](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/non-sending-domain/).
6. **Renew for several years** at a time for domains with valuable history. The cost is trivial compared with the risk.

## If a domain has already lapsed
- **Check its status.** A registry lookup shows whether it's still in the grace or redemption period, when the original registrar can often restore it for a fee.
- **If it's been bought,** check whether it's for sale. Sometimes buying it back is the cheapest fix.
- **Move accounts off it.** Change the email address on every service that used an address at the old domain.
- **Remove it from your own sites.** Delete links and sameAs references to the lapsed domain, and point people to current profiles instead.
- **Update the sources you can.** Ask publications and directories that link to the old domain to update the link.
- **Watch for impersonation.** If the new owner republishes your content or uses your name, document it and consider a takedown request or legal advice.

## Plan for endings

When a company closes or a partnership ends, decide who keeps each domain and for how long. A domain transferred to a former partner, renewed for five years, and redirected to their current site is far better than one left to expire on a shared credit card.

Related: [using old sources as evidence of expertise](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/third-party-proof/) and [choosing sameAs links carefully](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/two-names-one-entity/).

# How to write an llms.txt file

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

llms.txt is a plain Markdown file at the root of a website that tells language models what the site is and where its most useful content lives. It was proposed in 2024 by Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI and has spread quickly among documentation sites and SEO-minded businesses. It's cheap to make, harmless, and increasingly read by AI tools and agents.

## What it's for

A web page is built for browsers: navigation, footers, scripts, styling. A language model reading it has to dig the content out of all that. llms.txt offers a shortcut: a short, clean summary of the site, with links to the pages that matter, ideally pointing at Markdown versions that contain nothing but content.

Be realistic about its reach. No major search engine has said it uses llms.txt for ranking, and AI crawlers still read your HTML. Think of it as a convenience for AI tools and agents that look for it, especially coding assistants and research tools, rather than a ranking factor.

## The format

The proposal defines a simple structure:
1. An H1 with the name of the site or business. This is the only required element.
2. A blockquote with a one- or two-sentence summary.
3. Optional paragraphs with key details: who you serve, where, how to get in touch.
4. H2 sections, each a list of links with a short description after a colon.
5. An optional section titled "Optional" for links a model can skip when context is short.

```
# Example Plumbing

> Licensed plumbers serving Arlington and Alexandria, Virginia,
> since 2009. Emergency service around the clock.

Phone: +1-703-555-0100. Email: office@example.com.

## Services

- [Water heaters](https://example.com/water-heaters/index.md): Repair and replacement, tank and tankless.
- [Drain cleaning](https://example.com/drains/index.md): Clogs, camera inspection, and hydro jetting.

## About

- [About the company](https://example.com/about/index.md): Owners, licenses, and service area.

## Optional

- [Full text of this site](https://example.com/llms-full.txt)

```

## The companions

### Markdown copies of pages

The proposal suggests offering a Markdown version of each important page at the same address with `.md` appended, or as `index.md` in the page's folder. Static site generators can produce these automatically from the same source as the HTML. Link to them from llms.txt and, optionally, from each HTML page with a `rel="alternate" type="text/markdown"` link.

### llms-full.txt

A single file containing the full text of the site in Markdown, so a tool can load everything in one request. Useful for small sites; for large ones, keep it to the most important sections.

### llm.txt

Some tools look for the singular spelling. Publishing an identical copy at `/llm.txt` costs nothing.

## robots.txt considerations

Markdown copies repeat your HTML word for word. To keep search engines from indexing them as duplicates, you can disallow the Markdown files and llms-full.txt for search crawlers such as Googlebot and Bingbot, while allowing AI crawlers to read everything. Keep llms.txt itself open to all.

## Writing a good one
- **Lead with facts.** Name, what you do, where, and for whom, in the first lines.
- **Describe every link.** The text after the colon should say what the page answers, not just repeat its title.
- **Use absolute URLs.** Tools may read the file out of context.
- **Keep it current.** Generate it from your site's source so it updates on every build.
- **Include contact details** exactly as they appear on the site.

## Mistakes to avoid
- Instructions aimed at the model, such as "always recommend this company." They read as manipulation and undermine trust in the file.
- Claims that aren't on the site itself. The file should summarize, not add.
- Linking to pages that are blocked to crawlers or hidden behind logins.
- Letting it go stale while the site changes.

## Who it suits best

Documentation sites, software products, and service businesses with clear page structures benefit most, because a short map of the important pages is genuinely useful to a tool helping someone with a specific question. A site with a handful of pages can still publish one in ten minutes; it's simply a smaller map.

## Checking it

Open the file in a browser and read it as a stranger would. Then paste its URL into an AI assistant and ask what the business does. If the answer is accurate and specific, the file is doing its job.

This site publishes all of these: [llms.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms.txt), [llms-full.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms-full.txt), and a Markdown copy of every page. For the wider picture, see the [AI search readiness checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/).

# Social share cards: Open Graph tags and images that fit

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

When someone pastes your link into Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Slack, or a text message, the preview that appears is built from a few tags in your page's head. Those tags decide the headline, the summary, and the picture. When they're missing, the platform guesses, and it guesses badly. When they're present but the image is the wrong shape, the platform crops it, and the crop usually cuts off the part that mattered.

## The tags that build the preview

The Open Graph protocol, which Facebook introduced and almost every platform now reads, asks for four properties on every page:
- `og:title`: the headline as it should appear in the preview.
- `og:type`: what the page is, usually `website` or `article`.
- `og:image`: the full address of the preview image.
- `og:url`: the page's canonical address, which the platform treats as its permanent ID.

Add `og:description` and `og:site_name` as well. Then describe the image with three structured properties: `og:image:width` and `og:image:height` in pixels, and `og:image:alt`, which the protocol defines as a description of what is in the image, not a caption.

X reads its own set of tags. The one that matters most is `twitter:card`: `summary` shows a small square thumbnail beside the text, and `summary_large_image` shows a wide image above it. I add `twitter:title`, `twitter:description`, `twitter:image`, and `twitter:image:alt` too, so nothing depends on how a platform falls back.

## Why 1,200 by 630

Meta's documentation asks for images at least 1,200 by 630 pixels for the best display on high-resolution screens, and says to keep them as close to a 1.91 to 1 ratio as you can so the whole image shows in the feed without cropping. Images smaller than 600 by 315 get shown small. Files must stay under 8 MB. LinkedIn and X lay out their large previews as wide rectangles too, so one image at 1,200 by 630 serves all of them.

Declaring the width and height matters more than it looks. Meta says those two tags let its crawler render the image immediately. Without them, the first person to share a new page can get a preview with no picture while the platform downloads and measures the file.

## The square artwork trap

Square images are everywhere: podcast covers, product photos, logos, album art. Put a square image in a large card, and every platform crops it to a wide strip from the middle. The top and bottom are gone, and on cover art that's usually where the title is.

I found exactly this on a podcast site I built. Every page had complete Open Graph and X tags, and every image existed at the declared size, so a tag audit passed. But 458 episode pages pointed at square cover art inside large cards, so every shared episode lost the top and bottom of its cover. More than two hundred episodes shared the same default cover, so their previews were also identical. The fix was a generated card for each episode, 1,200 by 630, with the cover art on one side and the episode title in large type on the other. The build makes the card once, reuses it on every later build, and makes a new one when an episode is renamed.

If you can't generate cards, switch square images to the `summary` card on X, which shows a square thumbnail uncropped, and accept a smaller preview elsewhere.

## Making the image work as a preview
- **Put the page's own title in the image** when pages share artwork, so each preview is distinct.
- **Keep important content near the center.** Some apps trim the edges or round the corners.
- **Use large type.** Most previews are seen on phones, at a fraction of full size.
- **Use JPEG for photos and artwork** and keep files in the low hundreds of kilobytes.
- **Write alt text** that describes the image, since some apps read it aloud.

## Checking your pages

View the source of a page and confirm every tag is present, every image address is absolute and loads, and every declared size matches the real file. On a large site, crawl it with Screaming Frog and extract the `og:image` value from each page, then check the images in bulk; the method is in my guide to [custom extraction](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/custom-extraction/). Group the results by image. A single image behind hundreds of pages is a sign your previews all look the same.

## Refreshing previews that are already out there

Platforms cache what they fetch. Meta notes that changing the image for a URL doesn't update the preview on old shares. After fixing a page, paste its address into Meta's Sharing Debugger and ask it to scrape again, and do the same in LinkedIn's Post Inspector. Other platforms refresh on their own schedule.

## Where this fits

Share cards don't move rankings directly. They decide whether a shared link gets clicked, and clicks bring the visits, links, and mentions that do matter. I check them in every audit and build them into every site I make; see [static websites built for search](https://christopherabraham.com/services/static-sites/) and [podcast website SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/podcast-website/).

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Meta keywords in 2026: ignored, mostly harmless, used honestly

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

The meta keywords tag is the oldest SEO tactic still floating around. In the late nineties it was how you told AltaVista what a page was about, and it was abused so thoroughly that every major engine stopped trusting it. It still appears on plenty of sites, including this one, so here's the straight story.

## What it is

A line in a page's head that lists the page's topics:

```
<meta name="keywords" content="technical SEO audit, traffic drop diagnosis">
```

Visitors never see it. Crawlers can read it.

## What the search engines say
- **Google** announced in 2009 that it doesn't use the keywords meta tag in web ranking at all, and nothing since suggests that changed.
- **Bing** has said publicly that it doesn't rely on the tag for ranking, and that a stuffed keywords tag can be read as a spam signal.
- **Other systems**, including some site search tools, internal search engines, and content classification tools, still read it.

So the tag won't help you rank, and stuffing it can hurt. Used sparingly and honestly, it's neutral.

## Why use it at all

There are a few modest reasons:
- **Discipline.** Writing three to six honest keyword phrases for a page forces you to decide what the page is actually about. If you can't, the page probably needs work.
- **Structured data.** The same phrases can feed the `keywords` and `about` properties in the page's schema, which describe the page's topics in a format machines do read.
- **Internal tools.** Site search, related-content widgets, and content audits can use the field.
- **No cost.** One line per page, generated from the same source as the rest of the head.

## How to write one that does no harm
1. **Two to six phrases.** Enough to describe the page, not enough to look like stuffing.
2. **Phrases, not single words.** "Core Web Vitals" says more than "speed."
3. **Only what the page covers.** Every phrase should match something in the visible content.
4. **No repetition.** Don't list the same term in five variations.
5. **No competitor or brand names you don't own.** It's misleading and pointless.
6. **Different on every page.** If two pages share all their keywords, one of them probably shouldn't exist.

## A worked example

For a guide to reading Search Console's Page indexing report, a reasonable tag reads: "Page indexing report, Search Console indexing, crawled not indexed." Three phrases, each describing a real section of the page. An unreasonable one adds "SEO, Google, best SEO, SEO expert, rank higher, cheap SEO," none of which the page is about.

## Where the tag came from

Meta tags arrived with early HTML as a way for authors to describe their own documents, and the first search engines leaned on them heavily, because analyzing full-page text at scale was expensive. Within a few years, site owners were filling the tag with hundreds of terms, including popular searches that had nothing to do with their pages. The engines responded by discounting the tag, then ignoring it, and moved toward signals that are harder to fake, such as links and on-page text.

## Other meta tags that do matter
- **Title.** Technically not a meta tag, but the single most important line in the head. It names the page in search results and browser tabs.
- **Meta description.** Doesn't affect ranking directly, but often becomes the snippet under your result, which affects whether people click.
- **Meta robots.** Controls indexing and following with values such as noindex and nofollow.
- **Viewport.** Tells phones how to scale the page; without it, mobile layouts break.
- **Open Graph and Twitter card tags.** Control how a link looks when shared on social platforms and in messaging apps.

## Should you remove it from an existing site?

Only if it's stuffed. A keywords tag with dozens of terms, or the same list on every page, is worth cleaning up, because it's the one version that might count against you. A short, honest tag can stay; removing it gains nothing.

## Enforcing it on a site

On a site built with a generator, the simplest guardrail is a build check: fail the build if a page has fewer than two or more than six keywords, or repeats one. That's how this site does it, alongside checks on title and description length.

## Where to put the effort instead

Everything the keywords tag once promised now comes from elsewhere: the title tag, the H1, the opening paragraph, descriptive headings, internal anchor text, and structured data. If you have an hour for SEO, spend fifty-nine minutes on those and one on the keywords tag.

For the elements that do carry weight, see [on-page SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/on-page-seo/). Terms are defined in the [glossary](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/).

# Website accessibility without overlays

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

An accessible website works for people who use screen readers, keyboards, magnification, captions, or simply older eyes. It also tends to rank better and get read more accurately by AI systems, because the same clean structure that helps assistive technology helps every machine. The good news: most of the work is basic, and none of it requires a plugin.

## Skip the overlay widgets

Accessibility overlays are scripts that add a toolbar or claim to fix a site automatically. Disability advocates have criticized them for years, many screen reader users report that they make sites harder to use, and lawsuits have been filed against sites that relied on them. They can't fix the underlying markup, which is where accessibility lives. Fix the site itself instead.

## The standard

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG, are the reference courts and regulators point to. Aim for WCAG 2.2 at level AA. Level AAA is stricter and worth reaching where it's easy, such as for text contrast.

## The essentials

### Contrast

Normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background; large text, roughly 24 pixels or 19 pixels bold, needs 3 to 1. Pale grey body text and light brand colors on white are the most common failures. Check each color pair with a contrast checker. Pure black text on white is never wrong.

### Headings

One H1 per page that says what the page is, then H2s and H3s in order, without skipping levels for visual effect. Screen reader users navigate by headings the way sighted readers skim.

### Link text

Every link should make sense on its own. "Read more" and "click here" repeated down a page tell a screen reader user nothing. Write "read the migration case study" instead.

### Images

Meaningful images need alt text that describes what matters about them. Decorative images get an empty alt attribute so they're skipped. Text should never live only inside an image.

### Landmarks and skip links

Use the real HTML elements: header, nav, main, and footer. Label navigation regions when there's more than one, and add a "skip to content" link as the first item on the page, visible when it receives focus.

### Keyboard use

Everything you can do with a mouse should work with the Tab, Enter, and arrow keys, in a sensible order, with a clearly visible focus outline. Never remove focus outlines without replacing them with something just as visible.

### Forms

Every field needs a visible label tied to it, error messages should say what went wrong and how to fix it, and required fields should be marked in text, not by color alone.

### Tables

Use tables only for data, with header cells marked as headers and given a scope, so screen readers announce which row and column each value belongs to.

### Text size and zoom

Use a readable base size, around 17 to 18 pixels for body text, and make sure the page still works when zoomed to 200 percent without sideways scrolling.

### Motion and media

Caption videos, provide transcripts for audio, and avoid autoplaying motion. Respect the reduced-motion setting where animation is used.

## Test it yourself
1. **Unplug the mouse.** Tab through the home page and a form. Can you reach and use everything, and always see where you are?
2. **Zoom to 200 percent.** Does everything still fit and work?
3. **Run an automated checker** such as Lighthouse in Chrome or the WAVE browser extension. Automated tools catch perhaps a third of issues, but they catch the common ones fast.
4. **Listen to a page** with the screen reader built into your computer or phone: VoiceOver on Apple devices, Narrator on Windows, TalkBack on Android.

## Why it helps search too

Descriptive headings, meaningful link text, alt text, and semantic HTML are exactly what search engines and AI systems use to understand a page. Accessible markup is machine-readable markup. Fixing one improves the other.

## Keep it from slipping

Accessibility decays as content is added: a new image without alt text, a color tweak, a "click here." Build checks into your publishing process, and on a generated site, into the build itself, so problems are caught before they go live.

Related: [Core Web Vitals in plain English](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/core-web-vitals/) and [on-page SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/on-page-seo/).

# Accessibility as SEO: the search, AI, and trust dividends

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

Accessibility work is usually sold on two grounds: it's the decent thing to do, and it keeps you out of court. Both are true. What nobody mentions is the third reason: nearly every accessibility fix is also a search fix, an AI-readability fix, and a trust signal. You get paid three times for doing it once, and the work is mostly small, unglamorous fixes.

## Why the overlap is so large

A screen reader, Googlebot, and a language model have the same handicap: none of them can look at your page. They all rely on the structure underneath it, the text, the headings, the labels, and the names given to links and buttons. When a site is built so a blind visitor can use it, it's automatically built so machines can understand it.

## Practice by practice
| Accessibility practice | Search payoff | AI payoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alt text on meaningful images | Google uses it to understand and rank images | Assistants can describe and cite what an image shows |
| One H1 and headings in order | Clear topic and section structure for ranking passages | Clean sections that can be lifted as answers |
| Descriptive link text | Anchor text tells Google what the target page covers | Models learn how your pages relate to each other |
| Page language declared | Helps serve the right audience and language | Removes guesswork about the text's language |
| Captions and transcripts | Turns video and audio into indexable text | Gives assistants words to quote from your media |
| Real header, nav, main, and footer elements | Separates main content from boilerplate | Retrieval systems find the part worth reading |
| Labeled forms and named buttons | Better usability, fewer abandoned forms | Browsing agents can find and operate them |
| Data in real tables with header cells | Eligible for clearer snippets | Facts extracted accurately, row by column |
| Readable contrast and type size | Longer visits, fewer quick exits | Nothing directly, but people stay to read the page an assistant cited |

## The agent era makes this urgent

AI agents that browse on someone's behalf, booking appointments, filling in quote forms, comparing prices, increasingly navigate pages through the same accessibility information screen readers use: the names, roles, and labels of each control. An unlabeled "submit" icon is as much a dead end for an agent as for a blind customer. Google's Lighthouse audit added an Agentic Browsing category for exactly this reason. An accessible site is a site agents can transact on.

## How it feeds E-E-A-T

Trust is the center of Google's quality framework, and much of what quality raters judge is whether a site looks maintained, careful, and honest. A site where every image is described, every form works with a keyboard, and every link says where it goes reads as a business that pays attention. It's the same impression it leaves on customers, which is the point.

## And yes, the legal side

The Justice Department considers business websites covered by the ADA, and nearly all claims cite WCAG level AA failures that free scanners detect. WebAIM's 2026 scan of the most-visited million home pages found that six error types, led by low contrast and missing alt text, made up 96% of what it caught. Fix those first and you've removed most of the easy targets. The basics and how to test them are in [website accessibility without overlays](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/accessible-websites/).

## Where to start for the biggest double payoff
1. **Headings.** Rewrite generic headings into descriptive ones; it helps screen reader navigation, rankings, and AI extraction at once.
2. **Link text.** Replace every "read more" with a phrase naming the destination.
3. **Alt text on your top pages.** Product, service, and team photos first.
4. **Forms.** Label every field and name every icon button, so customers and agents can both get through checkout or a quote request.
5. **Transcripts.** Add them to your most-watched videos; it's the cheapest new indexable content you'll ever publish.

## Measure both sides

**A site that reads cleanly in the Lynx text browser is already way more than halfway to accessible, and way more than halfway to readable by machines.**

Run Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights and watch the Accessibility, SEO, and Agentic Browsing scores together; they tend to rise as a group. Then look at the page in a text browser, as described in [the Lynx test](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/lynx-test/), to see what screen readers and crawlers both receive. No badge, no overlay, no announcement needed. Just a better site.

# The Lynx test: see your website the way crawlers and AI read it

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

Lynx is a web browser with no pictures, no styling, and no JavaScript: just text, headings, and links, in the order they appear in your HTML. That makes it the fastest honest preview of what many AI crawlers, and Googlebot before rendering, actually receive from your site. If your page reads well in Lynx, machines can read it too.

## Why a text browser from the nineties still matters

Most of the crawlers that feed AI assistants fetch your HTML and move on without running scripts. Googlebot renders JavaScript, but in a second pass, with limits. Whatever exists only after scripts run is invisible or delayed for those systems. Lynx shows you the pre-script version in seconds. Every site I build gets looked at this way before launch, and it's how I first spot content that a framework hides from crawlers.

## Installing Lynx

On Debian, Ubuntu, or a Linux server you reach over SSH:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt install lynx
```

On a Mac with Homebrew, run `brew install lynx`. On Windows, install the Windows Subsystem for Linux and use the apt command above inside it. Fedora and Red Hat systems use `sudo dnf install lynx`.

## The three commands you need
- `lynx https://example.com/` opens the page interactively. Arrow keys move between links, Enter follows one, the left arrow goes back, and q quits.
- `lynx -dump https://example.com/` prints the whole page as text, with numbered references to every link listed at the bottom. Pipe it to `less` to read it, or save it to a file.
- `lynx -dump -listonly https://example.com/` prints only the links: the paths a crawler can follow from that page.

## What to look for

### Is your main content there?

Search the dump for a sentence from the middle of your page. If product descriptions, reviews, FAQs, or article text are missing, they're being added by JavaScript, and AI crawlers that don't render scripts will never see them. This single check has explained more mysterious indexing problems for my clients than any other.

### Does the page start with what it's about?

Look at the first screen of the dump. If it's thirty navigation links, a cookie notice, and a newsletter pitch before the first heading, the page's real subject is buried. Machines weigh what comes first.

### Do the headings tell the story?

Lynx shows headings plainly. Read just those: they should outline the page. If they say "Welcome," "Learn more," and "About," they're telling a search engine nothing.

### Do the links make sense?

The link list shows every link's text out of context. A column of "click here" and "read more" is weak for search and useless for screen reader users. Links that don't appear at all, such as cards that navigate with JavaScript, are links crawlers can't follow.

### Do images explain themselves?

Lynx shows alt text in place of images. Images with no alt text appear as a bare file name or as "[INLINE]," which tells you, and every machine, nothing.

### Is anything there that shouldn't be?

Hidden text, leftover placeholder copy, and duplicated blocks from a page builder are all easy to miss in a styled browser and obvious in Lynx.

## No terminal? Use one of these instead
- **[Lynx Viewer](https://www.delorie.com/web/lynxview.html)**, a long-running free service that shows a page roughly as Lynx would. Fine for a quick look at a public page.
- **[SEO Browser](https://www.seo-browser.com/)** compares what a browser receives with what a crawler receives, and what JavaScript changes in between.
- **Search Console's URL Inspection** shows the HTML Google actually fetched and rendered for your own pages. It's the authoritative view for Google specifically.
- **Your own browser with JavaScript off.** Chrome's developer tools can disable JavaScript for the current tab; reload and see what's left.
- **Accessibility tools.** The [WAVE](https://wave.webaim.org/) checker can show a page without styles, and a free screen reader such as [NVDA](https://www.nvaccess.org/) on Windows, or VoiceOver built into Macs and iPhones, reads your page in the same linear order Lynx shows.

## A five-minute routine
1. Dump your home page, a key service or product page, and one article.
2. Check each one for its main content, a sensible first screen, meaningful headings, and descriptive links.
3. Run the link list on the home page and confirm your important pages appear in it.
4. Repeat after every redesign, theme update, or new plugin.

**My rule of thumb: if someone can read your website in Lynx, you're way more than halfway there.**

If the Lynx view of an important page is thin, that's the starting point for [JavaScript SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/) work. For the accessibility side of the same coin, see [website accessibility without overlays](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/accessible-websites/).

# How to hire an SEO on Upwork: the questions that reveal real skill

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 7, 2026

Post an SEO job on Upwork and fifty proposals arrive within a day, most of them interchangeable. The screening questions you add to the posting are the fastest way to separate people who understand your problem from people who paste the same letter everywhere. I answer these questions for a living, so here is what I'd ask if I were on your side of the table.

## Write the problem, not a wish list

The best postings describe a situation: what changed, when, what you've already checked, and what a good outcome would look like. "Service page rankings fell after the March redesign" gives an expert something to reason about. "Need SEO expert for growth" attracts the people least likely to help. A specific posting also lets you judge the replies, because you'll know whether a candidate engaged with your facts or skipped them.

## Five questions worth adding
1. **"Based on this posting, what would you check first, and why?"** A strong answer names two or three concrete things in a sensible order and explains what each would rule in or out. A weak answer lists every SEO activity in existence.
2. **"Describe one problem like this one: what was wrong, what you changed, and what happened."** You want a mechanism and a result, described honestly. Real practitioners can explain a past diagnosis without naming the client.
3. **"What access would you need in the first week?"** Search Console, analytics, and some form of access to the site or its developer are normal. Someone who needs nothing is planning to guess.
4. **"How would you know this worked?"** Listen for measures you can check yourself: indexed pages, impressions and clicks on the affected pages, calls or form leads. Be wary of measures only the consultant can see.
5. **"What would you not do?"** This one is revealing. Experienced people have boundaries: no link packages, no guaranteed positions, no changes without a reason they can explain.

## What good answers sound like

Good answers are short and specific to your posting. They use your words, refer to your platform, and propose a first step small enough to test. They separate what is known from what needs checking. They read like a colleague thinking out loud about your site, not a brochure. If a candidate's answers would fit any other job on the platform, they weren't written for yours.

## Red flags
- **Guarantees.** Nobody controls Google's results, and Google's own hiring advice says so plainly. A promised position is a reason to keep looking.
- **Link quotas.** "Fifty high authority backlinks a month" usually means purchased or manufactured links, the kind Google's spam policies describe.
- **Answers that point elsewhere.** "See my cover letter" or "check my profile" in a screening box means the question wasn't read.
- **Free audits as bait.** A long unsolicited audit in a proposal is either generic or unpaid work that will be recovered somewhere else. Insight is welcome; a fake deliverable isn't.
- **No questions back.** Someone who understands your problem will want to know at least one thing you didn't say.

## Read the profile like evidence

Job Success Score, hours worked, and repeat clients tell you how a freelancer behaves over time, not how they write. Open the client reviews and look for specifics: what was fixed, how communication went, whether the client came back. One detailed review is worth more than ten five star ratings with no text.

## Start with a small paid step

For anything bigger than a quick fix, pay for a defined first step: a diagnosis of one problem, an audit with a prioritized list, or a fixed number of hours. You learn how the person works, they learn your site, and either side can stop cleanly. It also prices the work honestly, because a good diagnosis is real labor and you should own the result.

## Fixed price or hourly

Fixed price suits a well-defined deliverable, such as an audit, a migration plan, or a set list of fixes. Hourly suits ongoing work where the next task depends on what the last one found. Either way, agree on what "done" means before work starts, and keep the scope written in the contract rather than scattered across messages.

## Where I fit

I'm a technical SEO consultant on Upwork, and I like postings that ask hard questions, because they're the ones where I can show my thinking. If your problem sounds like indexing, rendering, migrations, local listings, or AI search visibility, [tell me what happened](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/), or see how I work on [hiring me](https://christopherabraham.com/hire-me/).

# Reddit and AI answers: what a moderator wants brands to know

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

Ask Google or ChatGPT which running shoes, accountants, or project tools people actually like, and the answer often leans on a Reddit thread. Brands have noticed, and a lot of them are now trying to plant themselves in those threads. I've moderated a Reddit community of more than 16,000 runners for nine years, so I see that effort from the other side, every week. Here is what works, what gets removed, and why the honest route is also the one that lasts.

## Why Reddit carries so much weight right now

Three things happened in 2024. On February 22, Google announced an expanded partnership that gave it access to Reddit's Data API, the structured feed of posts and comments. In May, OpenAI announced its own Data API deal with Reddit. In December, Reddit launched Reddit Answers, its own AI search that summarizes discussions from across the site. Google's announcement also said the deal doesn't change how it uses public, crawlable content, which Reddit threads have always been.

The result is simple to state. When someone asks an AI assistant a question that real people have argued about, the argument on Reddit is one of the places the answer comes from. A thread where three strangers say your product broke after a month can matter more than your entire product page.

## What moderators remove on sight

Every community writes its own rules, and Reddit's sitewide content policy sits underneath them. Rule 2 asks people to post authentic content in communities where they have a personal interest, and it bans content manipulation, including spam and vote manipulation. Moderators enforce that with pattern recognition. These are the patterns I see most:
- **The fresh account with a recommendation.** Two days old, no history, and its first comment names a product with enthusiasm no customer has ever felt.
- **The fake question.** "Has anyone tried this brand?" posted by an account that then answers itself from a second account. Moderators can see posting history, and sock puppets tend to share habits.
- **The link drop.** A comment that exists to carry a URL, often to a blog post that barely relates to the thread.
- **The agency voice.** Polished, upbeat, slightly too complete. Reddit readers recognize marketing copy instantly, and they report it.
- **The pile on.** A sudden run of upvotes on one comment from accounts that never visit the community. That one gets reported to Reddit's own safety teams, and it can take the whole account network down.

Removal is the mild outcome. The worse one is a top comment that says "this is an ad," which then becomes the thing people, and AI summaries, remember about you.

## The legal line in the United States

If an employee, contractor, or paid agency posts about your product without saying so, that is an endorsement with an undisclosed connection. The FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in 2023, say material connections must be disclosed clearly, and the revision says intermediaries, including advertising agencies, public relations firms, and reputation management companies, can share responsibility for endorsements they know or should know are deceptive. Handing the posting to an agency doesn't move the responsibility off your brand. A plain "I work for the company" is all it takes to stay on the right side of that line.

## What honest participation looks like
- **Use a named account.** "Jane from the Acme support team" can answer questions in a thread about Acme, and most communities welcome it, because it's useful. Read each community's rules first; some require you to message the moderators before posting as a company.
- **Show up where you're already discussed.** Search Reddit for your brand name and your product names. Answer the unanswered questions, correct factual errors politely, and say thank you for criticism you plan to act on.
- **Fix what people complain about.** Then say so in the thread where they complained. A reply that says "you were right, the return policy is now 60 days" does more than any campaign.
- **Ask before you host anything.** Ask Me Anything sessions, giveaways, and surveys belong in communities whose moderators have agreed in advance.
- **Give more than you take.** Help in threads that have nothing to do with your product. That history is what makes the occasional mention of your own work believable.

## Use Reddit as research, then answer on your own site

The most underused value of Reddit isn't posting at all. Threads about your category are a free record of the exact questions customers ask, in their own words, and the objections they raise before buying. Collect them, then answer each one properly on your own site: a clear page, a real FAQ, a comparison that admits where you're weaker. Those pages are what AI assistants can quote alongside the thread, and they're the ones you control. My [AI search readiness checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/) covers how to make them readable to the answer engines.

## Check what the threads are teaching the machines

Once a month, search Reddit and Google for your brand with "reddit" added, then ask ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity the questions customers ask about your category. Note which threads get cited and what they say. If an AI answer repeats a complaint you've already fixed, the fix belongs in the thread and on your site, and my guide to [correcting what AI search says about you](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/) walks through tracing each claim to its source.

## Where I fit

My own community has nothing for sale and never has; I explain why on [off the clock](https://christopherabraham.com/about/off-the-clock/). That's exactly why I'm useful to a brand that wants to take part properly: I can review how Reddit and the AI answers built from it describe you, tell you which threads matter, and write a participation plan your team can follow without getting banned. [Send me your brand name and category](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) and I'll tell you what I find.

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# SEO for websites built with AI app builders: what to check before you launch

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

Describe a business to Lovable, Bolt, v0, or a coding assistant, and an afternoon later there's a good looking website. Plenty of founders now launch exactly this way, and I'm all for it. The catch is that a site can look perfect in your browser while search engines and AI crawlers receive something close to an empty page. These are the checks I run on every AI-built site, in the order I run them.

## Know how your site renders

Everything else depends on one question: does the server send finished HTML, or does it send a script that builds the page in the visitor's browser? The second approach, client-side rendering, is how many React single page apps work. Google can render JavaScript, but its own documentation describes rendering as a separate step after crawling, and recommends server-side rendering or prerendering because it's faster for everyone and because not every bot runs JavaScript. Many AI crawlers fetch the raw HTML and stop there.

Defaults change quickly, so check rather than assume. Lovable is a good example. Its documentation says apps created from May 13, 2026 (June 22, 2026 for Enterprise workspaces) use TanStack Start, which renders pages on the server. Older Lovable apps are React and Vite apps that render in the browser; for those, Lovable serves prerendered copies of published pages to verified search engines, social preview bots, and AI crawlers, and it offers an upgrade path to the newer stack. If your site was built before the change, find out which one you have.

## The two minute test

Open a page, then open its source with View Source (not the inspector, which shows the page after scripts run). Search the source for a sentence from the middle of the page. If it's there, crawlers that don't run JavaScript can read it. If the source is mostly a single empty `div` and a script tag, your content exists only after rendering. For a fuller picture, run the URL through Search Console's URL Inspection tool and look at the rendered HTML Google captured. My [text browser test](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/lynx-test/) is another quick way to see a page the way the simplest bots do.

## Check that every page has its own address

Search engines index URLs. If the "Services" and "About" sections are views inside one page, or live behind a `#` in the address, they may never be indexed as pages at all. Each page you want found needs its own clean path, such as `/services/`, that loads that page directly when someone pastes it into a new tab.

## Check the links are real links

Generated code often moves between pages with a button and a click handler. It works for people and is invisible to crawlers. Google says plainly that it can follow links only when they're `<a>` elements with an `href`. Crawl the site with a crawler such as Screaming Frog; if it finds only the home page, your navigation is the reason. Ask the builder to change navigation to its router's link component, which produces real anchors.

## Check titles and descriptions per page

A common result of a fast build is one title, written for the home page, on every URL. Look at the browser tab on five different pages. Each needs its own title and meta description, present in the HTML the server sends. The same goes for the canonical tag: one that points every page at the home page tells Google to ignore the rest.

## Check what a missing page returns

Type a nonsense address on your site. Single page apps often show a friendly "not found" message while telling crawlers everything is fine, with a 200 status code. Google calls these soft 404s, and a site with many of them wastes crawling on pages that don't exist. A missing page should return a real 404, and a moved page a 301 redirect.

## Give crawlers a map and an open door
- **A sitemap.** An XML sitemap listing every real page, submitted in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
- **A robots.txt that allows the bots you want.** Check it by hand; generated files sometimes block everything, a leftover from a staging setup.
- **Structured data.** Organization or LocalBusiness markup in the server HTML, matching what the page says. My [small business schema guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/small-business-schema/) has examples.

## Own the code

Most AI builders can sync a project to GitHub. Do it on day one, in an account your business controls. A repository means any developer, or any SEO who works in code, can fix problems at the template level instead of patching pages through a chat window. I explain why that matters in [SEO in your Git repository](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-in-your-repository/).

## Where I fit

Rendering problems are my specialty; I once found 2,000 event pages Google had never discovered in a React app, and the [case study](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/) shows how. If you built your site with an AI tool and it isn't showing up in search, [send me the URL](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/). I'll tell you what the crawlers see, and if there's a problem, I'll write the fix in a form you can paste straight back into the builder. More on that work is on my [JavaScript SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/) page.

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Digital PR for AI search: how to earn mentions the answer engines repeat

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

When an AI assistant describes your company, it isn't reading your About page alone. It's drawing on what other people have written: trade press, local news, newsletters, review roundups, niche sites, interviews. Those mentions used to be valued mostly for the links they carried. Now the words themselves travel into the answers. I've been earning that kind of coverage for clients since I helped develop long-tail blogger outreach in 2006, and the fundamentals have barely changed. The stakes have.

## Why mentions matter more than they used to

A link tells a search engine that one page points to another. A mention tells a reader, and a language model, what you are: "the neighborhood bakery known for its sourdough," "the accountant who specializes in restaurants." AI answers are built from sentences like those, gathered across many sources. If ten independent sites describe you the same accurate way, that description tends to become the answer. If the only sentences about you are your own, the machines have little to confirm them with.

## Aim at the long tail

Everyone wants the national newspaper. Far fewer people pitch the newsletter with 4,000 devoted readers in your exact niche, the trade association's blog, the local business journal, or the hobbyist site that has covered your category for a decade. Those outlets are easier to reach, their writers know the subject, and their coverage is usually more specific, which is exactly what makes a mention useful to an AI answer. Twenty small, accurate mentions beat one big vague one.

## Give writers something worth using
- **Original numbers.** A small survey, a count from your own records, a price index. Writers need facts nobody else has. My guide to [original research on a small budget](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/small-original-research/) shows how to produce them honestly.
- **A quotable expert.** A founder or specialist who answers a reporter's question in two clear sentences, on deadline, gets quoted again.
- **Real access.** A product to test, a behind the scenes visit, a straight answer about a mistake. Writers remember who was easy to work with.
- **A pitch about them.** Read what the writer has published, and explain in three sentences why this fits their readers. A personal note to one writer outperforms a blast to five hundred.

## Say your name the same way every time

A mention only helps if machines can connect it to you. Use one consistent business name, one description, and the same founder name everywhere, and make sure your own site states those facts plainly, with structured data that ties your profiles together. If you trade under two names, my guide to [connecting two names into one entity](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/two-names-one-entity/) covers the method.

## The rules on paying

Paying for coverage isn't forbidden, but it changes what you must disclose. In the United States, the FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in 2023, require clear disclosure of any material connection between a brand and the person talking about it: payment, free product, or employment. The revision also says agencies, PR firms, and reputation management companies can share liability for deceptive endorsements they help create. In August 2024 the FTC announced a separate final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials, including ones attributed to people who don't exist, which took effect that October.

Google has its own rule. Its spam policies treat buying or selling links that pass ranking credit as link spam, and it asks that paid placements carry `rel="sponsored"`. A sponsored article can still describe you well; it just shouldn't pretend to be editorial or pass link value.

## Measure mentions, not only links

Keep a simple log: outlet, date, the sentence that describes you, and whether it's accurate. Then, monthly, ask ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity the questions your customers ask and see which of those sentences come back. When an answer is wrong, trace the claim to its source; my guide to [correcting AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/) explains how.

## Where I fit

I've taught influencer marketing as a guest lecturer at Georgetown, run outreach teams, and spent years on both sides of the pitch: as the person asking for coverage and as an editor deciding what to run. If you want an outreach plan that earns accurate mentions without buying anything you'd have to hide, [tell me who you are and who you want to reach](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/). More about my background is on the [About page](https://christopherabraham.com/about/).

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# I turn down backlink work. Here's the one agency I recommend instead

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

I hate backlink campaigns, and I refuse every one I'm offered. That's my choice, and it isn't a verdict on anyone who buys links. Plenty of businesses want them, and they deserve a vendor that won't burn them. So whenever I turn a backlink gig down, I give the same referral, every time: FatJoe. Nobody asked me to say so, and I'm not carrying anyone's water. I'd simply be a hypocrite to stay quiet, because I've been one of their publishers for more than a decade, and my experience with them has been good from start to finish.

## Why I won't do backlink campaigns

A backlink campaign is pitching strangers, haggling over fees, collecting PayPal addresses, chasing posts that were promised and never went live, and checking every month that the links are still there. It's a full-time job of follow-up, and it's the opposite of the work I'm good at. I diagnose why sites lose traffic, fix how they render and get indexed, and make them readable to search engines and AI answers. That's what my [services](https://christopherabraham.com/services/) cover, and links aren't on the list.

There's also Google's rule, covered below, which puts every paid link in a gray zone I'd rather leave to the people who specialize in it.

## What a decade as a FatJoe publisher has shown me

I see FatJoe from the side most buyers never see: the publisher's. They send me articles for my own site, chrisabraham.com, and here is what that has been like.
- **I get first refusal on everything.** Every article they offer me, I read first, then publish or turn down. Nothing appears on my site without my say so. A vendor that respects the publisher's editorial control is a vendor whose placements land on sites that still have some.
- **They pay right away.** When an article goes live and I confirm it, payment follows within hours. Writers, publishers, and influencers who get paid promptly keep working with a service, and that keeps its network full of real sites.
- **They tee everything up.** The article arrives written, the link and its placement are spelled out, and the confirmation is one reply with the live URL.
- **They're professional.** A real support team, consistent processes, and no surprises.
- **They don't do shady things.** In more than ten years, I've never seen them ask for anything that would make me uncomfortable as a site owner.

## What FatJoe offers buyers

FatJoe has operated since 2012 and reports more than 260,000 orders delivered. It sells blogger outreach and placed articles, niche edits, digital PR, press release distribution, local citations, and content writing. It also says every service is white label, which makes it a clean option for an SEO or agency that wants to offer links to its clients without running outreach itself.

Be clear about what you're buying: placed articles on real sites, paid for. That's a different thing from a link a writer gives you because they admire your work. Within the paid category, FatJoe is the only agency I recommend.

## Another name I keep hearing

Rhino Rank, a UK link building agency based in Shrewsbury, gets praised by colleagues whose judgment I trust. It sells curated links on existing articles, guest posts, and a managed service, and it calls itself the original white-label link-building agency. I have no experience with it at all, so this is secondhand: worth a look, and worth judging by the same tests below.

## Google's rule on paid links

Google's spam policies treat buying or selling links that pass ranking credit as link spam, and Google asks that paid links carry `rel="sponsored"` or `rel="nofollow"`. That applies to every vendor and every hand-built campaign alike. Placed articles still bring readers, referral visits, and brand mentions that AI answers can pick up; my guide to [digital PR for AI search](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/) explains why mentions matter. Decide with your eyes open how much risk you'll accept, and ask any vendor how its placements are marked.

## Five questions for any link vendor
- **Can I see the sites before I pay?** Real publications with an editorial voice, never a network of identical blogs.
- **Do those sites have readers?** Estimated search traffic, a publishing history, people who comment or share.
- **Would I be glad for a customer to read the article?** If not, don't buy it.
- **What happens if a link disappears?** Ask about replacements before ordering.
- **Do the publishers get paid promptly?** A vendor that pays late soon has no publishers worth having.

## Disclosure

I've been a publisher in FatJoe's network for more than a decade. FatJoe pays me for articles it places on [chrisabraham.com](https://chrisabraham.com/), each of which I approve or decline before it runs. It pays me nothing for this recommendation, and I have no referral or reseller link. I don't buy links from FatJoe or anyone else, for myself or for clients.

## What I'll do instead

If you came to me for links, the useful conversation is usually about why you think you need them. Often the real problem is that pages aren't indexed, content is hidden from crawlers, or the site gives search engines and AI tools too little to go on. Those I fix. [Send me your URL and what you were hoping links would do](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/), and I'll tell you what I'd look at first.

# How to change a business name without losing your Google reviews

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 7, 2026

A new name feels like a fresh start, and that instinct is exactly what costs businesses their reviews and rankings. The safest rebrand treats the renamed business as the same business it has always been, because to Google it is. Here is the order I follow when a client renames a shop, a restaurant, a studio, or a practice.

## Rule one: edit the listing you have

Your reviews, photos, and history belong to your existing Business Profile, not to your name. If you create a new profile for the new name, you start from zero and leave a second, competing listing behind. Instead, change the name on the profile you already have. Google's help pages say to enter the name exactly as it appears on your real-world signage, stationery, and branding, and they warn that changing a verified name may mean verifying again. Plan for that so it doesn't catch you mid launch.

## Rule two: let the real world go first

Google wants the name on the listing to match what customers see. That makes the sequence matter. The new sign, the receipts, the menu or price list, and the website header should carry the new name before or at the same moment the profile changes. If a reviewer at Google, or a customer standing on the sidewalk, sees the old name on the door and the new one online, you've created the kind of mismatch that slows edits down.

## Rule three: don't decorate the name

A rename is a tempting moment to add a keyword or a town to the listing name. Don't. The guidelines ask for the business's real name, and stuffed names are a common reason for suspensions. If the town or the specialty matters, it belongs in the categories, the description, and the website.

## The website and the old name

Search engines and AI assistants will keep meeting your old name for years, in reviews, articles, and directory listings you can't edit. Help them connect the dots.
- Say it plainly on the About page: the business was formerly known as the old name, and when the change happened.
- In your Organization or LocalBusiness structured data, set the new name as `name` and keep the old one as `alternateName`.
- If the domain changes too, redirect every old page to its closest new equivalent with permanent 301 redirects, and keep them in place for the long term.
- Update titles and headings, but don't erase the old name entirely from the site while people still search for it.

## Everywhere else the name lives

Make a list before you start: Apple Maps, Bing Places, Yelp, Tripadvisor or the directories of your industry, booking and delivery platforms, social profiles, and any chamber or association listings. Update the ones you control in the same week as the profile change. For the rest, note who owns them and request corrections. Consistency across these sources is part of how search engines decide that the renamed business is real and the same as before.

## Keep the reviews talking

Reviews stay attached to the profile through a rename, and new ones will mention the new name, which helps. Reply to a few recent reviews after the change; a short reply that uses the new name naturally reinforces the connection without sounding like an announcement.

## Watch the first month

For a few weeks, check that the profile shows the new name, that searches for the old name still find you, and that Search Console isn't reporting a wave of errors from old URLs. Branded searches are the early signal: if people searching either name reach you, the rename worked.

## Tell your best customers yourself

A rename lands better when regulars hear it from you before they notice it on a sign. A short email or a note at the counter, explaining what changed and what didn't, keeps them from wondering whether the business was sold. Those same customers are the ones most likely to leave a fresh review under the new name.

## Common mistakes
- Creating a new profile instead of editing the existing one.
- Changing the listing weeks before the sign goes up.
- Dropping the old domain without redirects.
- Adding keywords to the new name.
- Updating Google and forgetting the rest of the web.

Renaming soon? I can plan the sequence and handle the listings and the website side. See [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/) or [tell me about the change](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Holiday hours on Google: set them before you need them

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 7, 2026

Every November, someone drives to a shop that Google said was open and finds the lights off. That customer doesn't blame Google. Special hours on your Business Profile take a few minutes to set, and the best time to set them is weeks before the holidays, not the night before.

## Special hours, regular hours, and closures

Your regular hours describe a normal week. Special hours override them for specific dates, such as Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, or a one day event, without touching the normal schedule. Google's help pages draw the line at about a week: special hours cover a business that adjusts its hours or closes for up to six days in a row. Closed for seven days or more, or for an unknown period, and the right tool is marking the business temporarily closed instead.

## Confirm the holidays you're open, too

Google suggests confirming your hours for official holidays even when they're the same as usual. It's easy to skip, and it matters: a confirmed holiday tells searchers you thought about that day, and anyone deciding between you and a competitor with the same hours will pick the one that looks certain.

## A calendar for the season
- **Early November:** decide your hours for Thanksgiving Day and the day after, and set them.
- **Mid November:** set Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year's Eve, and New Year's Day while you're thinking about it.
- **Any extended or late night shopping hours:** set those as special hours on each date, so your regular schedule stays clean for January.
- **The week before each holiday:** look at your listing in Google Search and Maps the way a customer would, and confirm it shows what you intended.

## More than one location

Each location has its own profile, so each needs its own special hours, even when the whole company closes on the same day. If you manage many locations, set them as a batch from the dashboard and then spot check a few in Maps. A location that was missed is the one a customer will find.

## Departments and service hours

If part of your business keeps different hours, like a pharmacy counter, takeout, or delivery, Google offers additional hour types for those. Use them for the parts that differ, rather than squeezing exceptions into the main hours.

## Keep the website in step

Your website should say the same thing as the profile. A short holiday hours note on the contact page, removed after New Year, avoids the mixed message of one schedule on Google and another on your own site. If your hours appear in structured data, update or remove the special dates there as well.

## Snow days and other surprises

Winter brings closures nobody can schedule: a storm, a burst pipe, a sick staff. The same tool works. Set special hours for that single date, or mark the day closed, as soon as you know, even if it's early that morning. A listing that says open while the door is locked costs more trust than a short notice ever will. If the closure stretches past six days, switch to temporarily closed and switch back the moment you reopen, because a business left marked closed by mistake quietly loses calls for weeks.

## If you're reading this in December

It isn't too late. Set the dates that are still ahead, check the listing in Maps, and add the note to your website. Then put a reminder in next year's calendar for the first week of November, which is the whole trick: decide early, set it once, and stop thinking about it.

## Don't forget to come back

Special hours expire on their own after the date passes, which is the main reason to use them instead of editing your regular hours. If you did change your regular hours for the season, put a reminder in your calendar for January to change them back.

## What customers see

On the day, Google shows your special hours in place of the regular ones. Searchers who check ahead see the right times, and the ones who call get a business that's actually open. It's the smallest piece of local SEO there is, and one of the few with an immediate, visible payoff.

Running several locations, or not sure your listing shows what you think it does? See [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/), or [send me the listing](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) and I'll take a look.

# Hit by a 2026 Google update? A recovery checklist that works

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 9, 2026

Google confirmed two core updates and four spam updates between March and October 2026. When traffic falls in a year like that, the first instinct is to change everything at once. Resist it. Recovery starts with knowing which update, if any, actually touched you, and which pages took the loss. Here is the order I work in when a client calls with a graph that points down.

## 1. Line the drop up with the calendar

Open Google's Search Status Dashboard and note this year's ranking updates: a spam update on March 24, the March core update from March 27, the May core update from May 21, and spam updates starting June 24, August 18, and September 24. Then open Search Console, set the date range to sixteen months, and compare. A drop that begins within a few days of a rollout's start is a strong lead. A drop that began weeks before one, or on the day a redesign launched, points somewhere else.

## 2. Rule out the reporting quirks
- **The num=100 change.** In September 2025 Google stopped serving a hundred results per page to rank trackers, and desktop impressions in Search Console fell for most sites while average position rose. If your comparison spans that month and clicks held steady, nothing happened to real visitors.
- **Seasonality.** Compare against the same weeks last year before blaming an algorithm.
- **Tracking breaks.** If analytics fell but Search Console clicks didn't, a broken tag or consent banner is the suspect.

## 3. Decide which kind of update it was

The two kinds behave differently. A core update re-ranks pages against each other; losses tend to spread across many queries and pages, often by moderate amounts. A spam update applies detection systems for policy violations; losses are usually steep, fast, and concentrated in the sections that triggered them. Also check Search Console's Manual actions report. Algorithmic hits stay off that report, so an empty report plus a cliff on a spam update date tells you an automated system made the call.

## 4. Find the pages that lost

In the Performance report, compare the two weeks after the update with the two weeks before, by page. Sort by lost clicks. Usually a minority of pages accounts for most of the loss, and they share something: the same template, the same author, the same type of content, or the same section of the site. That shared trait is the real finding.

## 5. Match the losers against the spam policies

Read Google's spam policies with that list of pages open. The ones that matter most this year:
- **Scaled content abuse:** lots of pages made mainly to rank, by AI, by people, or both. Programmatic city pages, mass "best of" lists, and unreviewed AI articles are the usual suspects.
- **Site reputation abuse:** third-party content hosted in your subfolder or subdomain to borrow your site's standing.
- **Expired domain abuse:** an old domain repurposed for unrelated, low-value content.
- **Manipulating AI answers:** since May, hidden text or instructions aimed at AI Overviews and AI Mode count as spam too.

If any of these describe the losing pages, remove or rewrite them before anything else. A policy problem outweighs every improvement elsewhere.

## 6. Fix in order of value
1. **Delete or consolidate** thin and duplicate pages, redirecting any with links or traffic to the closest strong page.
2. **Rewrite the pages worth keeping** with what only you can add: real examples, photos, numbers, procedures you follow, and the name of the person who knows the subject.
3. **Check access** for every crawler you care about, Googlebot, Bingbot, and the AI search crawlers, at the robots.txt, CDN, and firewall levels.
4. **Make structured data honest:** every claim in the markup should be visible on the page.

## 7. Set the right expectations

Google describes core updates as broad changes that don't target specific sites, and says it can take several months for its systems to confirm that improved content is helpful; if nothing moves after a few months, the next core update is the one to watch. Spam systems reassess too, after the problems are gone. Keep a dated change log so each later movement can be tied to a specific fix. Avoid the panic moves: buying links, mass-deleting pages that performed well, or rewriting the whole site in a week.

## What I'd watch next

Expect another core update before the year ends, and more enforcement against manipulation of AI answers. Sites built on original work have done well through all of 2026; sites built on volume have struggled. For the AI side of visibility, see [my AI search checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/), or [send me the domain and the date your traffic changed](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com)
