# Where to get reliable SEO and AI search news in 2026

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 9, 2026

Search the phrase "best SEO news sites" and the first things you see are ads for AI visibility audits, then an AI summary, then lists of lists. Most of it is marketing for whoever wrote it. Staying current takes a short reading list, an order to read it in, and the habit of checking the claim before repeating it. Here is mine, built over decades of doing this work and refreshed for the AI search era.

## Start with the people who make the rules
- **Google Search Central Blog.** Official announcements: core updates, policy changes, new Search Console reports. Recent posts covered the site reputation policy update on August 28 and new multimodal performance reporting on September 24.
- **Google Search Status Dashboard.** The authoritative record of every ranking update, with start dates and durations. When an article and the dashboard disagree, the dashboard wins.
- **Google's documentation changelog.** Quiet but important. On October 1, Google's guidance on AI-generated content began calling manual fact checking and review of AI output critical before publishing.
- **Bing Webmaster Tools and its blog.** Bing's AI Performance report is the closest thing to a first-party view of AI citations.
- **The AI companies' own policies.** OpenAI's crawler documentation, and usage policies like the one Anthropic updated on October 8, change what is allowed faster than any trade article can summarize.

## Then the daily trade press
- **Search Engine Roundtable.** Barry Schwartz's site is the fastest on tests, volatility, and small interface changes, often within hours.
- **Search Engine Land.** Broad daily coverage and analysis from many contributors. Its footer notes that it is a trademark of Semrush, the SEO software company, which is worth knowing when a story touches SEO tools.
- **Search Engine Journal.** News plus long columns from practitioners, published by Alpha Brand Media.

Read at least two for anything big. They often break the same story with different details.

## A weekly digest

Aleyda Solis' SEOFOMO newsletter arrives every Sunday with the week's news, guides, tools, and events. If you read only one thing a week, make it this.

## Research, with a grain of salt

The big tool makers, Ahrefs and Semrush among them, publish large studies on AI Overviews, citations, and click rates. They are valuable and they are also marketing for the tools that produced the data. Independent practitioners who publish their own tracking, such as Lily Ray and Marie Haynes, are worth following for the same reason: you can see their method and their sample.

## Three habits that keep you from repeating mistakes

### 1. Check dates against the primary record

This month a widely read write-up gave the start of Google's September spam update as "Thursday, September 28." The dashboard says September 24, which was the Thursday. Small slip, easy check, and the kind of error that spreads when everyone copies everyone.

### 2. Compare studies before quoting one

Three studies this fall measured how often AI Overviews appear for brand searches. Ahrefs reported 83 percent of branded searches; DemandSphere data reported in Search Engine Land showed a jump from 26 to 80 percent; a third found summaries for 93 of 100 brands. Different samples, different methods, same direction. The direction is the finding. The exact number belongs to its study.

### 3. Read the footnote on every bold claim

One agency's ad this month promises a 100 percent success rate at increasing AI visibility. The footnote defines success as an increase in any one of several visibility metrics from the start of a campaign to its latest measurement. Another vendor reports a "100% client success rate" for making reviews crawlable. Neither claim is false. Both describe something much smaller than the headline suggests.

## What to skip
- "Best agency" lists written by an agency that ranks itself first.
- Statistics with no named study, sample, or date, especially round ones repeated by AI summaries.
- Anyone claiming a secret formula for AI Overviews. Google's own documentation says there are no special requirements beyond ordinary search eligibility.

## How I use all this

Every guide on this site starts with these sources and ends with a list of them, so you can check my work the same way. For what the news has added up to this year, see [my recovery checklist for 2026 Google updates](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/update-recovery-2026/) and [my AI search checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/), or [ask me what a headline means for your site](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# WordPress SEO 101: the settings and habits that matter most

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 9, 2026

WordPress runs a huge share of the web, and it is a genuinely good platform for search right out of the box. Most WordPress SEO problems I'm hired to fix come from a handful of settings nobody changed, a few plugins that fight each other, and habits like linking the words "read more" a thousand times. Here is what a beginner should do, in order, on a new site or an old one.

## Day one: five settings to check
1. **Settings, then Reading:** find "Discourage search engines from indexing this site" and make sure it is unchecked. Developers tick it while building and forget it at launch more often than you'd believe. One checkbox can keep an entire business out of Google.
2. **Settings, then Permalinks:** choose "Post name," so addresses read `/kitchen-remodeling/` instead of `/?p=123`. On an established site, change this only with redirects in place.
3. **Settings, then General:** set a real Site Title and a tagline that says what you do. Many themes print them on every page.
4. **HTTPS:** both addresses in General settings should start with `https://`. Your host can install a free certificate.
5. **Users:** give every author a real display name and a short bio. Pages signed by an actual person are easier to trust.

## The plugins I recommend

These are my personal picks after years of building and fixing WordPress sites. Install one SEO plugin only; two will fight over your titles and sitemaps.
- **[Yoast SEO Premium](https://yoast.com/wordpress/plugins/seo/).** The free version handles titles, meta descriptions, XML sitemaps, schema, and archive settings well. Premium adds a redirect manager, so changed or deleted pages never strand a visitor, and internal linking suggestions that help you connect related posts as you write. It pays for itself the first time you rename a page.
- **[WPCode](https://wpcode.com/), and WPCode Pro for schema.** The safe way to add snippets: a verification tag, a tracking code, a small PHP tweak. It keeps them in one place, survives theme changes, and spares you from editing `functions.php`, where one typo can take the site down. I use the paid Pro version for structured data: it lets me add bespoke schema to any individual page or post, so a service page, an event, or a case study can each carry markup written for exactly what that page says. Keep it consistent with what Yoast already outputs, and test every page in Google's [Rich Results Test](https://search.google.com/test/rich-results).
- **[Site Kit by Google](https://sitekit.withgoogle.com/).** Google's own plugin connects Search Console, Analytics, and PageSpeed Insights to your dashboard and verifies site ownership for you. It hardwires your site into Google's tools in a few clicks, and puts the numbers where you'll actually see them.

## Archive pages: keep the duplicates out of search

WordPress automatically makes extra pages that list your posts by tag, category, date, and author. On most small sites those pages repeat content that already lives on the posts themselves. In Yoast's settings I set tag archives, date archives, and author archives on single-author sites to stay out of search results, and leave categories indexed only when each one has a real introduction of its own. Media attachment pages, which give every uploaded image its own thin page, have been off by default for new sites since WordPress 6.4; on older sites, Yoast can redirect them to the image itself.

## Writing a post that ranks
- **The post title is your H1.** Use Heading 2 and Heading 3 blocks for sections, in order. Never pick a heading level for its size.
- **Fill in the SEO title and meta description** in the Yoast box under every post: a unique title around 50 to 60 characters and a description around 150.
- **Edit the slug** to a short, readable phrase before you publish.
- **Answer the question early,** in plain words, and add what only you know: prices, photos of your work, your process, your results.

## Alt text in the media library

Every image block and every media library item has an "Alternative text" field. Describe what the image shows in a short sentence, including any words visible in it. Leave out "image of," because screen readers already say that. Leave the field empty only for purely decorative images, so screen readers skip them. Fill it in once in the media library and WordPress reuses it wherever you insert that image.

## Kill "read more" for good

Many themes end every excerpt with a "Read more" or "Continue reading" link. On a blog page with twenty posts that's twenty identical links, each one telling crawlers and screen reader users nothing about where it goes. Link the post title instead, or change the theme's excerpt link to include the post's name. In your own writing, put links on words that describe the destination: "my [guide to accessible websites](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/accessible-websites/)," never "click here." Link new posts to your older related posts, and older posts forward to new ones; this is the internal linking that helps both readers and crawlers find your best pages.

## Put Cloudflare in front of WordPress

After the plugins, my strongest advice is to move the domain's DNS to [Cloudflare](https://www.cloudflare.com/) and route the site through it. Even the free plan speeds up WordPress, manages certificates, and fends off attacks, and the paid features are worth their price on most WordPress sites. My [guide to Cloudflare for WordPress](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/cloudflare-wordpress/) walks through the setup, the plan I'd choose, and the budget.

## Tell the search engines
1. Verify the site in [Google Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console/about) (Site Kit can do it for you) and submit the sitemap Yoast creates at `/sitemap_index.xml`.
2. In [Bing Webmaster Tools](https://www.bing.com/webmasters/), use the import from Google Search Console option. It copies every verified site and sitemap across in a few clicks.
3. Make sure IndexNow is on. Yoast SEO Premium includes it and pings Bing and the other participating engines every time you publish or update a post.
4. Check both consoles every few weeks for sitemap errors and pages that aren't indexed.

## Speed
- **Hosting matters most.** A good managed WordPress host beats any plugin on cheap shared hosting.
- **Use fewer plugins.** Each one can add scripts to every page. Remove what you don't use.
- **Upload sensible images.** WordPress already creates smaller sizes and lazy loads images below the fold, but a 6 MB photo straight from a phone still slows the first view. Resize before uploading, or use an image optimization plugin.
- **Add caching** if your host doesn't provide it, and test in PageSpeed Insights. My [Core Web Vitals guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/core-web-vitals/) covers what the scores mean.

## Accessibility

Choose a theme tagged "accessibility ready" in the WordPress theme directory; those themes have passed a review for keyboard navigation, contrast, and structure. Then keep your content accessible with real headings, alt text, descriptive links, and captions on video. Accessibility and SEO reward the same work; see [the SEO dividends of accessibility](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/accessibility-seo-dividends/).

## Updates and spam

Keep WordPress, your theme, and your plugins updated; hacked sites get spam pages injected and drop out of search fast. Turn off comments if you don't moderate them. And treat any offer of cheap backlinks, guaranteed rankings, or "AI content at scale" as the spam it is.

## Further reading
- [WordPress: the Reading settings screen](https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/settings-reading-screen/) and [the Permalinks screen](https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/settings-permalinks-screen/)
- [WordPress's built-in XML sitemaps](https://make.wordpress.org/core/2020/07/22/new-xml-sitemaps-functionality-in-wordpress-5-5/) and [the attachment page change in 6.4](https://make.wordpress.org/core/2023/10/16/changes-to-attachment-pages/)
- [WordPress performance optimization](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/performance/optimization/)
- [Accessibility ready themes](https://wordpress.org/themes/tags/accessibility-ready/) and the [WordPress accessibility handbook](https://make.wordpress.org/accessibility/handbook/)
- [Yoast help center](https://yoast.com/help/), [WPCode on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/insert-headers-and-footers/), and [Site Kit on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/google-site-kit/)
- [Google's SEO Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide) and [Google's link best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/links-crawlable)
- [Google's image SEO best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) and [WebAIM on alt text](https://webaim.org/techniques/alttext/)
- [Google Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console/about) and [PageSpeed Insights](https://pagespeed.web.dev/)

# Cloudflare for WordPress: setup, plans, and what to budget

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 9, 2026

If I could make one change to most of the WordPress sites I'm asked to look at, it would be putting them behind Cloudflare. It makes them faster, safer, and cheaper to run, and the free plan alone covers a lot of ground. My own experience and every AI assistant I've put the question to agree. For the record, Cloudflare pays me nothing for saying so, which, given how often I say it, is a little sad.

## Two ways to use Cloudflare

Every DNS record in Cloudflare shows a cloud. A gray cloud means DNS only: Cloudflare tells browsers where your server is, then steps aside. An orange cloud means proxied: visitors reach Cloudflare's network first, and it serves what it can from the data center nearest them before passing the rest to your host. The speed and protection only apply to orange records.
- **Gray, DNS only:** if Cloudflare just registers the domain and answers DNS, the free plan is all you need.
- **Orange, proxied:** this is where WordPress gains the most, and where the paid features become worth considering.

## What the free plan does once you're proxied
- Caches your images, scripts, and stylesheets close to visitors. HTML pages aren't cached by default; that takes APO or a cache rule, below.
- Compresses files on the way out.
- Provides HTTPS certificates at no cost.
- Absorbs denial of service attacks before they reach your host.
- Tells Bing and other engines that support IndexNow when your content changes, through a free feature called Crawler Hints.

## The paid features that matter for WordPress
- **Automatic Platform Optimization (APO):** caches whole WordPress pages at Cloudflare's edge, so even the first byte arrives fast from anywhere. It works with the official Cloudflare WordPress plugin, comes included with the Pro plan and above, and costs $5 a month on the free plan.
- **Polish:** compresses images and can convert them to WebP automatically. Available on Pro and above.

Even though Cloudflare can cost nothing, when a WordPress site runs through it I recommend budgeting about $50 a month for Cloudflare's paid services, starting with Pro. WordPress almost always benefits. I pay for Pro on my own main site.

## Setting it up
1. **Add the site** in a free Cloudflare account. Cloudflare scans your existing DNS records; compare them against your current DNS provider line by line, especially mail records, before going further.
2. **Change the nameservers** at your registrar to the two Cloudflare gives you. Or transfer the domain to Cloudflare Registrar, which charges the registry's wholesale price with no markup on renewals.
3. **Turn the website records orange.** Leave mail records gray.
4. **Set SSL/TLS to Full (strict)**, which requires a valid certificate on your host; most hosts provide one free. Flexible mode can trap WordPress in an endless redirect loop.
5. **Switch on Always Use HTTPS,** then HSTS once every page loads securely.
6. **Install the official Cloudflare WordPress plugin,** connect it, and turn on APO if you have it, so your cache clears automatically when you publish or edit.
7. **Check the bot and AI crawler settings.** Make sure search engines and the AI crawlers you want, such as the ones behind ChatGPT search and Perplexity, aren't blocked. I let them in; being cited by AI assistants is part of being found.
8. **Turn on Crawler Hints** under Caching.
9. **Test** your home page and a post in PageSpeed Insights before and after.

## What to leave alone
- **Rocket Loader** rewrites how scripts load. It can speed up a simple site and break a complex one, including forms, analytics, and cookie banners. If anything acts strangely, turn it off first.
- **Caching the admin.** Never cache `/wp-admin/`, the login page, carts, checkouts, or account pages. APO is built to skip logged-in visitors and the admin; any cache rule you write by hand has to exclude them too.
- **Under Attack Mode** challenges every visitor, search engine crawlers included. Use it during an actual attack only.

## When Cloudflare isn't the right layer

If a site runs on a hosted builder such as Shopify, Squarespace, or Wix, the builder already provides a CDN and certificates. Cloudflare can still hold the domain and answer DNS, but keep those records gray and follow the builder's own connection instructions. Some managed WordPress hosts also bundle Cloudflare or their own CDN; ask before stacking two.

For the rest of the WordPress basics, see [WordPress SEO 101](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/wordpress-seo-101/), and for what the speed scores mean, my [Core Web Vitals guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/core-web-vitals/). Want Cloudflare set up on your site without the guesswork? [Tell me about it](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Will Google penalize AI-written content? What Google actually says

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 9, 2026

Almost every client asks me some version of this: if I use ChatGPT or Claude to help write my pages, will Google punish me? The short answer is no, Google doesn't punish content for being written with AI. It punishes content for being unhelpful, inaccurate, deceptive, or mass-produced to game rankings, and AI makes all four of those very easy. Here is what Google has said, in its own words, and how to use AI without risk.

## What Google said in 2023, and still says

When ChatGPT arrived, Google published its position plainly: appropriate use of AI or automation is not against its guidelines. It defined inappropriate use just as plainly: generating content primarily to manipulate search rankings, which violates its spam policies. Google's ranking systems look for helpful, reliable content, and they don't care whether a person, a tool, or both typed the words.

## What changed on October 1, 2026

Google rewrote its page on using generative AI content, and it now says: "It is critical to manually factcheck and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing." The same review applies to the parts of a page people forget about: title tags, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text, all of which can appear in search results. If an AI tool wrote your metadata, a person should check it.

The page also suggests telling readers how content was created, in a way that makes sense for your audience. Sellers using Google Merchant Center have firmer rules: AI-generated product images need embedded metadata saying so, and AI-generated product titles and descriptions must be labeled.

## Fake authors are now named as deception

Google's guide to people-first content encourages accurate bylines and warns against "deceptive authorship information." Its examples are exactly what some AI content shops sell: AI-generated headshots, made-up names, and false credentials meant to make a page look written by human experts. Google calls any form of deception a reason to treat a page as untrustworthy. If a real person reviewed the work, put that real person's name on it.

## Where AI content really gets sites in trouble

The risk is scale without value. Google's scaled content abuse policy covers producing many pages mainly to rank, whether people, AI, or both made them, and it was the focus of reporting on Google's 2026 spam updates. The pattern that gets hit looks like this:
- Hundreds or thousands of pages published quickly, often one per keyword or city.
- Text that summarizes what's already ranking and adds nothing new.
- No named author, no first-hand detail, and no review before publishing.
- Factual errors nobody caught, because nobody read it.

## What the data shows

In July 2026, Ahrefs examined pages ranking in Google and estimated how much of each was written by AI. In the top three positions, about 5 percent of pages appeared to be entirely AI-generated and roughly 9 percent at least 80 percent AI. Its conclusion was in the title: Google doesn't punish AI content; it punishes bad content. Two cautions: AI detectors produce probabilities, never proof, and the study shows correlation rather than cause. Still, AI-assisted pages clearly can and do rank at the very top.

## A safe way to use AI for your site
1. **Use AI where it's strong:** research, outlines, first drafts, summaries of your own notes, and variations to choose from.
2. **Add what only you have:** your prices, process, photos, customer stories, mistakes, and opinions. This is the part search engines and AI assistants can't find anywhere else.
3. **Fact check every claim,** every number, every quote, and every link before publishing. Treat the draft as a confident intern's work.
4. **Review the metadata too:** titles, descriptions, structured data, and alt text.
5. **Put a real name on it,** the person who knows the subject and stands behind the page.
6. **Publish at a human pace.** Ten excellent pages beat a thousand thin ones.
7. **Be open about your process** where readers would want to know.

## About AI detectors

Clients sometimes run their pages through an AI detector and panic at the score. Don't. Detectors guess, they disagree with each other, and they flag plenty of human writing. Google's question is whether a page helps the person who searched, and no detector measures that.

## How I work

I use AI tools every day, for research, drafts, and checking my own work. Every guide on this site is drafted with AI assistance under my direction, checked claim by claim against named sources, and published with those sources listed at the bottom. That is the standard I'd hold any client's site to. For the broader picture of this year's updates, see [my 2026 update recovery checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/update-recovery-2026/); if you're worried about pages you've already published, [send me the site](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) and I'll tell you which ones need a human pass.

# Is a Screaming Frog licence worth $279 a year? Mine was

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 11, 2026

For years I was too cheap to pay for the Screaming Frog SEO Spider. I ran the free version, slurped up 500 URLs at a time, and got a tip of the iceberg view of what was going on with a site. I wasn't using a ten thousandth of what the tool can do. This year I finally bought a licence. Paying $279 stung. It also leveled me up more than any tool purchase I've made, and I should have done it a decade ago. It's legit my secret weapon now. Don't make my mistake. Here is what the free version leaves out and everything the paid version can do.

## What it costs, as of October 2026

The SEO Spider is a desktop program for Windows, macOS, and Linux. The free version needs no sign up. A licence costs $279 (£199) per user per year, and Screaming Frog discounts bulk purchases:
| Licences bought at once | Price per licence, per year |
| --- | --- |
| 1 to 4 | $279 |
| 5 to 9 | $265 |
| 10 to 19 | $249 |
| 20 or more | $235 |

Licences are per person, so two people need two licences, and each one lasts a year before it needs renewing. There's no per page or per project metering: the only ceiling on crawl size is your computer's memory and storage.

## What the free version gives you

The free version is genuinely useful, which is exactly how it kept me from paying. It crawls up to 500 URLs and will:
- Find broken links, server errors, and redirects.
- Check page titles and meta descriptions.
- Show meta robots and other directives.
- Audit hreflang attributes.
- Find exact duplicate pages.
- Generate XML sitemaps.
- Draw site visualisations.

For a ten page brochure site, that's plenty. For anything bigger, 500 URLs runs out fast, because every image, script, and stylesheet the crawler finds can count toward the limit, and you can't change the crawl settings to leave them out.

## My defense: the Rumsfeld

When anyone asks why I waited so long, I plead the Rumsfeld:

>

"There are known knowns; there are things we know we know. We also know there are known unknowns; that is to say we know there are some things we do not know. But there are also unknown unknowns, the ones we don't know we don't know."

Donald Rumsfeld, U.S. Secretary of Defense, Pentagon news briefing, February 12, 2002

That was me and the free version. The 500 URL cap was a known unknown: I knew there were pages past it I wasn't seeing. Everything in the next section was an unknown unknown. I never saw most of it, so I never missed it, and I never knew what it would have caught. You can't price a tool by the features you've never seen.

And when I couldn't plead ignorance, I pleaded his other famous line, from a town hall with troops in Kuwait on December 8, 2004:

>

"As you know, you go to war with the Army you have. They're not the Army you might want or wish to have at a later time."

Donald Rumsfeld, U.S. Secretary of Defense, town hall meeting, Camp Buehring, Kuwait, December 8, 2004

The free version was the army I had, and I made do with it. Five hundred URLs at a time, I patched together a picture of each site from slices. The difference is that I never had to wait for anyone's production line. The army I wanted was one $279 purchase away the entire time.

## What the licence unlocks

Here is the part I spent years ignoring. According to Screaming Frog's own comparison, everything below is paid only.

### Crawl the whole site, your way
- **No 500 URL limit.** Crawl sites with hundreds of thousands of pages; the tool can store crawl data on disk instead of in memory.
- **Full crawl configuration.** Include or exclude sections, set speed, change the user agent to Googlebot, Bingbot, or an AI crawler, and decide which resources to check.
- **Save and reopen crawls.** In the free version, closing the window throws the crawl away.
- **Forms based login.** Crawl staging sites and member areas that sit behind a login page.
- **Custom robots.txt.** Download, edit, and test a site's robots.txt rules against the crawl before you change the live file.

### See what Google sees on JavaScript sites

The licence turns on rendering with built-in headless Chromium, so the crawler runs the JavaScript on React, Angular, and Vue sites and reads the finished page. Crawl the same pages with rendering off and then on, compare word counts by template, and content that only exists after scripts run stands out immediately. Rendered screenshots and stored rendered HTML let you see exactly what the crawler saw.

### Catch the problems that cost rankings
- **Near-duplicate content.** Beyond exact copies, it finds near duplicates and semantically similar pages using algorithmic checks and vector embeddings.
- **Structured data validation.** Extracts schema markup and checks it against Schema.org and Google's rich result features.
- **Accessibility auditing.** Runs the open-source axe rules against WCAG on every page.
- **Spelling and grammar** checks in more than 25 languages.
- **Mobile usability** checks using Lighthouse.
- **AMP crawling and validation** with the official AMP validator.
- **Uncrawlable links.** Since version 24.0, a filter shows pages whose internal links don't follow Google's link best practices, such as a link that only works through an onclick handler.

### Pull any data off any page
- **Custom search** looks for anything in the source code: a missing analytics tag, an old phone number, a retired product name.
- **Custom extraction** scrapes any element with XPath, CSS selectors, or regex: prices, SKUs, authors, publish dates, stock notices.
- **Custom JavaScript** runs your own snippets during the crawl, so you can scroll pages, trigger events, or extract nearly anything you could in the Chrome console.

### Layer real data on top of the crawl
- **Google Search Console:** clicks, impressions, and index status in bulk through the URL Inspection API.
- **Google Analytics:** users and conversions for every crawled URL.
- **PageSpeed Insights:** Lighthouse scores, diagnostics, and Chrome UX Report field data for every page at once.
- **Link metrics:** Ahrefs, Majestic, and Moz data next to each URL, useful for content audits and deciding which pages deserve redirects.

Put those side by side and the crawl answers the question that matters: which pages earn traffic and have a technical problem? Fix those first.

### Use AI inside the crawl

The licence connects the crawler to OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, and Ollama, so you can run your own prompt against every page as it's crawled: draft missing meta descriptions, write alt text, classify page intent, or flag thin content. Any AI-written metadata still needs a person to check it before it goes live.

Version 24.0, released May 19, 2026, also added an MCP server, so you can run crawls and analyze, export, and reshape the data from inside AI assistants such as Claude, in plain English. Screaming Frog says plainly that it isn't a replacement for an experienced SEO, and not every feature is available through it yet.

### Put audits on autopilot
- **Scheduling:** crawls run on their own at set intervals and export to a folder or Google Sheets.
- **Command line:** run the whole thing from a script on a server.
- **Crawl comparison:** see what changed between two crawls, and map staging URLs to production URLs to check a redesign before launch. Since version 24.0, scheduled crawls can compare the last two crawls automatically.
- **Email alerts:** get a summary of issues when a crawl finishes, including what changed, and send a chosen export (say, weekly broken links) straight to a developer.
- **Data Studio crawl reports** for site health dashboards over time.
- **Segmentation** to report on sections of a site, such as products versus articles, separately.

### Support from the people who build it

Licence holders get free technical support. Free users don't.

## Who should buy a licence
- **Buy it** if you do SEO for a living, look after any site over a few hundred pages, run a JavaScript framework, or are planning a migration or redesign.
- **Skip it, for now,** if you own one small site that stays under 500 URLs and you only need to find broken links once in a while.

Screaming Frog is a technical crawler. It doesn't track rankings or research keywords and competitors, so it complements a keyword tool rather than replacing one.

## What I'd tell my younger self

The math is embarrassing in hindsight. $279 a year is about 76 cents a day. One recovered redirect, one page that was quietly invisible to Google, or one launch that didn't break pays for years of licences. I spent a decade reading the first 500 URLs of every site and guessing at the rest, when the whole iceberg was right there the whole time.

If you want to see what a properly configured crawl turns up on your own site, [that's where my audits start](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/). For what the finished audit should look like, see [what a technical SEO audit should give you](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-audit-deliverables/).

# Why your SEO should work in your Git repository, with AI at their side

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 11, 2026 · Updated October 15, 2026

Most SEO stops at the admin screen: plugin settings, a crawler export, a spreadsheet of recommendations. Your website doesn't live in the admin screen. If it was built by developers, it lives in a code repository, and that's where its search problems are caused and where they get fixed. An SEO who can work in the repository, with an AI coding assistant doing the heavy reading, fixes causes instead of reporting symptoms. That's how I work, and here is what it means for you.

## What a repository is, in plain English

A repository is the master copy of your site's code, with its entire history. Almost every team now keeps it in Git, the version control system Linus Torvalds and the Linux community created in 2005, usually hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Older systems such as CVS and Subversion did the same job before Git took over.

The history is the point. Every change is recorded with who made it, when, and why. Changes are proposed as pull requests that someone reviews before they go live, and any change can be rolled back. That's exactly the discipline SEO changes have usually lacked.

## Plugins and crawlers report. The code is where it's fixed.

Yoast is a fine plugin and Screaming Frog is the best crawler I own. Both tell you what's wrong on the pages they can see. Neither can tell you why a template produces the problem, and neither can change the template. On a site built with Next.js, Nuxt, Astro, Shopify themes, or a headless CMS, there may be no SEO plugin at all. The titles, canonicals, structured data, redirects, robots rules, and sitemaps are all code.

When the SEO can read that code, the work changes:
- **One fix instead of a thousand.** A duplicate title on 3,000 product pages is one line in one template.
- **Redirects where they belong:** in the framework's configuration or the host's rules file, tested before launch.
- **Structured data built into components,** so every new page gets it automatically.
- **JavaScript problems traced to the line.** When content only appears after a scroll or a click, the cause is in a component, and that's where to look.
- **No lost work.** Every SEO change has a commit, a reviewer, and a way back.

## What AI coding assistants add

A medium sized site can have thousands of files. Reading them used to be the developer's job alone. Now AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot can read an entire codebase, explain how it's organized, trace a problem to the files that cause it, and draft the change. GitHub describes Copilot planning changes, editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests. Claude Code works the same way from a terminal.

That puts an SEO who knows what to look for within reach of answers that used to take a developer a week. Two examples from my own client work:
- During [a clinic's move from WordPress to Next.js](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/), a read-only analysis of the repository with an AI coding assistant found thousands of image references still pointing at the old media library and traced them to a handful of central files. The developer got a short, concrete plan.
- For [a local business on Sanity, Vercel, and GitHub](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/headless-local/), I made the metadata changes myself in a pull request the developer reviewed and merged.

The assistant is fast, tireless, and sometimes confidently wrong. The skill is knowing what search engines need, asking the right questions of the code, and checking every answer. AI doesn't replace that judgment; it multiplies it.

## How I work in a client's repository

I work primarily with Codex and Claude Code, and also use Copilot. The repository, the written brief, and the checks carry the work between assistants, so the process does not depend on a single AI provider.
1. **Read-only first.** I start with read access, map the templates and routes, and compare the code to what crawlers actually see.
2. **Findings tied to files.** Every issue comes with the file and line that cause it, so your developer can act without guessing.
3. **Small pull requests.** When you want me to make changes, each one is a separate branch with a clear description, reviewed by your developer before it merges.
4. **Nothing reaches production without your approval,** and no passwords or API keys go into the code or into an AI tool.
5. **Verified on the live site** after deploy, with a crawl and Search Console.

## Questions to ask any SEO you're about to hire
- Can you read the site's templates, or only the pages they produce?
- Will you hand the developer findings tied to specific files?
- Can you open a pull request, and will you follow the team's review process?
- How do you use AI tools on the code, and how do you check what they produce?
- What access do you need, and what will you never touch?

For the broader hiring checklist, see [how to hire an SEO on Upwork](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/hiring-an-seo/).

## Work with me

I've built websites since 1994 and practiced SEO since 1998, and today I work the way modern sites are built: in the repository, through pull requests, with AI coding assistants doing the heavy reading under my direction. If your site lives in GitHub and your SEO lives in a spreadsheet, [send me the site](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) or see my [sitewide technical SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/sitewide-technical-seo/), [JavaScript SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/), and [technical audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/) services. I'll tell you what the code is doing to your search visibility and how to fix it.

# How to find near-duplicate pages and multiple H1s across a whole site

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

Two findings turn up in almost every full crawl I run: clusters of pages that say nearly the same thing, and headings that don't describe the page. Neither can be judged one URL at a time. Here is how I find both across every page, and how I decide what to do about each.

## Crawl the rendered page, not only the source

Set Screaming Frog to JavaScript rendering under Configuration > Spider > Rendering before you start. On sites built with React, Next.js, or a page builder, the H1 a browser shows can differ from the one in the raw HTML. A component may replace it after load, or a script may inject a second one. If you crawl only the source, you're auditing a page nobody sees.

## Turn on near-duplicate detection

Screaming Frog finds exact duplicates by default. Near duplicates need switching on, under Configuration > Content > Duplicates, which tells the crawler to store each page's text. The default similarity threshold is 90%, and you can lower it to cast a wider net. By default it compares only indexable pages, which is usually what you want.

Before crawling, open Configuration > Content > Area and exclude the navigation, header, and footer elements. Otherwise every page shares hundreds of words of menu text, and pages that differ in their main content can still score as near twins. You can adjust the content area and threshold after a crawl without crawling again.

One step trips people up: the Near Duplicates filter stays empty until you run Crawl Analysis at the end of the crawl. The overview pane marks the filters that are waiting on it. Once the analysis finishes, the Content tab lists each page's closest similarity match and how many near duplicates it has, and the Duplicate Details tab shows the matching text and highlights where the pages differ.

## Count headings with custom extraction

The crawler's H1 columns show you the heading text page by page. A custom extraction gives you a number you can sort by. Under Configuration > Custom > Custom Extraction, add an XPath rule in Function Value mode with `count(//h1)`. Every URL gets a column with its H1 count. Add `count(//h2)` alongside it if you want to see which templates skip a level. Group the results by URL pattern and the template behind each problem usually becomes obvious.

## What multiple H1s actually cost you

Less than most audit tools suggest. Google's SEO Starter Guide says headings in semantic order are fantastic for screen readers, and that from Google Search's perspective it doesn't matter if they're out of order. There is no ranking penalty for two H1s. The W3C's accessibility tutorial explains why order still matters: people using screen readers move through a page by its headings, so the ranks should describe how the page is organized.

So I treat headings as a clarity and accessibility problem. The cases worth fixing are:
- **No H1 at all,** often because a theme styles the page title as a div.
- **The logo wrapped in an H1** on every page, so the site name is the main heading of every URL.
- **An H1 split across styled elements,** such as two spans with no space between them, so extracted text reads "BestPrices" instead of "Best Prices."
- **The same H1 sitewide,** usually from a layout that hard codes it.

Each of these is one template fix. That's the payoff of finding them by count rather than by spot checking.

## Where near duplicates come from

When I group near-duplicate clusters by URL pattern, the same handful of causes come up again and again:
- **City swap location pages,** where the only difference is the town name.
- **Tag and category archives** that list the same posts under different labels.
- **Parameter URLs** for sorting, filtering, or tracking that serve the same content.
- **Printer friendly versions** of articles and recipes.
- **Quiz or calculator variants** that share an explanation and change a few inputs.

## Decide, cluster by cluster

Every cluster gets one of three decisions:
1. **Differentiate.** If each page has a real reason to exist, such as location pages for offices that actually differ, rewrite them so each carries information the others don't: staff, services, directions, local proof.
2. **Merge and 301.** If the pages serve the same purpose, keep the strongest, fold in anything useful from the rest, and permanently redirect the others to it. Google's documentation calls a redirect a strong signal, and recommends redirects when you want to get rid of duplicate pages.
3. **Canonicalize.** If the duplicates have to stay reachable, as parameter and printer versions usually do, point them at the main version with rel="canonical." Google treats that as a strong signal too.

Noindex is rarely the right tool here. Google specifically advises against using noindex to steer canonical selection within a site, since it removes the page from Search entirely. I reserve it for pages that should never appear in results at all.

## Check the fix with a second crawl

After the changes ship, crawl again with the same settings and compare the two crawls. The clusters you merged should now show redirects, the canonicalized URLs should point where you meant, and the H1 count column should read 1 across the templates you fixed. Then give Google a few weeks and check the Page indexing report in Search Console for duplicates it has resolved.

If heading and title patterns are the main issue, see [on-page SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/on-page-seo/). Unfamiliar terms are in the [glossary](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/).

# Screaming Frog custom extraction recipes for sitewide SEO audits

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

The standard Screaming Frog tabs answer the standard questions. Custom extraction answers yours. With a few lines of XPath or regex, every URL in a crawl gets a new column holding exactly the fact you need, and a question like "which templates are missing a canonical?" becomes a sort and a filter. These are the extractors I load into almost every audit.

## Setting it up

Custom extraction needs a paid licence. Open Configuration > Custom > Custom Extraction and click Add. Each extractor gets a name, which becomes its column heading, a type, and an expression. You can run up to 100 extractors in one crawl.

There are three types:
- **XPath,** which selects elements and attributes from the HTML. Most of my recipes use it.
- **CSSPath,** the same idea using CSS selectors, often the quickest to write.
- **Regex,** for anything that isn't an HTML element, such as JSON inside a script tag or an ID in inline JavaScript.

For XPath and CSSPath you then choose what to return: the whole element, its inner HTML, its text, or, with Function Value, the result of a function such as a count. If you'd rather not write expressions at all, the visual extraction browser lets you click an element on a sample page and suggests the expression for you.

One setting matters more than any recipe. Screaming Frog extracts from the raw HTML unless JavaScript rendering is on, in which case it reads the rendered page. On a React or Next.js site, run the same extractors in both modes and compare. Any column that fills in only after rendering is content that depends on JavaScript to exist.

## Heading recipes
- **H1 count** (XPath, Function Value): `count(//h1)`. Sort descending to find templates with two or more, ascending to find pages with none.
- **All H1 text** (XPath, Extract Text): `//h1`. Shows when a logo or a hidden mobile heading is the H1.
- **H2 count** (XPath, Function Value): `count(//h2)`. A zero on a long page usually means the template styles its subheads as plain text.

## Indexing and canonical recipes
- **Canonical count** (XPath, Function Value): `count(//link[@rel='canonical'])`. More than one canonical tag on a page is a conflict worth fixing at once.
- **Canonical target** (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): `//link[@rel='canonical']/@href`. Screaming Frog reports canonicals already; I extract it anyway when I need it beside other custom columns in one export.
- **Robots meta** (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): `//meta[@name='robots']/@content`. Catches noindex left behind from a staging site.
- **Hreflang values** (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): `//link[@rel='alternate'][@hreflang]/@hreflang`. A quick check that every language version lists the same set.

## Structured data recipes

JSON-LD lives inside a script tag as JSON, so element selectors can't reach the fields inside it. Screaming Frog's own guidance is to use regex for any JSON in the code.
- **JSON-LD block count** (XPath, Function Value): `count(//script[@type='application/ld+json'])`. Zero on a template that should carry schema is the first thing to fix.
- **Schema types** (Regex): `"@type"\s*:\s*"(.*?)"`. Lists every type declared on the page, so you can see which templates emit Product, Article, or nothing at all.
- **The whole block** (Regex): `<script type="application/ld\+json">(.*?)</script>`. Useful for exporting and validating a sample per template.

## Content and authorship recipes
- **Published date** (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): `//meta[@property='article:published_time']/@content`. Finds articles with no machine readable date.
- **Author meta** (XPath, Extract Inner HTML): `//meta[@name='author']/@content`. Many themes leave this blank or set it to the site name.
- **Images with no alt attribute** (XPath, Function Value): `count(//img[not(@alt)])`. Counts per page, so you can see which template is the repeat offender.
- **Links inside the main content** (XPath, Function Value): `count(//main//a)`. Separates contextual internal links from the menu and footer, assuming the template uses a main element.

## Tracking recipes
- **Google Tag Manager container** (Regex): `["'](GTM-.*?)["']`. Shows pages with no container, or two different ones.
- **GA4 measurement ID** (Regex): `["'](G-[A-Z0-9]+)["']`. Same idea for sites that load GA4 directly.

## Reading the results

A column of numbers is only useful once it's grouped. Export the crawl, add a column for the URL pattern or template, and pivot. When every product page reports two H1s and every blog post reports one, the cause is in the product template, and one change fixes thousands of URLs. That is the habit that turns a crawl from a list of warnings into a short list of causes.

Check a few rows by hand before you trust a recipe. View the source of one page, confirm the extracted value matches, and adjust the expression if a theme uses different markup from the one you expected.

## Where this fits

Custom extraction is how I make a full crawl answer the specific questions in a [sitewide technical SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/sitewide-technical-seo/) engagement. For the licence question itself, read [whether a Screaming Frog licence is worth it](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/screaming-frog-licence/), and for two problems these recipes surface constantly, see [finding near duplicates and multiple H1s](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/near-duplicates-and-h1s/).

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# How to prove an SEO fix actually worked

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

"Done" is the most dangerous word in SEO. A developer marks the ticket closed, the CMS shows the new titles, and three months later a crawl finds the old ones still live on half the site. A cache never cleared, a second template was missed, or the change only applied to new pages. I don't call a fix finished until two crawls and Search Console agree that it is. Here is the routine.

## Step 1: crawl before you change anything

The baseline is the step people skip, and without it there's nothing to compare. Before any fix ships, crawl the site with the settings you'll use afterward: the same start URL, the same rendering mode, the same exclusions, the same custom extractors. Save it.

In Screaming Frog, comparison needs a licence and database storage mode, which you switch on under File > Settings > Storage Mode. Database storage saves every crawl automatically and lists it under File > Crawls, and it copes with large sites far better than memory storage. Crawls saved in the old file format can be imported and converted.

## Step 2: crawl again after the release

Once the fix is live and caches have cleared, crawl again with identical settings. Then switch to Mode > Compare, pick the two crawls, and run the comparison. The newer crawl becomes Current and the older one Previous.

## Step 3: read the four change columns

For every tab and filter, the comparison sorts URLs into four groups, and the difference between them is the whole point:
- **Added:** URLs present in both crawls that have moved into this filter. If the filter is an error, these are new problems on existing pages.
- **Removed:** URLs present in both crawls that have left this filter. For an error filter, these are your fixes.
- **New:** URLs found only in the current crawl.
- **Missing:** URLs found only in the previous crawl.

If you fixed duplicate titles on 600 product pages, you want to see roughly 600 in Removed under Page Titles > Duplicate, and close to zero in Added. A large New count after a fix that wasn't supposed to create pages tells you something else changed, often a parameter or a pagination pattern now exposed to crawlers.

## Step 4: turn on change detection

Filters only notice changes that move a URL between filters. A title rewritten from one acceptable wording to another triggers nothing. For that, open Config > Compare before you run the comparison and select the elements you changed: page titles, meta descriptions, H1s, word count, crawl depth, internal links, structured data, or content. A Change Detection tab then lists every URL where those elements differ between the crawls.

This is how I answer the question every client eventually asks: did the new titles actually go live everywhere? The tab gives a URL by URL answer, and the pages that didn't change are the ones to chase.

## Step 5: check structure and internal links

The Site Structure tab in a comparison shows the directory tree with URLs added and removed, and how crawl depth shifted. The lower window's inlinks view can filter to links added or removed. When a menu change quietly pushes a section of pages one click deeper, this is where it shows up, along with the exact links that went away.

## Comparing staging with live

Before a migration or a redesign launches, URL Mapping under Config > Compare lets you compare crawls whose URLs differ. A regex maps the previous crawl's URLs onto the current crawl's, so a staging hostname can be compared page for page with the live site. Run it before launch and you'll catch missing titles, dropped schema, and lost internal links while they're still cheap to fix.

## Step 6: confirm with Google

A clean crawl proves what your site serves. Search Console shows what Google has noticed.
- **URL Inspection** on a handful of representative URLs. The live test shows whether Google can index the page as it stands now, and the indexed result shows the version Google currently holds, including its chosen canonical.
- **Validate fix** in the Page indexing report, once every instance of an issue is fixed. Google rechecks the affected URLs and emails you when the fix is confirmed or when it finds one still broken, which stops the validation. Google says this typically takes up to about two weeks and sometimes longer.
- **A smaller sitemap** for speed. Google suggests submitting a sitemap of your most important affected pages and filtering the report to it before validating, since a smaller set can finish sooner.

## Write it down

A verification note after each release can be short: the two crawl dates, the counts in Removed and Added for each targeted issue, a list of any URLs that didn't change and why, and the Search Console validation status with its date. It turns "fixed" into a record anyone can check, and it catches the missed template before Google does.

Verification is built into my [sitewide technical SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/sitewide-technical-seo/) work and every [site migration](https://christopherabraham.com/services/migrations/). The extractors I use for before-and-after comparisons are in [Screaming Frog custom extraction recipes](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/custom-extraction/).

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# How to measure your share of voice in AI answers

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

Share of voice in AI answers is the share of relevant questions where an assistant names you, measured against the competitors it names instead. You get a number you can track by asking the same set of buyer questions every month, with web search turned on, and recording four things from every answer: who it names, where you rank among them, the tone toward you, and the sources it cites. I run this on my own name, and the first run told me more than a year of guessing would have.

## Why a fixed question set beats screenshots

AI answers change from run to run. Ask ChatGPT the same question twice and the list of names shifts. A screenshot someone sends you on a Tuesday proves only that the answer looked that way once. A fixed set of questions, asked on the same schedule with the same settings, turns that noise into a trend: one run is a reading, and three monthly runs show a direction.

The set stays stable from month to month. New questions go on the end so earlier months still compare. Change the wording of an old question and you have started a new series.

## Build the question set from three kinds of question

I split every set into three groups, because they measure different things and a single blended number hides the gap that matters.
- **Branded questions** name you: "Who is this company?" "Is this consultant any good?" They test whether assistants know you and describe you correctly.
- **Open questions** are the ones buyers ask before they have a name: "Who should I hire to fix my JavaScript indexing?" "Recommend an agency for a B2B AI search program." These measure whether you are in the consideration set at all.
- **How-to questions** ask for an answer your content provides: "How do I fix Crawled, currently not indexed?" They show whether your guides get cited as a source.

Pull the wording from places buyers speak in their own words: Search Console queries, sales call notes, the first lines of inbound emails, and the questions clients ask on a first call. Sixteen questions is a workable start for one person or a small firm. A client program usually runs forty to a hundred.

## Record four things from every answer

For each answer, I record the providers it names in the order they appear, my position in that list, the tone toward me (positive, neutral, negative, or mixed), and every URL it cites. I also copy out each factual claim it makes about me, word for word, because tone and accuracy are separate questions. A warm answer with the wrong founding date still needs fixing.

Share of voice for a group is the number of answers that name you divided by the number of answers in that group. Report it per group, beside the names that appear most often in the answers where you are missing. Those names are your real competitors in AI search, and they are often different from the ones your sales team worries about.

## What my own first run showed

In October 2026 I asked Claude, with live web search, sixteen questions a prospect of mine might ask. It named me in all three branded answers and cited my sites in each. It named me in none of the nine open hiring questions and cited none of my guides on the four how-to questions. The answers about me were mostly accurate, with two dated facts and one sentence that had merged two of my companies into one founding year.

The sharpest line came from the answer to "Is Chris Abraham a good SEO consultant to hire?" It noted that almost everything it found about me was written by me. That is the finding that sets the work: the sites are readable and current, and the rest of the web hasn't caught up with them.

The run cost $1.88 in API fees. Web search on both Anthropic's and OpenAI's APIs is billed at $10 per thousand searches plus tokens, so a monthly run of this size stays in the single dollars.

## Read the competitors from the answers

The names that appear when you are absent tell you what the assistants are working from. In my run, the hiring answers drew names from marketplace listing pages and "best consultants" roundups, and the how-to answers cited vendor blogs. Each pattern points at a different fix: listings and roundups are an outreach problem, and how-to citations are a content problem. My guide to [earning mentions that last](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/) covers the first.

## Know the limits before you report the number

An API call with web search is close to what a person sees in the assistant's app, and the two are not identical. The app adds memory, personalization, and the user's location. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode use different models and techniques, so their answers and links vary between the two features as well. Report the trend across runs, name the engine and the date on every figure, and keep the raw answers so anyone can check a number against the words behind it.

Bing Webmaster Tools now reports citations of your pages in Copilot answers, and Search Console includes AI features in its performance data. Use both beside the question set: they count what actually happened on those platforms, and the question set shows what you would see if you asked.

## Where I fit

I build and run these question sets for companies and agencies, and I use the results to decide what to fix first. If you want a baseline for your brand, [tell me who you compete with and who your buyers are](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/). When the answers about you are wrong, my guide to [correcting AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/) walks through tracing each error to its source.

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Topic clusters for AI search, without your pages competing with each other

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

A topic cluster is one hub page that defines a subject and routes readers, plus a set of pages that each answer one buyer question in full, all linked to each other. AI search rewards the shape because Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode break a question into subtopics and run a separate search for each one. Every subtopic page you publish is another chance to be the page that search returns. The discipline that makes it work is one page per question, and no two pages answering the same one.

## Why the shape suits AI search

Google's documentation says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a "query fan-out" technique, issuing multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources to build a response. Elizabeth Reid, Google's head of Search, described it when AI Mode launched in May 2025: the system breaks a question into subtopics and runs many queries at once. A buyer's one question becomes a dozen narrower searches behind the scenes.

A single long page that covers everything competes in each of those searches with one URL and a diluted focus. A cluster puts a page with a clear, specific answer in front of each subtopic search. To be eligible as a supporting link, Google's guidance adds, a page only has to be indexed and eligible for a snippet in ordinary search. The cluster changes how many questions you can be the best answer to.

## Start from questions, not keywords

I build a cluster from the questions buyers ask, in their own words. The best sources are the Search Console query report for the pages you already have, the first lines of inbound emails, notes from sales calls, and the open questions in an [AI share of voice question set](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/). Group the questions by what the buyer is trying to decide. Each group that needs more than a few paragraphs to answer properly becomes a page.

Keyword tools still help with volume and wording, and they come second. A cluster planned from a keyword export tends to produce pages that differ by one modifier and answer the same thing, which is how a site ends up competing with itself.

## One page per question

When two pages on your site answer the same question, search engines have to pick one, and they often alternate between them or choose the one you'd rank lower. Google's canonicalization guidance exists for exact and near duplicates; the softer version, two different pages chasing one intent, gets no such help. The fix is a decision for each pair: merge them and redirect the weaker URL, or rewrite one so it answers a different question.

I enforce this mechanically on my own sites. The script that builds them refuses to publish a page that shares more than 15 percent of its phrasing with another page on the same site, or a sentence of ten words or more that already appears elsewhere. A human editor misses overlap across eighty pages; a check that runs on every build doesn't.

## Build the hub to route, and the spokes to answer

The hub page defines the subject in its first paragraph, says who it's for, and links to every spoke with anchor text that names the question the spoke answers. Google's starter guide asks for exactly that: link text that tells people and Google something about the page it points to. A hub that tries to answer every question itself becomes the long page the cluster was meant to replace.

Each spoke opens with a direct answer in two or three sentences, then supports it. Every section should make sense if it is the only part an AI system lifts. Spokes link back to the hub and to the other spokes a reader would naturally need next, and nowhere else by habit.

## A cluster on this site

My [AI search service page](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ai-search/) is the hub for one cluster. Its spokes each answer one question: whether a site is ready (the [AI search readiness checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/)), how to fix a wrong answer ([correcting AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/)), how to earn the mentions answers repeat ([earned mentions](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/)), what [llms.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/llms-txt/) does, and how to [measure share of voice](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/). None of them answers another's question, and each links back to the hub.

## Check the cluster every quarter

Open Search Console's performance report, filter to the cluster's pages, and look at the queries. When two pages draw impressions for the same query, one of them is drifting into the other's territory. When a page draws queries you never planned for, the buyers are telling you what the next spoke should be. Add it, link it from the hub, and keep the rule of one question per page.

## Where I fit

I plan clusters from real buyer questions, find the pages already competing with each other, and decide what to merge, rewrite, or add. If your site has grown by accretion and you suspect it is splitting its own signals, [send me the domain](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) and I'll tell you where I would start.

Once the questions and their pages are mapped, the [internal linking guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/internal-linking/) takes that structure down to individual sentences and destinations, with a worksheet for recording each proposed connection.

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# How to load Google Analytics 4 without hurting PageSpeed

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

On a lean site, the Google Analytics tag can be the heaviest thing on the page. When I tested this site in October 2026, gtag.js accounted for most of the main-thread work during load on mobile, about twice what the site's own code used. Loading the tag after the visitor's first scroll, tap, or key press, or four seconds after the page finishes loading, took the home page from a mobile Lighthouse score of 73 to 80 up to 100. Pageviews still count. The cost is the visitors who leave within a few seconds without touching the page.

## What the tag costs

The standard GA4 snippet loads gtag.js asynchronously, which keeps it from blocking the HTML parser. It still runs on the main thread once it arrives, and the script is large: about 176 KB on my pages. On a phone, parsing and running it lands in the same window as the page's first paint, and Lighthouse counts every long task in that window toward Total Blocking Time. On my home page, Total Blocking Time ran from 700 to 1,760 milliseconds, depending on the run.

Total Blocking Time is a lab measure. Google's ranking signals use field data, and the field measure for responsiveness is Interaction to Next Paint. Real phones on real networks still pay the cost of a large script parsed during load, so a lab fix that removes that work tends to show up in the field too, a month or so later, once enough visits have been recorded.

## Load the tag after the visitor acts

The fix keeps every analytics command and moves only the script download. The page defines dataLayer and the gtag function as usual, queues the consent defaults, the js timestamp, and the config call, and then waits. The first scroll, pointer press, touch, or key press loads gtag.js. If none comes, a timer loads it four seconds after the page's load event. When the script arrives it reads the queued commands in order, so the pageview is recorded with the right consent state.

```
<script>
  window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
  function gtag(){dataLayer.push(arguments);}
  gtag('js', new Date());
  gtag('config', 'G-XXXXXXXXXX');
  (function () {
    var done = false;
    function load() {
      if (done) return;
      done = true;
      var s = document.createElement('script');
      s.async = true;
      s.src = 'https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-XXXXXXXXXX';
      document.head.appendChild(s);
    }
    ['pointerdown', 'keydown', 'scroll', 'touchstart'].forEach(function (e) {
      addEventListener(e, load, {once: true, passive: true});
    });
    addEventListener('load', function () { setTimeout(load, 4000); });
  })();
</script>
```

Keep your consent mode defaults above the config line, exactly where they were. They are commands in the same queue and run before anything is sent.

## The result

I tested the original and the deferred version of the same page side by side, twice each, with Lighthouse in mobile mode on the same machine. The original scored 73 and 80, with 1,760 and 890 milliseconds of blocking time. The deferred version scored 100 both times, with 40 and 30 milliseconds. The two pages I measured on this site afterward scored 98 and 100.

## The cost, stated plainly

A visitor who opens a page and leaves within about four seconds without scrolling, tapping, or typing is never counted. On most sites that group is small and includes a share of bots, but it is real, and a client should hear it before the change ships. Bounce rate and short-session counts will shift on the day you deploy, so annotate the change in GA4 and compare like with like afterward.

Two cases call for the standard snippet instead. A site whose business depends on counting single-page visits exactly, such as a landing page measured by paid campaigns, should keep the tag loading immediately. So should any page where the tag fires conversion events the moment it loads.

## Check the rest of the page first

Deferring analytics is the right first move only when analytics is the problem. Run Lighthouse, open the diagnostics, and read which scripts take the main-thread time. If a theme, a page builder, or a chat widget is the larger cost, fix that first. My guide to [Core Web Vitals](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/core-web-vitals/) covers the other common causes.

## Where I fit

I find what is actually slowing a site, measure the fix before it ships, and explain the trade-offs to the people who own the analytics. If your PageSpeed scores are stuck and nobody can say why, [send me the URL](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).
