# Glossary of SEO and AI search terms

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026 · Updated October 26, 2026

The vocabulary of search and AI visibility, one or two sentences per term. Every entry carries an anchor, so a link can point straight at the definition you need. To find every page that discusses a term, use the [index](https://christopherabraham.com/site-index/).

**301 redirect**
A permanent forwarding instruction from an old address to a new one, which passes nearly all of the old page's ranking signals along.

**AEO (answer engine optimization)**
Shaping pages so that systems which reply with an answer rather than a list of links, from featured snippets to voice assistants to chatbots, can lift a passage and credit it.

**AI Overviews**
The generated summaries Google places on many results pages, citing the sites they borrowed from. AI Mode extends the idea into a back-and-forth conversation.

**AI share of voice**
The share of relevant buyer questions where an AI assistant names your brand, measured against the competitors it names instead, tracked with the same question set every month. Method in [measuring share of voice in AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/).

**Alt text**
Words attached to an image in the markup that describe it for people using screen readers and give crawlers a clue about the picture's subject.

**Anchor text**
The visible, clickable wording of a hyperlink. When it names the destination's topic, both readers and crawlers know what they'll find.

**APO (Automatic Platform Optimization)**
Cloudflare's WordPress feature that stores complete pages at the edge so even the first byte arrives quickly. Included with Cloudflare's Pro plan and above, or $5 a month on the free plan, per Cloudflare's pricing.

**Astroturfing**
Posting praise for a product while pretending to be an ordinary customer, often from new or borrowed accounts. Reddit moderators remove it on sight; see [Reddit and AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/reddit-ai-answers/).

**Bing Webmaster Tools**
Microsoft's no-cost dashboard for owners, covering crawl, index, and keyword data from Bing, whose index also supplies Copilot and several other assistants.

**Canonical tag**
A line in a page's head nominating which address should represent a set of duplicate or close copies. Google weighs it heavily but may overrule it.

**CDN (content delivery network)**
A network of servers spread around the world that keeps copies of a site's files and hands them to each visitor from somewhere nearby.

**Client-side rendering (CSR)**
Building a page in the visitor's browser with JavaScript, so the HTML the server sends starts nearly empty. Crawlers that skip scripts see little or nothing. See [SEO for AI-built websites](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-built-websites/).

**CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)**
The Core Web Vital that scores how far things jump around on screen during loading. Aim for 0.1 or lower.

**Comparison cohort**
A fixed group of pages evaluated across reporting periods so changes in the page inventory can be distinguished from changes in performance. See [Search Console comparisons](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/search-console-comparisons/).

**Core update**
A broad change Google makes to how it ranks everything, several times a year. Pages can rise or fall without anything being wrong with them; Google lists each one on its Search Status Dashboard.

**Core Web Vitals**
Three experience scores Google tracks, LCP, INP, and CLS, taken from Chrome users over a rolling four weeks.

**Crawl budget**
The practical ceiling on how much of a site a search engine will fetch in a given stretch of time. A concern for very large sites and those spawning endless URL variants.

**Crawler**
Software that requests pages on its own to read them, such as Googlebot, Bingbot, GPTBot, or ClaudeBot. People also say bot or spider.

**Custom extraction**
A crawler feature that pulls a chosen piece of every page, by XPath, CSS selector, or regex, into a column, so one crawl can audit headings, schema types, or tracking codes sitewide. Recipes are in [custom extraction](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/custom-extraction/).

**Digital PR**
Earning coverage and mentions on other people's sites, newsletters, and shows by giving writers something worth using. The sentences those mentions contain now feed AI answers; see [digital PR for AI search](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/).

**E-E-A-T**
Experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness: the qualities Google's quality raters look for in a page and its author, with trust counted as the most important.

**Earned media**
Coverage a business didn't pay for and doesn't control: a reporter's article, a reviewer's post, a mention in someone else's newsletter.

**Entity**
A single real-world thing, whether a company, person, place, or product, that search engines and AI models recognize as one concept however a page happens to phrase its name.

**Faceted navigation**
Category filters for attributes like color, size, or price. Left open to crawlers, the combinations can balloon into millions of addresses.

**Field data**
Speed and responsiveness figures gathered from actual visits, as opposed to one synthetic test run on a single machine.

**Free listings**
Unpaid product results Google shows across Shopping, Search, Images, Lens, and Maps, fed by a store's Merchant Center data. See [Merchant Center free listings](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/merchant-center-free-listings/).

**GEO (generative engine optimization)**
Work aimed at how generative AI tools portray and cite a company or a page. In practice it overlaps almost entirely with AEO and AI SEO.

**Google Business Profile**
The free Google listing that puts a business on Maps and in local results, carrying its hours, categories, photos, and reviews.

**GTIN (Global Trade Item Number)**
The barcode number a manufacturer assigns to a product, such as a UPC or EAN. Resellers put it in their product feed; makers of their own goods mark it as not applicable.

**hreflang**
Markup that pairs each language or country edition of a page with the audience that should see it.

**HSTS**
A security header telling browsers to reach a site only over HTTPS for a set period, so no visit ever falls back to an unencrypted connection.

**Hybrid business**
A business that both receives customers at a posted address and travels to them, such as a tile showroom with installation crews. Its profile shows the address and a service area. See [service-area businesses](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/service-area-business/).

**Index**
The store of pages a search engine considers eligible for results. Nothing ranks until it's in there.

**IndexNow**
A shared ping system: when a page appears, changes, or disappears, the site tells Bing, Yandex, and other members right away instead of waiting for a recrawl.

**INP (Interaction to Next Paint)**
The Core Web Vital that times the gap between a tap, click, or keystroke and the screen's visible response. Aim for 200 ms or lower.

**JSON-LD**
Google's preferred way to write structured data: a JSON object inside its own script element, kept apart from what visitors see.

**LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)**
The Core Web Vital that times how long the biggest image or text block in the opening view takes to finish drawing. Aim for 2.5 s or lower.

**llms.txt**
A suggested standard: a Markdown summary kept at the top level of a domain, pointing language models to the pages most worth reading.

**Material connection**
The FTC's term for any tie between a brand and the person endorsing it, such as payment, free product, or employment. In the United States it has to be disclosed clearly wherever the endorsement appears.

**Meta description**
The short summary written into a page's code that search engines often show beneath the title in results. It invites the click rather than setting the rank.

**Near-duplicate**
Two pages whose text is almost, but not exactly, the same, such as product variants or city pages built from one template. Crawlers can flag them by similarity score; see [near duplicates and H1s](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/near-duplicates-and-h1s/).

**Niche edit**
A paid link inserted into an article that's already published and indexed, rather than a new article written for the purpose.

**noindex**
A directive, set in a meta tag or a response header, asking search engines to keep a page out of results.

**Open Graph tags**
The og: meta tags in a page's head that set the headline, summary, and image Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, and most messaging apps show when someone shares the link. See [social share cards](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/social-share-cards/).

**Orange cloud**
Cloudflare's icon for a proxied DNS record, meaning visitors pass through Cloudflare's network, with its caching and protection, on the way to the site. A gray cloud means DNS only.

**Orphan page**
A page nothing else on the site links to. Only a sitemap entry or an outside link can lead anyone to it.

**Permalink**
The permanent address of a single post or page. In WordPress, the Permalinks settings screen decides its pattern; the post name pattern produces readable addresses.

**Place card**
Apple Maps' listing for a business: name, hours, phone, photos, and actions such as booking, managed through Apple's business tools. See [Apple and Bing listings](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/apple-and-bing-listings/).

**Placed article**
An article published on another site through a paid arrangement, usually carrying a link back. Google expects the link to be marked rel="sponsored"; see [why I turn down backlink work](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/buying-backlinks/).

**Prerendering**
Generating a finished HTML copy of a JavaScript page ahead of time and serving it to crawlers or visitors, so the content is readable without running scripts.

**Pull request**
A proposed change to a code repository, shown line by line for review before it's merged. SEO fixes made this way are recorded, reviewable, and easy to undo; see [SEO in your Git repository](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-in-your-repository/).

**Reddit Answers**
Reddit's own AI search, launched in December 2024, which summarizes discussions from across the site in reply to a question.

**Redirect chain**
Several redirects strung together before the visitor arrives. Every extra step costs time and can weaken the signals passed along.

**rel="sponsored"**
A link attribute that tells Google a link was paid for, so it passes no ranking credit. Google's spam policies ask for it on every paid or sponsored link.

**Rendering**
Running a page's scripts to produce what a browser finally shows. Anything that exists only after this step can escape crawlers that skip it.

**Review gating**
Screening customers before asking for a public review, so only satisfied ones reach the review site. Google's policies forbid it, and the FTC warns it can mislead. See [the FTC review rule](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ftc-review-rule/).

**Rich results**
Search listings dressed up with extra details drawn from structured data, like star ratings, prices, or breadcrumb trails.

**robots.txt**
A plain text file at the top of a domain that tells bots which folders to stay out of. It governs fetching; keeping a page out of results takes noindex.

**Scaled content abuse**
Google's spam policy against publishing many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, whether people, AI, or both produce them. The main target of Google's 2026 spam updates.

**Schema markup**
Structured data written in the Schema.org vocabulary to spell out the people, organizations, places, and products on a page.

**Search Console**
Google's free owner dashboard: clicks and impressions, index status, Core Web Vitals, and alerts about problems it detects.

**Server-side rendering (SSR)**
Assembling the complete HTML on the server so a crawler gets every word in the first response, no scripts required.

**Service-area business**
A business on Google that travels to its customers, such as a plumber or mobile groomer, and hides its street address from the public profile. It verifies by showing its tools, vehicle, and nearby street markers. See [video verification](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-video-verification/).

**Single page application (SPA)**
A website that loads one HTML shell and swaps content in with JavaScript as people click, instead of loading a new page for each address. Many AI app builders produce them.

**Site reputation abuse**
Placing a third party's low-value pages on a trusted site to borrow its standing in search, such as coupon or gambling sections rented out under a respected domain. Against Google's spam policies.

**Soft 404**
A URL that answers with a success code yet shows an empty or not-found page. Google files it with the real 404s.

**Spam update**
An improvement to the automated systems Google uses to detect pages that break its spam policies. Sites caught by one usually drop sharply and quickly.

**Title tag**
The headline written into a page's code that search engines usually show as the clickable link in results and browsers show on the tab.

**Topic cluster**
One hub page that defines a subject, plus a set of pages that each answer a single buyer question in full, all linked together. See [topic clusters for AI search](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/topic-clusters/).

**Vibe coding**
Building software by describing what you want to an AI tool and accepting what it writes, with little reading of the code itself. Andrej Karpathy coined the phrase in February 2025.

**Video verification**
Google's way of confirming a Business Profile from a single unedited phone recording of at least 30 seconds that shows the location, the business, and proof the owner runs it. Explained in [my video verification guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-video-verification/).

**White label**
A service delivered under someone else's brand: an agency resells the work, and its client never sees the vendor's name.

**XML sitemap**
A machine-readable list of the addresses a site wants crawled, often with the date each last changed.

These terms are used throughout the [guides](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/) and [services](https://christopherabraham.com/services/) pages.

# The show notes cascade: podcasting as an AI search strategy

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

Most podcasters treat show notes as a courtesy, a few lines typed after the episode is edited and forgotten by morning. I treat them as the most widely republished writing I do. Every episode I release copies its notes, word for word, onto hundreds of podcast indexes and directories, each one a page on a domain that search engines and AI assistants already trust. When someone later asks a machine about my subject, the answer often comes back built from sentences I wrote once, in a notes field, months earlier.

## How the cascade works

A podcast is distributed by a feed, and the feed is promiscuous. Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Podcast Index, Pocket Casts, Castbox, TuneIn, Podcast Addict, and a long tail of smaller directories and apps all read the same feed and republish what it carries: the episode title, the audio, and the full text of the show notes. Nothing about this requires outreach, pitching, or a link building campaign. Syndication is simply how the medium works, and it has quietly become an answer engine optimization channel hiding in plain sight.

The second half of the mechanism is newer. Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT, and Perplexity answer questions by gathering text from pages they can reach, and directory pages are easy for them to reach. A claim that appears in your notes therefore exists in hundreds of places at once, stated the same way everywhere, which is precisely the pattern these systems read as settled fact. Repetition used to be what links did for a page. Now the words themselves do it, and show notes repeat more faithfully than almost any other format on the web.

## The morning the machine quoted me to myself

On October 24, 2026, I searched Google for what I think about a television show I have covered on my own podcast, The Chris Abraham Show. AI Mode answered with my position, quoting my show notes for season 11, episode 3 nearly word for word: what I came for, what I stayed for, the themes I keep returning to. My essay on the same subject sat at the top of the ordinary results below it. Nobody had written about my opinion except me. The answer engine found my own sentences, syndicated across the podcast directories and my episode pages, and handed them back as the authority on the question.

That is the proof of concept in miniature. The query was about me, but the machinery does not care whose name is in the question. Ask what a company thinks about its own industry, what a founder believes about her market, what a consultant recommends about his specialty, and the same sources get consulted. If your positions live in your show notes, they are positioned to be quoted. If they live only in the audio, the machines mostly cannot use them, because an answer engine quotes text.

## Write the notes for citation

Once you see the cascade, the writing rules follow from it. Write every episode's notes as if a directory reader, and then a machine, will repeat them without you in the room.
- **Use full entity names.** Write the whole name of every person, company, show, and product, spelled the way it should be quoted. A first name alone cannot be connected to you, and a misspelling repeated in two hundred places is a misspelling with authority.
- **Phrase claims the way they should come back.** If you hold a position, state it in one clean, quotable sentence inside the notes. The engines lift sentences, not vibes. My guide to [correcting AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/) starts from the same principle: answers are built from sentences found somewhere, so make sure the findable sentences are yours and are right.
- **Include the canonical links.** Link each claim to the page on your own site that owns it. Directories carry links unevenly, but the ones that survive point the engines, and the occasional human reader, at your canonical version.
- **Say who is speaking.** Name the host and guests with their roles and affiliations. Attribution is what turns a floating opinion into a position a named expert can be cited for.

## Front load what matters

Platform notes do not all survive intact. Spotify trims episode descriptions at roughly 4,000 characters, and different directories cut or compress at their own limits. So put the citable material first: the episode's actual subject, the named people, the position sentences, and the key links, all before the credits, the chapter markers, and the housekeeping. Think of the first screen of notes as the press release and everything after it as the appendix. What travels is what appears early, so the sentences you most want quoted should be the sentences every copy is guaranteed to carry.

## Keep a mirror you own

Directories are landlords. They can trim your text, surround it with their own recommendations, or disappear, and you hold no deed to any of it. So the cascade needs a home base: a site you control that republishes every episode with the full notes, a transcript, and one permanent page per episode. My own show's website is the worked example I point clients to. It carries the complete notes with no character cap, full transcripts that give the engines thousands more quotable words per episode, and an llms.txt file that hands AI crawlers the whole catalogue in plain text. My guide to [what belongs in an llms.txt file](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/llms-txt/) covers that format. The directories supply the reach. The mirror supplies the canonical record the reach points back to.

## Every episode is a page that stays

A blog post fights for attention in the week it ships and then sinks into the archive. An episode behaves differently. It is a dated, permanent landing surface in every directory at once, still indexed and still quotable years later, and each new episode adds another one without disturbing the rest. A season of weekly episodes is fifty new surfaces a year, each carrying your names, your links, and your stated positions. That compounding is why I call podcasting an investment rather than a content chore: the production cost is paid once, and the citation surface keeps appreciating as the catalogue grows.

## Measure the position queries

None of this counts until you check what the machines actually say. Monthly, run a fixed set of position queries: what does this person think about that subject, who offers this service in this place, what is the difference between these two approaches. Record which sentences come back, which sources get cited, and whether your phrasing survives the round trip. My guide to [measuring AI share of voice](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/) describes the method I use. When an answer quotes your notes verbatim, the cascade is working. When it quotes a competitor's framing instead, you have found the next episode to record and the next notes to write.

## Where I fit

I run this play on my own show before I recommend it to anyone, and I build the same machinery for clients: notes written for citation, a mirror site with transcripts and permanent episode pages, and a monthly set of position queries that proves whether the answers are moving. If you want the baseline first, my AI visibility audit runs your money queries through the major answer engines and reports what they say about you today. [Book a thirty minute call on my calendar](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) to talk about your show or your site, or [write to me through the contact page](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) if you would rather start in writing.

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Case studies

Each case explains the problem, my role, what I found, what was done and by whom, how it was checked, and where things stand. Clients are described by industry, never by name.

## Content crawlers couldn't see
- [My own podcast: 458 episodes, each with a page of its own](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/podcast-site/). A feed turned into a static site that updates every morning, and a share card fix for every episode.
- [Equipment retailer: product details that loaded only on scroll](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/scroll-gated-products/). Magento and Hyvä, Alpine.js, and a backlink spike kept on its own track.
- [Film review site: a consent tool that emptied every article](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/consent-banner/). A cookie platform blocking the script that displayed the reviews.
- [Event discovery app: 2,000 pages with no way in](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/). A React app, a 13-page spec, and testable fixes.

## Modern stacks and migrations
- [Junk removal company on a headless stack](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/headless-local/). Sanity, Vercel, and SEO changes merged through GitHub.
- [Medical clinic: WordPress to Next.js](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/). A decision for every legacy URL and an AI-assisted code review.
- [Serialized novel: Movable Type to static HTML](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/movable-type-novel/). All 953 old URLs kept, with DNS moved before the site.
- [Fly fishing shop: cleanup after a Shopify move](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/shopify-cleanup/). 3,400 broken URLs and duplicate product markup.

## Indexing at scale and recovery
- [Trading card price site: 20,000 pages in the index](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/card-price-index/). Segmented sitemaps and parameter rules.
- [Health-testing store: after the SEO plugin went dark](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/plugin-outage/). Recovery checked in Google and Bing.

## Entities, local, and AI search
- [Custom closet brand: the company versus its first showroom](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/closet-locations/). Entity modeling and location pages.
- [Therapy practice: a suspended Business Profile reinstated](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/). An evidence-first appeal.
- [Private training gym: a brand name that is also a verb](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/training-gym/). Calls from the profile went from 7 to 56 a month.
- [AI research company: accurate AI answers for job seekers](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/recruiting-answers/). A GEO audit for recruiting.
- [My own consultancy: an AI visibility baseline](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/ai-visibility-baseline/). Named in 3 of 3 branded answers and 0 of 9 hiring questions.

## The common thread

Almost every case comes down to the same gap: what a business believes its site says versus what crawlers and AI systems actually receive. Finding that gap, proving it, and closing it is the work. If one of these sounds familiar, [tell me about your site](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

# Equipment retailer: product details that loaded only on scroll

An equipment retailer running Magento 2 with the Hyvä theme watched organic traffic slide for months. The odd part: non-brand category traffic was rising while brand searches and product pages fell.

## The engagement

Forensic diagnosis and technical direction. The client's contractor owned implementation; I owned the evidence and the specification.

## What the crawl showed

I crawled the site twice with Screaming Frog, once reading raw HTML and once rendering JavaScript, and compared extracted word counts by template. Category pages yielded thousands of words. Flagship product pages, each weighing more than 1.2 MB, yielded only 250 to 400.

## The mechanism

The product template wrapped its specifications, FAQs, and reviews in Alpine.js directives that created those sections only when a shopper scrolled them into view: an `x-intersect` trigger around an `x-if` block. Googlebot renders pages in a tall viewport without scrolling the way people do, so those sections were never built. Search Console agreed: a selective cluster of product URLs sat in "Crawled, currently not indexed" while the rest of the site was fine.

## The second problem, kept separate

During the same months, a burst of spam backlinks from cloud-hosting ranges arrived, along with a redirect fault. Tempting as it was to blame everything on one cause, I documented that track separately and requested fuller Search Console access to investigate it on its own evidence.

## Recommendations
- Render product sections in the server HTML; keep scroll animation as an enhancement on top.
- Remove the scroll gate on a test group of products first, so the effect is measurable before a sitewide rollout.
- A separate cleanup plan for the backlinks and redirects.

## The lesson

Page weight and word count can disagree wildly. When a heavy page yields little text to a crawler, look for content waiting on an interaction that bots never perform. More on this pattern under [JavaScript SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/).

Source: https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/consent-banner/
Updated: 2026-10-06

# Film review site: a consent tool that emptied every article for Google

A WordPress site publishing film reviews in English and Italian had a strange split: Bing indexed it normally, while Google left almost every review out. No crawl errors, no manual action, just a long list of pages marked "Crawled, currently not indexed."

## The engagement

A paid diagnosis for the owner, followed by a call to walk through what I found.

## The cause

Each review's text sat inside jQuery UI tabs. The site's cookie consent platform was set to prior-consent blocking, holding back scripts until a visitor clicked Accept. One of the scripts held back was the one that initialized the tabs.

Googlebot never clicks Accept. It visits every page as a visitor who has declined, so it rendered each review with the layout intact and the tab panels empty. Bing processed the pages differently, which explained the gap between the two engines.

## What made it worse
- 97% of pages carried identical hardcoded H2 headings from the theme.
- 95% of internal links had no anchor text at all.

Even the parts Google could see said almost nothing that distinguished one review from another.

## Recommendations
- Exempt content-building scripts from consent blocking, or put the review text directly in the HTML. Consent rules belong on analytics and advertising scripts, never on the article.
- Generate H2s from each review's own content.
- Add descriptive anchor text to internal links.

## How I confirmed it

Side-by-side browser sessions, one consenting and one not, showed the tabs empty in the second. The blocked script was identified in the consent platform's settings and matched to the exclusion pattern.

## Why it matters

Consent platforms are installed by legal and marketing teams and almost never tested against crawlers. If your site uses one, load a page with consent declined and check what's left. See [reading the Page indexing report](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/page-indexing-report/).

Updated: 2026-10-06

# Event discovery app: 2,000 pages with no way in

A nightlife and event discovery app built on Create React App needed roughly 2,000 event pages in Google. After three months, Search Console showed impressions for the home page and close to nothing anywhere else.

## The engagement

I diagnosed, wrote the specification, and verified the work. The founder's developer built the fixes.

## Four findings
1. **The home page was empty to crawlers.** The server returned a single empty root element; everything visible was drawn later by JavaScript.
2. **Event cards weren't links.** They navigated with click handlers, so there were no anchor tags for a crawler to follow.
3. **The event pages were orphans.** Ironically, the event pages already had server-side rendering and decent HTML. Nothing pointed to them.
4. **Canonicals pointed home.** The events and community sections declared the home page as their canonical, effectively telling Google they were copies of it.

## The deliverables

A short plain-language summary for the founder, and a 13-page specification for the developer covering 12 items ranked from P0 to P3. Each item carried the evidence, why it mattered, the build steps, and an acceptance test. The P0 items: real anchor links on every event card, server rendering for the home page and the event feed, and indexing requests for priority pages once those shipped.

## Verification

Every item had a test anyone could run, for example "event links appear in the server HTML of the feed" and "each section's canonical references itself." I checked the developer's work against those tests with a crawl and Search Console's live URL test.

## The takeaway

Good pages can still be invisible if nothing links to them in a way crawlers understand. Real links in real HTML remain the foundation of discovery. More under [JavaScript SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/).

# Junk removal company on a headless stack: SEO through the repository

A local junk removal company had a modern website: content in Sanity, hosting on Vercel, code in GitHub. It also had every classic problem of a client-rendered site, and with no SEO plugin to configure, every fix had to go through code.

## What I found
- Client-side rendering left crawlers with thin initial HTML.
- Many pages shared the same title and meta description.
- Heading levels were skipped or repeated.
- Missing pages answered with a 200 status, producing soft 404s.
- Canonical tags and structured data were missing or inconsistent.

## Division of labor

The developer handled the infrastructure: prerendered HTML and deployment changes. I set the order of work, specified what each page type needed, reviewed the developer's changes, and checked the production site independently. For metadata, I made the code changes myself in a pull request that the developer reviewed and merged.

## How the result was checked
- Crawls before and after prerendering, comparing extracted text.
- Raw HTML fetched from production to confirm content was present without scripts.
- Search Console's live URL test on representative pages.
- A sitewide review of titles, descriptions, canonicals, and status codes.

## Why this way of working helps

On headless sites, SEO lives in templates, routes, and build settings. Working through the team's pull requests means every SEO change has a commit, a reviewer, and an easy rollback, and nobody has to wonder who changed what.

## Status

Core fixes are live and verified, with a final audit under way. See [JavaScript and headless SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/javascript-seo/).

Updated: 2026-10-06

# Medical clinic: WordPress to Next.js without losing the trail

A clinical practice replaced its managed WordPress site with a new Next.js build hosted on Netlify. The developer built the site. My job was continuity: making sure people and search engines could follow every old address to the right new one, and investigating whatever went wrong after launch.

## A decision for every URL

I reviewed the legacy URLs and reconciled the redirect map line by line. Each URL got one of four outcomes: unchanged, redirected to an existing destination, given a new migration redirect, or deliberately retired. I also separated faults the migration introduced from faults the old site already had, so neither the developer nor the old host took blame that wasn't theirs.

## Reading the code with an AI assistant

Alongside crawls and exports, I ran a read-only analysis of the Next.js repository with an AI coding assistant. It surfaced thousands of image references still pointing at the old WordPress media library and traced them to a handful of central files. That became a short, concrete plan for the developer to move the media. No code was changed by the analysis.

## A conservative disavow

I reviewed the backlink profile and rebuilt the disavow file to drop truly toxic domains while keeping legitimate ones. Over-disavowing throws away the very equity a migration is trying to keep.

## After launch

Blurry images from the image CDN, script and stylesheet errors, instability, and analytics oddities all came up. When engagement dipped over a short window, the obvious story was that blurry images drove people away. I checked tracking, engagement, and stability separately before accepting any explanation, and found the data didn't yet support that one.

## The point

Migrations rarely fail on launch day. They fail weeks later, through media still on the old host, missing redirects, and stories told too early. Read my [rules for 301 redirects](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/redirect-rules/) or see [migration services](https://christopherabraham.com/services/migrations/).

# Fly fishing shop: cleaning up after Squarespace to Shopify

A family-owned fly fishing retailer moved its store from Squarespace to Shopify. The new storefront looked better, but the number of indexed pages kept shrinking and search visibility slipped month by month.

## A four-part audit
- **Duplicate product URLs.** Leftover Squarespace-style paths and Shopify's own collection paths were competing for the same products.
- **More than 3,400 404s** from old URLs that were never redirected.
- **A duplicated FAQ page.**
- **Brand misspellings driving most organic traffic**, a sign the shop wasn't being found for the gear it sells.
- **Broken and default meta descriptions** inherited from the theme.
- **Spammy backlinks, slow mobile pages, and almost no presence in AI answers.**

## Hands-on work

First, a pass through product titles, descriptions, metadata, and category assignments. Then structured data, done in a duplicate of the live theme so the store was never at risk. I added Organization markup and a Product block, then discovered the theme already emitted a more complete Product block of its own. I traced the overlap and left exactly one valid block. Review stars needed the reviews app's metafield namespace confirmed before they could be wired in correctly.

## Checks

Structured data validated on sample product pages, crawls compared before and after, and every change previewed in the duplicate theme before publishing.

## Status

The audit and the first product pass are delivered. Remaining items, including thin product descriptions and missing categories, are being reviewed with the owner before further edits.

## Lesson

A platform move isn't finished when the new store launches. It's finished when every old URL lands somewhere useful and the new theme's markup is checked rather than trusted. See [ecommerce SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ecommerce-seo/).

# Trading card price site: managing 20,000 pages in Google's index

A new site publishing prices for more than 20,000 trading cards, generated programmatically and launched on an expired domain, was indexed quickly at first. Then whole sections began dropping out.

## The engagement

Hourly technical SEO focused on crawling and indexing, working with the owner over Microsoft Teams and with access to the GitHub repository where the site is built.

## Thinking in collections

A site like this can't be managed page by page. The useful questions are about groups: which page types deserve to be indexed, which URL variations the site's tools and filters create, and how a crawler reaches a card page five levels deep.

## What I put in place
- **One sitemap per content type**, so Search Console reports coverage for each group on its own.
- **A baseline by segment**, so every later change is judged against numbers rather than impressions.
- **Robots rules for parameter-driven tools** whose endless URL variations add nothing to the index and pull crawl attention from the pages that matter.
- **Lag-aware checks.** Reports trail reality, so live behavior gets checked before any change is called a success or a failure.
- **The domain's past treated as one factor**, kept apart from the site's own technical issues.

## Working through the code

Because the site is built by developers, fixes go through the repository. Seeing how URLs are generated lets me specify changes precisely instead of describing symptoms. Every recommendation reaches the owner in writing, with its evidence attached.

## Status

Ongoing. I'm not claiming recovery numbers here; at this scale, indexing moves over weeks and months, and honest reporting means waiting for the trend. See [indexing repair](https://christopherabraham.com/services/indexing/).

# Health-testing store: recovering after the SEO plugin went dark

On a WooCommerce store that sells health tests, someone switched off the SEO plugin for a short time. Afterward, indexed pages, organic visits, and referrals from AI assistants all dropped. The owner isn't technical and needed the problem found, fixed, and the recovery demonstrated.

## The engagement

Three paid milestones: diagnosis, fixes, and verification. Because the store handles protected health information, the work ran under a HIPAA agreement and an NDA.

## Why a few hours matter

On WordPress, the SEO plugin quietly produces titles, descriptions, canonicals, robots directives, structured data, and the XML sitemaps. With it off, crawlers that visit see pages with no canonicals, default titles, and sitemaps that have vanished. Switching it back on doesn't erase what search engines recorded while it was off; they have to recrawl and reconsider.

## The work
- URL Inspection on the priority product and information pages.
- Crawl stats reviewed for changes in Googlebot's visit rate and what it fetched.
- Sitemaps checked and resubmitted to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
- A watch list of priority pages for the recovery period.
- Structured data, Cloudflare settings, and ghost traffic in GA4 reviewed in the same scope.

## Proving recovery

I tracked several indicators over time rather than trusting one dashboard, and took care to tell a stale report apart from a fault that was still active. Each milestone closed with a plain-language note for the owner, showing the before and after side by side.

## Status

Recovery checks continue, with redirects, merchant structured data, and crawler policy as possible next steps. Related: [WordPress SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/wordpress-seo/) and [Search Console setup](https://christopherabraham.com/services/search-console/).

# Custom closet brand: separating the company from its first showroom

A custom closet and wardrobe company with showrooms in several states ran everything from one website. Search engines kept merging the brand with its original showroom, and its location pages, Google Business Profiles, and town pages stepped on each other.

## The engagement

A fixed-price project in milestones, delivering recommendations and structured data ready for the developer to install.

## What I delivered

### A clear entity model

The company described as the parent organization, and each showroom as a branch of it, so search engines and AI assistants can tell which is the brand and which is one of its locations. The JSON-LD states that relationship explicitly.

### Organization and product markup

Home page and product JSON-LD, validated and ready to install.

### Location pages matched to profiles

Each Google Business Profile linking to a page about that specific showroom, rather than to the home page.

### Profiles and town pages with separate jobs

Guidance for areas where a profile and a town page cover the same ground, so they reinforce each other.

### Services, regions, and breadcrumbs

A structure for how services, regions, and showrooms link together, reflected in breadcrumb markup.

## Why it matters

When every page and listing describes the business the same way, search engines can't tell the locations apart, and each one competes with the others. Distinct entities and distinct pages let every showroom rank in its own area while the brand ranks for itself.

## Status

Delivered. See [schema markup and entity SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/schema/) and [local SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

Updated: 2026-10-06

# Therapy practice: a suspended Business Profile restored

Google suspended the Business Profile of a hypnotherapy office in western Canada. The practice depends on nearby people finding it, so the suspension left it close to invisible to the very clients most likely to book.

## My part

Auditing the listing against the office's real records, assembling proof, writing the appeal, and seeing it through with Google.

## Reconcile the listing with reality

Google suspends a listing when what it claims can't be squared with what Google is able to confirm. So I went field by field: the practice's legal and trading names, its street address, its categories, and whether it served clients on site. Anything on the listing that didn't match the paperwork was corrected before a word of the appeal was written.

## Lead with the best proof

The supporting file contained the office lease, the practice's business licence, an invoice billed to that office, and the business card carrying the same name and address. I ordered them from most to least authoritative, so a reviewer would see the strongest proof first, and the appeal made no claim that one of those documents didn't back up.

## File the appeal

The corrected listing and the ordered proof reached Google as one package, so the reviewer saw the fixes and the evidence side by side.

## Result

Google restored the profile in February 2025.

## How I handle these now

Google gives no timetable and no guarantee for appeals, and two cases that look alike can end differently. For that reason a suspension now starts with a paid written assessment: the likely trigger, the proof Google will expect, and an honest view of the odds. If an appeal makes sense, it's quoted on its own. I take the same approach with harder situations, like duplicate records, listings stranded with a former agency, or an established listing that should be repaired rather than replaced. See [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

# Private training gym: a brand name Google kept misreading

A members only gym in Northern Virginia, built around private lanes that personal trainers rent for their own clients, had a problem baked into its name: the brand was a single everyday verb. People who searched for it by name, plus the town, were competing with every generic workout query that used the same word.

## My part

An hourly engagement of a few hours a week: auditing the website and the gym's presence in Google, cleaning up its Business Profile, rewriting page titles and descriptions, and shaping the local targeting. The owner made the business decisions; I did the search work and reported on it monthly.

## Two audiences, one small site

The gym sells to two very different people. One is a member looking for a personal trainer nearby. The other is a trainer looking for a professional space to rent by the hour. The site had to answer both without blurring them, so the service, facility, contact, and FAQ pages each got titles and descriptions written for one clear intent, from "personal trainer" searches in the town to "rent gym space" searches from trainers.

## Make the name unambiguous

When a brand is also a common word, Google needs extra help deciding that a search means the business. I made the listing's name, category, address, and description agree exactly with the website and the signage, and removed photos on the profile that showed things the gym didn't actually have. Inaccurate photos are a quiet problem: they tell searchers and Google two different stories about the same place.

## Result

While I worked on it, the gym's Business Profile reports showed monthly interactions rising from 269 to 1,019 over about six months. Phone calls went from 7 a month to 56, direction requests from 108 to 754, and website visits from the profile from 153 to 209. In one spring month, Search Console recorded 138 clicks from 3,240 impressions, and the brand plus town search alone brought 40 of those clicks. A new facility was also becoming better known in that period, so I credit the work with removing the confusion rather than with every new member.

## What I'd do the same way today

Start with the name and the facts, then the pages. A listing that matches the real business, a site that answers each audience separately, and monthly numbers the owner can read in a minute are still the core of the job. For gyms, studios, and clinics with more than one location, the next step is a page and a profile per location that clearly belong to one company. See [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

# AI research company: accurate AI answers for job seekers

An AI research company was hiring engineers in Palo Alto and across the Bay Area. Engineers now ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI features who's hiring and what they pay, so the company wanted to know how it showed up in those answers.

A defined AI search visibility audit with recommendations.

- Whether, and how, the company appeared when assistants were asked the questions engineers ask about jobs, employers, and compensation.

# My own consultancy: an AI visibility baseline, with nothing redacted

In October 2026 an agency asked me for a sample AI visibility audit. Every audit I had run belonged to a client under confidentiality, so I ran one on myself. Claude, with live web search, answered sixteen questions a prospect of mine might ask. It found me every time someone asked for me by name, and never when someone asked who to hire.

## The engagement

My own name and sites, measured the way I measure clients: a fixed question set, every answer saved word for word, and a second pass that recorded who was named, my position, the tone, each factual claim about me, and every cited source.

## What I found
- **Branded questions:** named in 3 of 3 answers, with my sites cited in each.
- **Open hiring questions:** named in 0 of 9. The names came from marketplace listing pages, an agency directory, and "best consultants" roundups.
- **How-to questions:** 0 of 4 answers cited any of my guides. Vendor blogs supplied most of the citations.
- **Accuracy:** 46 factual claims about me across the branded answers. Most were right. Four needed action, and every one traced to a page I control.

## Tracing the wrong facts

One answer gave my consultancy the founding year of my earlier agency. The cause was a single sentence on one of my own About pages that named both companies and both years. The assistant kept the first year and attached it to the second company. I split the sentence into two lines, one company and one year each.

Another answer described my sites as a preview that hadn't launched. The source was a public GitHub repository README, still carrying launch instructions written before the site went live. I rewrote it to say the site is live and to point readers to it.

Older figures, a stale Upwork status and job count, came from a profile page on my personal site written two years earlier. A recognition the assistant called unconfirmed, a 2012 Forbes contributor's ranking, turned out to be real: the archived list shows me at number 33. It needed a link, which I added.

## What the gap means

The answer to "Is Chris Abraham a good SEO consultant to hire?" put it plainly: almost everything it found about me was written by me. The sites were crawlable and current. The rest of the web hadn't caught up. That finding sets the program: complete listings on the marketplaces the answers drew from, pitches to the roundups that supplied the hiring names, and independent coverage over the following months. My guide to [earned mentions](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/) describes the outreach side.

## Cost and method

The full run cost $1.88 in API fees and took about fifteen minutes. The same sixteen questions rerun monthly give a trend, and the method is in my guide to [measuring AI share of voice](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/). One engine on one day is a reading. The monthly series is the measure.

## Status

The errors on the sites I build from code were corrected the same day, and the older profile page is next. Outreach follows, and the next run will show whether the open questions start to name me. See [AEO and GEO consulting](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ai-search/) for the same audit on your brand.

# My own podcast: 458 episodes, each with a page of its own

My show, [The Chris Abraham Show](https://thechrisabrahamshow.com/), has published episodes since 2019, and for most of that time it lived only where the platforms put it. On October 8, 2026, I built it a website from its RSS feed with Claude Code. This is the site I point to when someone asks what a podcast website from me looks like, because you can open any page of it right now.

## What the build produced

Claude Code handled the original build described here. For ongoing site work I use OpenAI Codex as well, with the same requirements for stable episode URLs, readable HTML, and a checked build.
- 458 episode pages, one per episode, each at an address recorded once and never changed.
- Full transcripts on 151 episodes, every one the host provides, rendered in the HTML where crawlers can read them.
- A written description for each of more than 230 distinct cover images, done by looking at the art and quoting any words on it.
- PodcastEpisode and Person structured data, a 467-address sitemap, an llms.txt file, and IndexNow notices when pages change.
- An articles section, where episodes that drew a response grow into longer written pieces.

The generator is a single Python file. GitHub Pages hosts the site, Cloudflare handles DNS, and the domain is the only bill.

## It runs every morning

A scheduled GitHub Actions job reads the feed at 9:17 UTC, adds any new episode, picks up transcripts that arrive late, rebuilds, and commits. I record and upload as I always have; the site follows on its own.

## Tags that passed, previews that didn't

On October 14 I audited the social tags on all 469 pages. Every page had complete Open Graph and X card tags, and every image existed at its declared size. The audit still turned up a fault: episode pages offered square cover art inside large preview cards, so Facebook, LinkedIn, and X cropped off the top and bottom of every cover, and more than two hundred episodes shared one default cover and looked identical when shared. I added a generated 1,200 by 630 card for each episode, with the cover beside the episode title. Every one of the 469 pages now offers an image at the size the platforms ask for. The method is in my guide to [social share cards](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/social-share-cards/).

## Corrections, made in public

On one episode I misidentified a car I'd photographed. The episode's page now carries the correction, the photo, and the threads where readers identified it. Articles on the site go through a line-by-line fact-check before they're published, the same one I offer as [fact-checked articles written with AI](https://christopherabraham.com/services/fact-checked-articles/).

## The point

A podcast feed already holds everything a website needs. What keeps the site honest and current is a set of rules the build enforces every day. If you want the same for your show, see [podcast website SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/podcast-website/).

# A serialized novel: 17 years of Movable Type URLs, all kept

This one is my own work, not a client's. A serialized novel I published as a blog from 2005 to 2022 ran on Movable Type 3.33 until its CGI stopped working on the old shared host. I moved it to static HTML on free hosting, and every address the old site ever published still answers.

## Counting what the old site published

Movable Type publishes far more than its entries. Besides 309 chapters, the old site had monthly, weekly, daily, and category archive pages, per entry TrackBack files, three separate feed formats, and an images folder that other sites had linked to for years. I took the list from the database dump and the old web root, not from memory, and it came to 953 URLs.

## Same addresses, not redirects

Where I could, I kept each URL exactly rather than redirecting it. Each chapter carries an explicit permalink matching its original path. The 389 old archive addresses are generated stubs, and the few pages Movable Type left behind after entries moved get redirects. The TrackBack files still answer, minus the spam pings that had piled up in them. All three feed URLs still serve their original formats, and the images keep their paths.

## Cleaner for search than before

The archive pages repeat chapter text, so they are now noindex, follow and left out of the sitemap, and only the chapters and the main pages are indexable. Every chapter got a handwritten title and description, checked by a script. Spelling and typography fixes went into a log, one row per change, so any of them can be undone.

## Cutting over in the right order

The old host also ran the domain's DNS, so canceling hosting would have taken DNS down with it. I moved DNS first, with the old records and the Search Console verification record copied exactly, and only then switched the site. A check script confirmed all 953 URLs, the https and www redirects, and the canonicals before I told Google and Bing.

## The point

A small site gets the same discipline as a large one: count every URL first, keep the ones you can, and redirect the rest. The same approach carried a [medical clinic from WordPress to Next.js](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/). See my [migration services](https://christopherabraham.com/services/migrations/).

# About Christopher Abraham

I'm an independent SEO consultant in Arlington, Virginia, across the Potomac from Washington, DC. I've called the DC area home since college, and I take clients across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand.

## What I'm working on now
- Testing how AI assistants describe businesses and people, and fixing what they get wrong.
- Finding content that JavaScript frameworks hide from crawlers, on React, Next.js, Alpine.js, and headless builds.

## How I got here

My first online home was a text-based conferencing system, and I've kept an account on The WELL, one of the oldest online communities, for decades. That's where my email address comes from. I built my first websites in 1994, hand-coding HTML (with Macromedia Dreamweaver open in the other window) for anyone who asked, including my dad's company, Pacific Rim Productions, as well as urban.net and my own MemeSpace community. My search work began in the directory era, just before Google arrived in 1998, and only on my own projects: I submitted them aggressively to Yahoo, Ask Jeeves, and the other directories people browsed to find anything, and worked to get them talked about on Usenet, message boards, and forums. From 1998 I was also optimizing the pages themselves: titles, meta descriptions, page structure, and the meta keywords tag back when search engines still read it (the story of that tag is in [meta keywords in 2026](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/meta-keywords/)). I didn't do SEO for anyone else until New Media Strategies hired me in 2002. I've worked with open-source content management systems since 1999, starting with on-site blogs in Greymatter and Pyra's tools, Movable Type's Perl scripts, and PHP-Nuke and PostNuke portals, then Plone, Drupal, WordPress, and plenty of platforms that no longer exist.

Before the agencies, I started as the image center administrator at PNI, Picture Network International, part of SRA in Arlington, then became an associate at Rheingold Associates, the virtual community consultancy of Howard Rheingold, a Linux system administrator at Caucus Systems running professional online events, and a builder of websites for clients that included the Treasury Department. In 1996 I was part of the Proxima team, the firm that became Proxicom, that put Owens Corning's Pink Panther online: a 500-screen site with its own discussion community for homeowners, which won the first BOTI award for best website design, as [the firm's archived press release](https://web.archive.org/web/19980117033913/http://www.proxicom.com:80/press/owens.html) records.

In the agency years I was the technology strategist at New Media Strategies, one of the first firms to treat a brand's online reputation as something to manage, and then a senior account supervisor on the interactive team at Edelman's public affairs practice in Washington. In 2006 I developed long-tail blogger outreach: rather than pitching a handful of famous bloggers, my team researched and pitched thousands of niche writers who actually cared about a client's subject, treating it as earned media, closer to public relations than to paid social. In 2007 I co-founded Abraham Harrison, a digital marketing firm that ran search, content, and outreach programs from Washington, Portland, and Berlin. It ran as a fully virtual company before that was normal: two founders and fourteen contractors across the United States, Europe, India, and Africa, spread over ten time zones. Google liked the setup enough to publish [a case study about the firm](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/www.google.com/en//a/help/intl/en/admins/case_studies/pdf/abraham_harrison_cs.pdf), quoting me as president and COO. Later I was team lead for special projects at Reputation.com, working with high-profile individuals on search results that mattered to them.

A word about New Media Strategies, because it shaped everything after. I was employee number 13 there, from 2002 to 2006, in an open-plan former newsroom in a Rosslyn tower, back when word-of-mouth marketing meant joining online communities and becoming a real, contributing member of them for months before a client's name ever came up. The firm grew past 120 people and trained every new hire, me included, as if it were a discretion bootcamp. In 2002 I helped develop the practice that became online reputation management, which I've done in one form or another ever since. I've written the whole story up, tongue firmly in cheek, as ["I was a teenage Russian troll."](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/i-teenage-russian-troll-chris-abraham) I was neither a teenager nor Russian. And yes, working under a nom de guerre is an old habit.

I'm proud to work alongside two firms: as a digital strategist with [Meritus Media](https://meritusmedia.com/), a digital PR and marketing agency, where search, Google Business Profile, and reputation work sit beside the PR, and as a business partner at [Stainless Communications](https://stainlesscommunications.com/), a senior-led brand, PR, web, and growth firm.

My independent practice runs mostly through Upwork and centers on the technical end of search: why a page isn't indexed, why a template hides content from the crawler, why a migration lost traffic, and how a business shows up when someone asks an AI assistant about it.

## What I'm known for
- **Forensics.** I like the cases nobody else could explain. The answer is usually a mechanism: a script that never runs for Googlebot, a canonical pointing at the wrong page, a redirect chain that drops equity at every hop.
- **Working inside messy, inherited sites.** Twenty-year-old WordPress installs, half-finished migrations, themes three developers have patched. I'm comfortable there.
- **Translating between marketers and engineers.** I write tickets developers trust and summaries executives read.
- **Using AI with judgment.** I use AI tools for metadata drafts, topic gap analysis, FAQ coverage, and repository analysis. Every output gets checked by a human who knows what good looks like.

# Technical SEO skills, and the proof for each one

"Technical SEO" on a profile can mean anything from installing a plugin to rebuilding a rendering pipeline. So here's my list, specific enough to check. Every skill below is something I've done on a real site, and wherever I can show it, it links to the case study or guide that proves it. My full career history lives in my [CV on chrisabraham.com](https://chrisabraham.com/cv); this page is the technical inventory.

## Crawling and auditing whole sites
- Full site crawls in Screaming Frog with JavaScript rendering, run in raw and rendered modes and compared, so I can see which content exists only after scripts run.
- Custom extraction with XPath and regex to audit every URL for heading counts, canonicals, robots tags, schema types, and tracking IDs. My [extraction recipes](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/custom-extraction/) are published.
- Near-duplicate detection and multiple H1 audits across entire sites, with a decision per cluster. See [how I find both](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/near-duplicates-and-h1s/).
- XML sitemap audits that compare the file, a crawl, and Search Console, so every listed URL is canonical, indexable, and dated honestly. My checklist is in [XML sitemaps that tell the truth](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/xml-sitemaps/).
- Before-and-after crawl comparisons to prove a fix landed on every URL, described in [proving an SEO fix worked](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prove-seo-fixes/).
- Crawl and index management for a programmatic site of more than 20,000 pages: segmented sitemaps, robots rules for parameter URLs, and baselines per segment. [Programmatic price index](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/card-price-index/).

## JavaScript rendering forensics
- Traced a Magento and Hyvä store's traffic loss to Alpine.js sections that loaded specs, FAQs, and reviews only on scroll, and proved it with crawler extraction counts. [Hidden product content](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/scroll-gated-products/).
- Found 2,000 event pages Google never discovered in a Create React App build, and wrote the 13 page developer spec, ranked P0 to P3, that fixed it. [React event app](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/).
- Diagnosed a consent platform that blocked the script displaying every article, so bots saw empty pages. [Consent banner case](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/consent-banner/).
- Hunted hydration errors sitewide by loading every URL in scripted headless Chrome and collecting console errors by template.

## Working in the code
- Hacked Perl and PHP by the bucketful long before AI coding assistants: Movable Type's Perl CGI scripts, PHP-Nuke and PostNuke portals, and scripts of my own. Reading somebody else's codebase has felt like home ever since.
- Made metadata changes in a client's Sanity and Vercel codebase through a GitHub pull request the developer reviewed and merged, then verified prerendering. [Headless local business](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/headless-local/).
- Read whole repositories with OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to trace a crawl finding to the component or import script that causes it, checking every answer against the live site.
- Built SEO checks into the build of sites I run, so a page with a bad title, a duplicate description, a broken internal link, or borrowed phrasing fails before it publishes. That's how this site is built.
- Turned a podcast RSS feed into a static site that rebuilds itself every day, with a page, share card, and alt text for each of 458 episodes. [Podcast site](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/podcast-site/).
- Automated IndexNow submissions with GitHub Actions, gated on the new sitemap actually being live.
- Built a 12,000 line command line assistant in Python with 140 end-to-end tests, directing Claude Code the way a technical lead directs a team.

## Migrations, redirects, and recovery
- Audited a Squarespace to Shopify move that left 3,400 broken URLs and duplicate product paths, and did the theme schema work. [Shopify cleanup](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/shopify-cleanup/).
- Rebuilt the redirect map for a site that had lived on three platforms over fourteen years, by pulling every URL the Wayback Machine ever captured, testing all 848 against the live site, and redirecting every one that had ever served a page.

- Separated a multi-state brand from its first showroom in schema and on the page, so search engines stopped blurring the two. [Closet locations](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/closet-locations/).
- Fixed a gym whose brand name Google read as an ordinary word, which lifted calls and visits. [Training gym](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/training-gym/).
- Audited how ChatGPT and Perplexity described an AI company's jobs and pay, and planned the fix. [Recruiting answers](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/recruiting-answers/).

- Got my first root access on a Sun SPARCstation running Solaris, the pizza box kind, as the image lab administrator at PNI, Picture Network International.

- Run Google Workspace administration end to end: users, aliases, groups, Gmail routing, Calendar, and Drive sharing.

- Diagnose mail that bounces or lands in spam, and lock down domains that never send mail so nobody can borrow their names, as in [protecting a domain that sends no mail](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/non-sending-domain/).

## Local search and Google Business Profile
- Got a suspended profile reinstated with a documented appeal. [Profile reinstated](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/).

My [video verification checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-video-verification/) is published.
- Build appeals like a legal brief: the most authoritative document first, nothing that exposes private data, and no date claimed that the paperwork doesn't support.

## Data
- Wrote Python pipelines that built an 88,900 contact master list, merged two 28,800 record exports at 94% email coverage, and caught an AI-built tracker inventing its data.

## Strengths that don't fit on a skills list

These are habits, not tools, and they shape every engagement.
- **I keep two problems apart.** When a traffic loss and a spam spike land in the same month, I run them as separate investigations until the evidence connects them, so nobody spends a quarter fixing the wrong thing. It's built into every [technical SEO audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/).
- **I catch AI tools inventing things.** I use AI every day and trust none of it unchecked, which is how I caught an AI-built outreach tracker logging messages to contacts who didn't exist. My guide to [correcting what AI says about you](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/correct-ai-answers/) comes from the same habit.
- **I build a case like a brief.** I captained my high school speech and debate team, and my Google appeals still read that way: the strongest document first, nothing that exposes private information, and no date claimed without paper behind it. That's how a [suspended profile came back](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/).
- **I vet sources for a living.** At Edelman my job included checking online influencers for a genuine, multi-year track record before clients went near them. I bring the same suspicion to every crawl export, vendor dashboard, and confident AI answer.
- **I write for the developer and the owner at once.** The same finding becomes a ranked ticket with acceptance criteria for engineering and a plain summary for the person paying, as in the [13-page spec for a React app](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/).
- **I ship at speed without dropping the checks.** This site went from first commit to 75 pages and more than 50,000 words in a week, built with Claude Code under my direction, and every page passes automated checks for title and description length, duplicate wording, broken links, and voice before it publishes.
- **I've made myself machine readable.** Two decades of publishing under one name, tied together with structured data so search engines and AI tools know the profiles belong to one person. The method is in [two names, one entity](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/two-names-one-entity/).
- **I know how online communities behave from the inside.** I moderate a Reddit community of more than 16,000 runners and have for nine years, and Reddit threads turn up constantly in AI answers. The story is [off the clock](https://christopherabraham.com/about/off-the-clock/).
