# Off the clock

Clients hire me to read crawl data, but it helps to know the fellow reading it. I've been curious about nearly everything for as long as I can remember, and I've never been very good at picking just one thing. Here's the rest of the story, told plainly and with as little bragging as I can manage.

## A Honolulu boyhood

I grew up in Honolulu, in Salt Lake, the neighborhood next to the airport (not the one in Utah, whatever the AI summaries say). I went to Aliamanu Elementary, right there in the neighborhood, from kindergarten through sixth grade, then to Saint Louis School for seventh through twelfth grade, where I somehow ended up student body president while also doing JROTC, the Ranger Club, wrestling, the newspaper, the yearbook, the photography club, and the Bullseye Club. I ran out of high school courses before I ran out of high school, so I took philosophy classes at Chaminade University, which shared the school's campus.

My father was a photographer, and my mother had traveled through Europe and the United States before I came along, so hopping on a plane was simply normal in the Abraham household. Once, when an eruption was announced, my dad pulled me out of elementary school to fly to the Big Island and see it. Tramping around on lava flows at nine years old makes a lasting impression on a kid.

## College, crew, and a year abroad

Washington got me first through Close Up, a summer program on politics for high school students. Then a GW catalog arrived at home in Honolulu with a photo of the crew rowing across a glassy, misty Potomac at dawn, and that was that. I came to Washington for The George Washington University. I started in political science, switched to American literature, and minored in creative writing; I'm told mine was one of the last American literature degrees GW ever granted. I'd never rowed a stroke, but I'd seen [Oxford Blues](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Oxford+Blues+1984+Rob+Lowe&tag=gerris-20) in high school, so naturally I rowed heavyweight crew, was a founding father of the Phi Kappa Psi chapter on campus, hosted a weekly house music and comedy show on WRGW radio, interned in the Washington bureau of The Baltimore Sun, and edited the English department's newsletter.

My adviser, the English professor Robert Combs, steered me toward a year abroad, so midway through I spent a year at the University of East Anglia in Norwich, England, reading postwar American literature. I rowed for UEA too, worked the door as a bouncer at the student nightclub, spent weekends in Paris whenever the budget allowed, and once left class for two weeks to trek the Kathmandu Valley. Then I took a year off before my senior year and went home to Honolulu to work as a commercial photographer, studying French at the University of Hawaiʻi on the side. Later I sold my work as a stock photographer through an agency in New York.

GW Today, the university's news site, once [wrote up some of this story](https://gwtoday.gwu.edu/marketing-online-and-around-world), and I'll admit I still think of old buff and blue every time I get all the cartoons in The New Yorker.

## Languages, mostly attempted

French in Hawaii, German at the Goethe-Institut in Washington and again in Berlin. My German is solidly A2, which is enough to order lunch with confidence and apologize for it fluently. Abraham Harrison, the firm I co-founded, ran for a time from Washington, Portland, and Berlin, so the lessons got real use.

## Online before it was a career

Back when getting online meant a modem and patience, I joined ArtsWire, then The Meta Network, one of Washington's first online communities, then Brainstorms, and The WELL, where I've kept a home ever since; that's why my email ends in well.com. None of it would have happened without my first job out of college: administering the image center at PNI, Picture Network International, part of SRA in Arlington. Down in the basement of the same building worked Metasystems Design Group, which ran The Meta Network at tmn.com and doubled as an internet service provider. That basement is where I met my true mentors, a father and son: [Frank Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_L._Burns) and his son Scott Burns. Frank was a retired Army lieutenant colonel with a Silver Star from Vietnam, widely credited with the "Be All That You Can Be" slogan, and the director of the Army's Task Force Delta, the unconventional brain trust Jon Ronson later wrote about in [The Men Who Stare at Goats](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0743270606?tag=gerris-20). In retirement Frank led Metasystems Design Group, known for the Caucus conferencing software, with Scott beside him building tools for people to think together online, and I later worked in a support role on Frank's New MetaNet. Between the two of them I learned most of what I believe about online community, and a great deal about everything else.

I built websites by hand for anyone who'd let me, including sites for a consulting firm, a production company, the Shadow Conventions, and the Treasury Department, and I worked as a Linux system administrator at Caucus Systems, hosting professional virtual events on its conferencing software.

I also co-taught, with Ginny Little, one of the first fully accredited online high school courses: creative writing for EFA, a magnet program of the Kalamazoo Public Schools in Michigan, with more than sixty students logging in from around the area. The lesson I took from it, and later wrote a column about, is that children naturally want to show what they know. And I became an associate of Howard Rheingold, the author of [The Virtual Community](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0262681218?tag=gerris-20), at Rheingold Associates; [my old team bio is still up](https://rheingold.com/Associates/team_abraham.html), which delights me more than it should.

I published a memetic lexicon at Memes.org, founded MemeSpace, a free online community of more than 800 "memebers" that The New York Times once wrote about, running its first version on Caucus, which its creator, Charles Roth, generously let me use for free, and ran a little online publication called The Caffeinated Magazine. Caucus deserves its own footnote in internet history: Charles Roth conceived and built it at Wayne State University in the early 1980s, then formed Camber-Roth to distribute it, and it went on to power web-based learning, collaborative forums, and a good many of the first virtual communities. I'm happy to be one of the people carrying that story forward. These days I'm the founding moderator of [r/slowjogging](https://www.reddit.com/r/slowjogging/), a Reddit community of more than 16,000 people practicing the gentle, smile-while-you-run method of the late Japanese exercise physiologist Hiroaki Tanaka. After nine years it still has nothing to sell: no coaching funnel, no membership tier, no merchandise. Watching ideas spread and mutate online for as long as I have turns out to be excellent training for understanding how AI assistants pick up and repeat what they read.

>

"I met Chris … as part of my work for Arts Wire, an online network for artists. He was an early adopter of the Web and has context."

Beth Kanter, master trainer and nonprofit innovator in networks, learning, and social media

## Hyperfiction

Before anybody called it electronic literature, I was writing it. I was one of the eight writers of Name is Scibe, a collaborative hyperfiction that Judy Malloy, one of the true pioneers of the form, began on Arts Wire and The WELL. [Her own history of the piece](http://www.judymalloy.net/intaud.html) lists the writers, and [The WELL still hosts the original text](https://people.well.com/user/jmalloy/scibe/), my entries included. Then I led my own: 8: A Collaborative Hypernarrative Fiction, or Collabor8, written over a full year by a group of friends, with each story broken into linked fragments that readers wandered through in their own order. Pieces of it survive as found poems with titles like "Chocolate City," "TheBUS," and "Blue plastic kayaks." Afterward I started Coelaboration, a site for collaborative writing with a featured writer each month and the beginnings of yet another hypernarrative.

It turns out that writing stories as a web of linked pages is decent preparation for a career thinking about how crawlers move through websites.

## Lodge, rite, and parish

I'm a Master Mason at Naval Lodge No. 4 on Capitol Hill, the oldest continuously operating lodge in the District of Columbia, first chartered in 1805. I'm also a 32nd degree Scottish Rite Mason in the Southern Jurisdiction, whose headquarters, the House of the Temple, sits on 16th Street in Washington. Before that I served on the vestry of St. Monica and St. James, an Episcopal parish on Capitol Hill, and, naturally, I ended up as its webmaster too.

## Renaissance Weekend

I've been a member of Renaissance Weekend for many years, though I haven't made it to one in a while: invitation-only, off-the-record gatherings where a physicist, a poet, a senator, and a teenager might share a panel. I've moderated sessions and worn the blue dot. It's the closest thing I know to a polymath's playground, and it's taught me that the best ideas come from people outside your own field.

At one Renaissance Weekend I shared a panel with Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, the two engineers who designed the internet's core protocols. Just those two and me. At others I spent a lot of happy hours with Esther Dyson, the investor and early internet thinker who trained as a backup cosmonaut, in her trademark jeans.

Away from Renaissance Weekend, the early internet has been a small and generous world. Howard Rheingold brought me into his consultancy as an associate, and I once found myself at a house party at Guy Kawasaki's home in Silicon Valley, which is about as Valley as an evening gets.

## Miriam's Kitchen

For years I volunteered as a sous chef at Miriam's Kitchen, which works to end chronic homelessness in Washington. Cooking for guests who deserved a good meal was the most useful work I did all week, nobody in that kitchen cared about my rankings, and I hope to be back at the cutting board one day.

## On the water and on the road

I was a senior member of the Potomac Boat Club, founded in 1869 and one of the oldest rowing clubs in the country, and I may well be again someday. For years I kept my own racing shell, a heavyweight Hudson carbon single, at Thompson Boat Center, and I eventually gave it to the club to join its fleet of training singles, where it can teach somebody else what Oxford Blues taught me. On land I'm a slow jogger, which is exactly as fast as it sounds. If I'm honest, these days it's not enough jogging and plenty of modding.

## Teaching and talking

I've been a guest lecturer at Georgetown, GW, American University, the University of Maryland, the University of Oregon, and Columbia, and I taught blogging and early SEO at The Writer's Center in Bethesda. I've been called on by BBC World Service and CNN Radio to talk about technology and the internet, and I spoke on a panel at South by Southwest.

## Why any of this matters to you

I spent a good part of my career on the bleeding edge: online events before anyone had heard of webinars, hyperfiction before e-lit had a name, memes before they were jokes, reputation management before it was an industry. These days I'm happy on the bleedy edge, early enough to put new tools to work for clients and seasoned enough to know which ones have earned it.

A polymath is a big word for a modest man, so I'll settle for generalist with a specialty. Literature taught me to read closely, photography taught me to notice what's in the frame and what isn't, rowing taught me that nothing moves unless everyone pulls together, and the lodge taught me patience with ritual and process. All of it shows up when I'm looking at your site. Back to the [work side of my story](https://christopherabraham.com/about/), or [say hello](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

Links to books and films on Amazon carry my Amazon Associates tag. As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

# How these pages are written and checked

Everything on this site is published by me, Christopher Abraham, and I'm responsible for every word of it. Here's how the guides, case studies, and service pages are made, so you can decide how much to trust them.

## Written from the work

The case studies describe engagements I worked on myself: the problem, my role, what I found, what was done and by whom, and where it stands. The guides come from the same work. When I explain how to read the Page indexing report or how to lock down a domain that sends no email, it's because I've done it for clients or for my own sites, often in the same week.

## Primary sources for every factual claim

Where a guide states how Google, Bing, a standard, or a protocol behaves, it links to the primary documentation: Google Search Central, Bing Webmaster Guidelines, the W3C's accessibility standards, the RFCs that define email records, and the specifications for files like llms.txt. Those links are listed under "Sources" at the end of each guide, and in the page's structured data as citations. When the official documentation and common practice disagree, I say so.

## How I use AI tools

My workflow is platform agnostic. OpenAI Codex and Claude Code do most of my coding work; I also use GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and sometimes Perplexity for assistance with research, writing, and checking ideas. A tool gets chosen for the task, and I remain responsible for the result.

I use AI assistants the way I'd use a capable junior colleague: to draft outlines and first passes, to check code and markup, and to build and test this site's generator. I don't publish anything they produce until I've read it, corrected it, and checked its claims. Two rules are absolute:
- **Personal and biographical details come only from my own records** and verifiable published sources, never from an AI summary. AI search tools have confidently told the world things about me that aren't true, and none of those get a second life here.
- **Technical claims are checked against primary documentation**, not against what an assistant remembers.

## Clients and confidentiality

Case studies describe clients by industry and problem, never by name, and leave out anything that could identify them: addresses, revenue, account details, and screenshots of private dashboards. Where a client's engagement is ongoing or paused, the case study says so. I don't claim results I can't show, and I don't round up.

## Quotes and testimonials

Quotes from clients and colleagues are reproduced as written, with attribution. Where I've shortened a quote, an ellipsis marks the cut. Upwork figures, such as my Job Success Score and job counts, are copied from my profile with the date they were taken, and the profile itself is linked so anyone can check the current numbers.

## Independence
- No sponsored posts or paid placements, anywhere on the site. The one kind of affiliate link here is my Amazon Associates tag on books and gear, and every page that carries one says so at the bottom.
- Tools and platforms are named because I use them or because clients run on them, not because anyone pays me to mention them.
- The firms I'm affiliated with are named on the About page, so you can weigh any recommendation with that in mind.

## Dates and updates

Every guide shows when it was published and when it was last updated. Search changes quickly, so I revise guides when Google, Bing, or a standard changes, and the updated date moves with the revision. Pages describing my own memberships and activities use past and present tense carefully, and I correct them when something changes.

## Corrections

If you find an error, email [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com) with the page and what's wrong. I'll check it against the source, fix it if you're right, and update the page's date. Significant corrections to a guide are noted on the guide itself.

## Who's behind the site

This is a one-person practice. My background, credentials, and the third-party sources that confirm them are on the [About page](https://christopherabraham.com/about/), and the life behind the work is [off the clock](https://christopherabraham.com/about/off-the-clock/). You can also find me on [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham) and [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chrisabraham), or [get in touch directly](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

# Colophon

Book publishers end a fine edition with a colophon, a few lines on the type, the paper, and the press. Here are the equivalent details for this website.

## Look and type

The design is deliberately plain, after the classic Plone theme: a row of tabs, a breadcrumb trail, and generous black text in Verdana. The CA monogram and the social sharing card were drawn in code with Python and the Pillow imaging library. My name is set in burnt orange, page titles in blue, and section headings in teal, and every one of those colors clears the 4.5 to 1 contrast ratio that accessibility guidelines ask for.

## Under the hood

I now maintain this site with both OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. My wider toolkit includes GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and occasional use of Perplexity; the original build credit below records how the site began.

Each page is a hand-written HTML file with a few lines of metadata on top. A short Python script assembles them into the finished site and generates the extras machines look for: a Markdown version of every page, llms.txt and llms-full.txt, an XML sitemap and a readable one, RSS and Atom feeds, and structured data describing every page, every guide's sources, and me. The script also refuses to publish anything that breaks the house rules, from title length to repeated sentences to any slip into the royal plural.

I built it in a terminal session from a [ThinkPad X220](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Lenovo+ThinkPad+X220&tag=gerris-20), connected over SSH to a DigitalOcean droplet, with Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant, as my collaborator. I decided what the site would say and checked every fact in it; the assistant handled much of the typing. The rules for that collaboration are spelled out in [how these pages are written](https://christopherabraham.com/about/editorial-policy/).

## Where it lives

GitHub Pages serves the static files over HTTPS, and Cloudflare handles DNS. Nothing on the server runs code, which keeps the site fast and leaves nothing to hack. Google Analytics is the one script on the page, with advertising features off and no analytics cookies for visitors in Europe and the UK; the [privacy page](https://christopherabraham.com/privacy/) has the details.

## How it's checked
- Every page read in Lynx, the text-only browser, as described in [the Lynx test](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/lynx-test/).
- PageSpeed Insights scores of 100 for performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO on mobile and desktop, plus 3 of 3 for agentic browsing, as of October 6, 2026.
- Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, with IndexNow notifying Bing whenever a page changes.

## Code and launch

The source is public at [github.com/chrisabraham/christopherabraham](https://github.com/chrisabraham/christopherabraham). The site launched on October 6, 2026, the same day the first line of it was written.

As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

# Hire me

Every engagement follows the same arc: a defined question, a paid audit that answers it, a ranked plan, the fixes, and a verification pass once the fixes are live. Here's how each step works and what I need from you.

## Two ways to hire me
- **On Upwork.** Most of my clients hire me through [my Upwork profile](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham). Engagements there run as fixed price contracts with milestones, and Upwork handles the contract, invoicing, and payment protection for both sides.
- **Directly.** Email [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com) and I'll send a written scope.

## The process
1. **A short conversation.** You tell me the symptom; I ask what changed, when, and who has access to what. A few emails or a [30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) is usually enough.
2. **A written scope.** The questions the audit will answer, what you'll receive, the access I'll need, the timeline, and the price.
3. **The audit.** Crawls, Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools data, rendered HTML, server responses, and whatever else the question calls for. You receive a findings report with the cause, the evidence, and a ranked list of fixes.
4. **The fixes.** I make the changes I have access to, such as metadata, redirects, schema, plugin settings, and Cloudflare rules. For everything that needs a developer, I write tickets with steps and acceptance criteria.
5. **Verification.** Once changes ship, I check the live site, request recrawls where they help, and watch the reports until the trend is clear.

## What I need from you
- Access to Google Search Console and, if you have it, Bing Webmaster Tools. Full user access is ideal; I'll explain why when it matters.
- Read access to analytics, usually GA4.
- A content management login with a role that fits the work, or a staging copy.
- An introduction to whoever deploys code, if that isn't you.
- A named person who answers questions and approves changes.

## Where the work lives

I keep every engagement in writing: Upwork messages, email, or your project tool, whether that's Basecamp, Asana, Jira, or a shared Google Drive folder. Calls are welcome for kickoff and walkthroughs, and each call gets a written follow-up so decisions survive. A written record makes the work easier to review, easier to hand to a developer, and easier to pick up six months later.

## Pricing

I quote every engagement as a fixed fee. Audits are scoped and priced before they start, so you know the cost of an answer before you commit to it. Follow-on work is quoted per milestone on the same basis, and retainers are a fixed monthly fee for an agreed scope, with a report every month. The price is settled in conversation before the work begins, never by a clock.

## What I sell, and what nobody can

I sell expertise, diagnosis, and hands-on work. Rankings, indexing decisions, AI answers, and Google Business Profile reviews belong to the platforms, and each one decides on its own schedule. So I commit to the work and the evidence, and I report honestly on what the platforms do in response.

Questions about time zones, access, and invoicing are answered in the [FAQ](https://christopherabraham.com/faq/). Ready to start? Head to [contact](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

# Frequently asked questions

Practical answers about how an engagement runs. For the overall process, see [Hire Me](https://christopherabraham.com/hire-me/).

### How long does an SEO audit take?

Most audits take one to two weeks from the day I have access. Large sites, sites with many subdomains, or questions that need server logs take longer, and the scope states the timeline up front.

### What do I receive at the end of an audit?

A written findings report: the question, what I examined, what I found, the evidence for each finding, and a prioritized list of fixes with an owner for each one. Developer items come as tickets with acceptance criteria. I walk you through it on a call if you'd like.

### Do I have to hire you through Upwork?

No. Upwork is convenient for many clients because it handles contracts and payments, and that's where my reviews live. You can also hire me directly by email, with payment in advance.

### What access will you need?

Usually Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, GA4, and a login for your content management system. For JavaScript and headless sites, read access to the code repository helps a great deal. I'll list exactly what's needed in the scope.

### Will you change things on my live site?

Only with your approval, and only changes that are in scope. Theme and template work happens on a staging site or a duplicate theme first. Every change I make is logged so you can see what moved and when.

### Can you work with my developer?

Yes, and I prefer it. I write specifications developers can build from, review pull requests when I have repository access, and verify the live result after deployment.

### What time zone do you work in?

US Eastern time. I schedule calls across North America, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, and most of the work happens in writing, so time zones rarely slow a project down.

### How soon will I see results?

Technical fixes can show up in crawl data within days. Indexing changes usually take weeks, and ranking and AI answer changes can take months. I set expectations for each item in the plan and report on them as they move.

### Do you write content?

I write and edit metadata, FAQs, page outlines, and service page copy as part of SEO work, using AI tools for drafts and my own editing for the final version. For a full content program, I can brief and edit your writers.

### Do you offer monthly SEO?

Yes. A [retainer](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-retainer/) covers monitoring, fixes, and reporting each month, billed at the start of the month.

### Do you set up Cloudflare?

Yes, and I recommend it for nearly every site: DNS, caching, and HTTPS through Cloudflare, with the right settings for search engines and AI crawlers. Even the free plan helps, and for WordPress I usually suggest budgeting about $50 a month for its paid features. See [Cloudflare for WordPress](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/cloudflare-wordpress/).

### How do you handle confidential information?

Client details stay private. Case studies on this site describe clients by industry and problem, never by name. I'm happy to sign a nondisclosure agreement, and I've worked under HIPAA terms on a healthcare site.

Something else? Email [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com).

# Privacy

This site runs one script: Google Analytics 4, which tells me roughly how many people visit, which pages they read, and how they found the site. It runs no advertising, no remarketing, and no other tracking.

## Analytics, in detail
- **Advertising features are off for everyone.** Ad storage, ad user data, and ad personalization are all switched off in the site's consent settings, so visits here are never used to target ads.
- **Visitors in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom** get no analytics cookies at all. Google receives only cookieless, aggregate signals from those regions.
- **Visitors elsewhere** get first-party Google Analytics cookies, named `_ga` and `_ga_` followed by an ID, that tell repeat visits apart from new ones. They hold a random identifier, not your name or email.
- Google processes the data under its own privacy policy. I see aggregate reports: page views, rough location by country or city, device type, and referring sites, including AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity.
- **Your browser's privacy signals count.** If it sends Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track, analytics cookies stay off for you wherever you are. Google signals, which ties visits to signed-in Google accounts, is switched off for everyone.

To opt out on every site that uses Google Analytics, install Google's opt-out browser add-on, or block cookies for this site in your browser settings. Everything here works the same with analytics blocked.

## What the host sees

GitHub Pages serves the site. GitHub's servers receive the connecting IP address and the requested page, as every web host does, and may retain those logs for security under GitHub's privacy statement. I can't see them.

## Everything else on the page

Pages, images, and styles all load from this domain. There are no embedded videos, social buttons, third-party fonts, or pixels. Outbound links, such as those to Upwork and Calendly, lead to sites with their own policies.

## Messages and calls

An email, call, or text gives me your address or number and whatever you write. I use it to answer you and, if you hire me, to do the work. It's never sold, shared for marketing, or added to a list. Logins and analytics access granted during an engagement serve that engagement only, and I give them up when it ends or whenever you ask.

## Crawlers

Search engines and AI crawlers may read and cite the public pages, as described in [robots.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/robots.txt). No visitor information goes to them.

## Questions

Write to [cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com) with any privacy question, or to have me delete your past emails with me.

# Internal linking strategy: stitch your website together

You may already have the answer a visitor needs somewhere on your website. The problem is that the page they found never points to it. Internal linking joins those pieces: an explanation to a detailed guide, a guide to a relevant service, a service to the case study that shows the work. I call it stitching together all the pages of your site with text links and targets and anchors.

## Make existing work easier to find

A website accumulates knowledge over years. Articles arrive in the blog, services sit in another section, and older pages disappear from the paths a visitor normally follows. A linking strategy looks across that whole collection and asks which page would help somebody next. That can expose useful connections without commissioning another batch of articles or waiting for another website to link to yours.

## What I examine
- **The destinations that matter:** important services, products, categories, guides, and supporting evidence.
- **Existing routes:** navigation, breadcrumbs, body links, related content, and links generated by templates.
- **Missing connections:** relevant pages with few useful incoming links and pages found in exports but absent from the crawl.
- **The wording:** whether the visible anchor text explains the destination in the sentence around it.
- **The targets:** live canonical URLs, working section anchors, and links still aimed at redirects or retired pages.

## A plan an editor can implement

The deliverable is a source and destination map. Each proposed link names the page where it belongs, the paragraph or section that gives it context, the target URL, and suggested anchor text. I group template work separately from individual editorial additions so your developer and your content editor each get an actionable list. Where authorized, I can make the additions in the CMS or through a reviewed repository change.

## Choose a useful path, then a useful phrase

The link should earn its place in the reader's journey. A page about a missing product description might lead to an explanation of rendering, while a migration checklist might point to a redirect worksheet. The destination decides the wording. Repeating a search phrase across unrelated sentences makes the page harder to read and does not substitute for a relevant connection.

## When the link exists only after interaction

In my [event platform investigation](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/), the way an application exposed its routes affected discovery. That is why a linking review includes the HTML and rendering behavior, not just the words an editor sees. A visible card, a search box, and a normal text link can give crawlers different ways into the same content. I check the actual path.

## Measure the work in two stages

First I verify that the agreed links are present, readable, and aimed at the intended pages or sections. A fresh crawl shows changes to incoming links, discovery, and depth. Then I monitor the destination pages' search observations over an agreed period. The implementation record and the later search results stay separate, so a published link is never reported as a ranking gain before there is evidence.

## Internal linking questions

### Can you work with the pages I already have?

Yes. Existing content is the starting point. If a proposed destination does not answer a useful next question, I flag the content gap rather than forcing a link to an unsuitable page.

### Can this be a focused project?

Yes. A review can cover a particular service, a group of related guides, an ecommerce category, or the whole site. The agreed inventory sets the scope.

My [practical internal linking guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/internal-linking/) includes a planning worksheet. For help with your own pages, [send me the site and the destinations you want people to find](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/). This can also sit inside [sitewide technical SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/sitewide-technical-seo/) or an [ongoing SEO retainer](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-retainer/).

# SEO release QA: check the change before it reaches every page

A developer is ready to release a new template. The staging site looks good. What you need now is someone to check what that change does to search: the content crawlers receive, the URLs they follow, and the signals that tell them what belongs in the index. I can review that release as a defined piece of work.

## When to bring me in

This is useful before a redesign, a CMS upgrade, a new navigation system, a consent banner change, or a move from one rendering approach to another. It also fits a team that has already had an SEO audit and wants an independent check that its developer's implementation meets the brief. There is a specific release to examine, a list of expected changes, and a decision somebody needs to make.

## Agree the test before the release

I start with the pages and behaviors the change could affect. A product template needs product examples, an unavailable product, a category, and a route that should not exist. A navigation change needs the destinations it is supposed to expose. A media move needs the image and document addresses as well as the pages that contain them. The scope says which templates and URL sets will be checked in full and where a sample is appropriate.
- **Content:** the important text, links, and images in the initial response and in the rendered page.
- **Search signals:** titles, canonicals, robots directives, structured data, and the production sitemap.
- **Routing:** expected destinations, redirect behavior, missing pages, and any retired URLs.
- **Dependencies:** content held behind consent, interaction, old hosting, or an account that is about to close.

## What you receive

The deliverable is a release note with the test date, the build or deployment examined, the affected URLs, and a clear result for each agreed check. Failed checks include the observed behavior, the expected behavior, and enough evidence for a developer to reproduce the problem. Items I could not verify are labeled with the access or information needed to finish them. A green result for one template is not silently applied to the rest of the site.

## Why I look beyond the browser

My [consent banner investigation](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/consent-banner/) concerned article content that a normal browser session could show while a nonconsenting crawl could not. In the [event platform case](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/), discovery depended on how the application exposed its links. Those are examples of the gap this review is designed to find: an interface can look finished while an important search behavior is still broken.

## After deployment

I repeat the agreed checks against the public site, since staging cannot show every production redirect, cache rule, or domain setting. The handover separates release acceptance from later search observations. A response can be verified today; recrawling, indexing, and traffic changes need their own dated followup. My guide to [proving an SEO fix worked](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prove-seo-fixes/) explains that second part.

## Questions about a release review

### Can you review a site another developer built?

Yes. I can work from a staging address and the release brief. Repository access helps when a finding needs tracing to a template or component, and any proposed code change can go through your team's normal review.

### Does this replace a complete SEO audit?

The review answers whether the named release meets its agreed search requirements. A broader investigation of an unexplained traffic loss belongs in a separately scoped audit.

For a release involving old images or downloads, start with my [image and PDF migration checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/media-migration/). To arrange a review, [send me the release brief and staging address](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/); scope and terms follow the process on [Hire Me](https://christopherabraham.com/hire-me/).

# Internal linking: stitching your pages into a useful website

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 15, 2026

A visitor arrives on one page. That page can either end the visit or give them a sensible next step into the rest of your work. Internal linking is how individual pages become a website: a connected body of explanations, services, examples, and answers. The opportunities are often already there, waiting for a sentence that joins them.

## Start with the destination, then find its neighbors

Choose a page that deserves to be found: a service with a clear offer, a substantial guide, or a category that helps a buyer narrow the choices. Read it first. Write down which questions it answers and who would benefit from reading it. Then look for other pages where those questions arise naturally.

For example, an article about missing product specifications creates a reason to explain how JavaScript rendering works. A page about moving an old blog creates a reason to visit a redirect guide. The connection follows the subject and the reader's next question. A shared keyword alone is not enough to establish that relationship.

## Use a crawl and a content inventory together

A crawl shows the pages reachable through the paths it followed. A CMS export, sitemap, or approved list of production URLs can expose pages absent from that crawl. Compare the lists and investigate the difference. A page missing from a crawl may be orphaned, blocked, redirected, or simply outside the crawl's settings; the label needs checking before it becomes a task.

Record the pages worth retaining and the destinations visitors should reach from them. The [internal link planning worksheet](https://christopherabraham.com/downloads/internal-link-plan.csv) has columns for source, target, placement, anchor wording, reason, and verification. Its sample addresses are invented. A working copy should describe real paragraphs on real pages, not a list of hoped for keywords.

## Write the sentence before inserting the link

A useful editing test is to read the paragraph aloud with the link treated as ordinary text. Does the sentence still make sense? Does the phrase describe what somebody will find? If the destination takes a whole explanation to justify, move the link to a place where the subject is already being discussed.

Google's link guidance favors descriptive, concise, relevant anchor text and contextual connections between pages. It does not prescribe a magic number of links. In practice, I look for an actual reason for every addition. The destination's topic matters more than fitting an exact phrase into every sentence.
| Where the reader is | A useful next destination | Possible anchor wording |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A migration overview | A detailed media move checklist | check images and PDFs before retiring the old host |
| A service description | A relevant account of completed work | how the event links investigation unfolded |
| A diagnostic guide | A service that handles the same problem | independent SEO review of the release |
| A long reference page | A specific section of another guide | the section on checking destination URLs |

## Give anchors real targets

The word anchor can mean the text someone clicks, or a named section inside a page. Both deserve attention. A link to a whole page should point to the intended production URL. A section link adds a fragment such as `#checking-destinations`, which should match an actual element ID on that destination.

A section link helps someone arrive at the relevant part of a long document. It does not create a separate article. Keep the identifier stable when a heading is edited, and check it after a template or CMS change. A working page address with a missing fragment can still drop the visitor at the top, far from the promised answer.

## Check the markup and the route

Google's crawlable link examples use anchor elements with valid `href` values. Inspect what your template emits, especially when navigation depends on JavaScript. A card that reacts to a click can look like a link without providing the same route in the HTML. The [repository guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-in-your-repository/) explains how to trace that behavior back to the component.

Follow each proposed destination and record its final address. Avoid sending a new link through an old redirect when the final page is known. Check that the destination is the intended version and that its indexing signals agree with its role. Adding more routes to an accidental duplicate only adds another problem to untangle.

## Keep hubs and editorial links doing useful jobs

A hub gives people an overview of related material. A contextual link helps at the moment a particular question arises. They can support each other: a clear index introduces the topic, while the detailed pages provide the next connections. The [topic cluster guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/topic-clusters/) covers choosing distinct questions for those pages.

For a shop, think about routes between categories, subcategories, and products as well as editorial content. Google's ecommerce structure guidance discusses linking through that hierarchy. The practical question is whether a shopper can navigate to the relevant item without having to guess the phrase your search box expects.

## Verify additions before reporting results

Keep a before-and-after record of the changed source pages. Check that the links appear in the agreed locations, open their destinations, and land at the expected sections. Crawl again with comparable settings to inspect incoming links and changes to discovery. If you changed a shared component, sample its different uses rather than assuming one good page represents them all.

After the links are live, watch the destination pages over time and keep other changes in the record. Discovery and a successful fetch can be observed separately from indexing or traffic. This makes the result useful even when search takes time to respond, because the team can see exactly which connections were added.

I offer [internal linking strategy and implementation](https://christopherabraham.com/services/internal-linking/) as a focused engagement. A good first brief is the site address, the pages that matter most to the business, and the parts of the archive that visitors rarely find.

# Moving a website? Check its images and PDFs before closing the old host

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 15, 2026

A website can finish its move while its pictures are still living in the old house. Every article loads, the new domain works, and the migration looks complete until somebody cancels the previous hosting account. Then the photos, brochures, and link previews disappear together. Media deserves its own inventory and its own acceptance check.

## Make a second list for files

The familiar migration spreadsheet maps old pages to new pages. Add a separate sheet for images, documents, and other files. Google's site move guidance explicitly includes hosted images and downloads in the move. That matters because a page address and the files used by that page can belong to different servers, accounts, and caching systems.

Start with the old site's crawl, the media library or storage export, and any list of downloads linked from the content. Include files referenced in templates as well as files an editor inserted into an article. A crawl of visible links alone may miss a social image declared in metadata or an alternative image used on a narrow screen.

I provide a [media migration inventory worksheet in CSV format](https://christopherabraham.com/downloads/media-migration-inventory.csv). Its example rows are fictional. Replace them with the old file address, its new destination, the page that uses it, and the checks that establish whether the move is complete. Keep the worksheet private if the real inventory contains unpublished documents.

## Record what the file is supposed to be

A successful request does not prove the file is right. An image URL can return an HTML error page with a successful status. A brochure link can open a different brochure from three years earlier. Record the expected file type and, where useful, its dimensions, page count, or another detail that distinguishes it from a placeholder.
| Item | Check | Evidence to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Article image | The intended image opens at the new address. | Response type, dimensions, and a visual check. |
| PDF download | The document opens and contains the expected version. | Document title, version date, and referring page. |
| Share card | The page points to the correct public image. | Metadata URL, image size, and a preview check. |
| Responsive image | Each offered image variant can still be fetched. | The complete source set and its destinations. |

## Separate copying from updating references

There are two jobs. First, put the intended files somewhere the new site controls. Second, change the references that still ask for them at the previous location. Finishing the first does not finish the second. Search the repository or exported content for the retiring hostname, upload directory, and media delivery domain. Include any encoded versions your content system stores.

Look at image elements, responsive source sets, CSS backgrounds, document links, structured data, Open Graph images, and social card metadata. Check generated pages as well as source files: an import script may keep rebuilding the old addresses after a manual correction. Google's image guidance describes how standard image markup helps discovery; this inventory also checks whether that markup reaches a surviving file.

## Decide what happens at the old address

If the media URL changes, decide how visitors and existing links should reach the replacement. For a permanent move, Google's redirect guidance favors a permanent server redirect where possible. Map a file to its actual replacement rather than sending every missing image or download to the home page. A replacement page is a different thing from the image or document a browser requested.

Write down who controls the old hostname and how its redirects will be served after the old application closes. A redirect rule inside an account you are about to cancel will not provide continuity. If a particular hosting plan cannot keep those addresses working, resolve that limitation while the old service is still available.

## Check original artwork before resizing

A technically valid social card can still crop a face, stretch a square cover, or replace distinctive original artwork with a generic image. Compare the new card with the original. Decide whether the image should fill its frame or sit inside it with space around it, then inspect the result at the size a person will see. The [social share card guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/social-share-cards/) covers the metadata and preview side.

When a source file is small, record that fact instead of treating an enlarged copy as a new high-resolution original. Keep the source and the transformed output separately. That makes a later correction possible without downloading an already compressed derivative and processing it again.

## Test the dependency you intend to remove

Before shutting anything down, use a controlled test to find requests to the old media host. A developer can block that hostname locally in a test browser and load representative pages on the new site. Compare the network requests with the inventory. This is a diagnostic exercise in a test session, not a request to change public DNS or interrupt the live service.

Repeat it for a short article, an image heavy page, a page with a PDF, and a link shared on a social platform. Then run the wider crawl to find exceptions outside the sample. A cached picture in one browser is weak evidence that an external dependency has gone.

## Sign off the files as well as the pages

Close each inventory row with the destination checked, the references updated, the old address decision recorded, and any unresolved exception assigned to a person. Keep the date and the deployment being tested. That gives the owner a concrete basis for deciding when the old hosting can be retired.

My [clinic migration case study](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/) describes repository analysis that exposed references to the previous media library. I can review this part of your move through [migration oversight](https://christopherabraham.com/services/migrations/) or a focused [SEO release QA review](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-release-qa/).

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Website inquiry audits: find where contacts go missing

If the website seems busy but the inbox is quiet, more traffic may be the wrong first purchase. I test how a prospective customer reaches you, what happens to the submission, and whether your reporting describes that journey accurately.

## The problems this investigation addresses

A service button that opens the wrong form. A scheduler that no longer accepts bookings. A success message without a delivered notification. An analytics event that fires on every attempt, including failed validation. These are concrete defects that can obscure the value of your search traffic.

This service sits between a website review and a measurement audit. It is useful after a redesign, a form plugin change, a new booking provider, or a sudden disagreement between reported conversions and actual contacts. I begin with the affected routes rather than asking you to rebuild the whole website.

## What I test
- Priority landing pages and their contact, quote, or appointment buttons.
- The chosen form or scheduling destination, including mobile usability and required fields.
- Successful submissions, validation failures, and the confirmation experience.
- The resulting message or record in the systems you authorize me to inspect.
- The analytics event definition and whether overlapping triggers inflate the count.
- Consent behavior and whether identifying form data is being passed into analytics.

## What the delivery contains

You receive a route inventory and a test log with dates, observed behavior, and evidence for each finding. Every issue states the expected result, the actual result, its likely owner, and the next repair or diagnostic step. I distinguish confirmed failures from parts of the journey that remain unverified because access is unavailable.

The repair plan starts with contacts that cannot reach the business, followed by incorrect destinations and misleading measurement. Within agreed access, I can correct links, page copy, and supported website settings. Provider changes or custom integrations may need your developer or administrator. I write the acceptance criteria and retest the affected route when the repair is ready.

## How the scope is agreed

The starting engagement is a paid diagnostic for a named set of pages, forms, and destinations. I need the affected URLs, a receiving contact who can confirm labeled tests, and access to relevant reporting. Any live test is coordinated so it does not get mistaken for a customer request. Payment and booking commitments require a supported test route.

This is a focused website investigation. A larger CRM implementation, sales process redesign, or mail infrastructure repair can be identified as follow-on work with its own scope. I do not promise a particular number of leads. The immediate outcome is evidence about whether the agreed routes work and what your reported conversions mean.

## Before commissioning the audit

### Will this explain every difference between analytics and the inbox?

No single test can establish that. Consent choices, filtering, time windows, and multiple routes can create legitimate differences. I identify the causes supported by the available evidence and state which questions remain open.

### Can you test an external booking tool?

Yes, where the provider and your access allow it. I follow the handoff and confirm the resulting record, or document the point beyond which verification requires the provider's help.

For a self-directed starting point, use my [guide to testing website inquiries](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/test-website-inquiries/). Broader reporting problems belong with [Search Console and GA4 work](https://christopherabraham.com/services/search-console/).

# Your website form says success. Did anyone get the inquiry?

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 20, 2026

A visitor can press Send, see a reassuring message, and still fail to reach your business. Conversely, a real inquiry can arrive without appearing in your analytics report. Before treating a shortage of leads as a search problem, test the entire contact route and write down where the evidence stops.

## Choose one journey and agree on the test

Begin with a landing page that matters commercially. Follow its contact button as an ordinary visitor would, using a phone as well as a desktop when possible. Include any intermediate service page, embedded scheduler, or external booking screen. A homepage contact link may work while the button on a course or product page points to an obsolete destination.

Tell the person receiving inquiries that a test is coming. Use clearly labeled test content and an address you control. Agree whether the test may create a CRM record or trigger an automatic reply. If the route creates a paid reservation or another commitment, use the provider's supported test environment or stop before that action. Testing should produce identifiable evidence without confusing staff or customers.

## Distinguish five different events

A useful investigation separates the stages that dashboards often collapse into one conversion:
1. **Contact intent:** the visitor follows a contact or booking link.
2. **Submission attempt:** the visitor presses the form's submit button.
3. **Accepted request:** the form system confirms that it has accepted the information.
4. **Business delivery:** the intended inbox or CRM receives a usable record.
5. **Qualified conversation:** staff confirms that the inquiry is relevant and can be followed up.

These events need different evidence. A button click proves interest in a route, not that a message arrived. A confirmation screen alone does not prove inbox delivery. A delivered message is not automatically a sale. Name the stage in the report so nobody mistakes a convenient measurement for the business outcome.

## Check the visitor experience before inspecting tags

Look for the defects a customer encounters: the wrong form, a missing service option, a keyboard covering a required field, validation that clears the message, or a confirmation with no explanation of what happens next. Verify the destination of each priority call to action. Repeated buttons may share styling while leading to different places.

Try a deliberate validation failure as well as a successful submission. Leaving a required field empty should not produce the same success event as a completed request. Refresh the confirmation page and revisit it directly. If either action adds another apparent inquiry, the report may be counting page visits rather than accepted submissions. Record the behavior before changing the setup.

## Follow the message into the business

Record the submission time and check the form provider's record where available. Ask the recipient to confirm arrival in the expected inbox, not just in a forwarding account or spam folder. Check that the reply address works and that the message includes the context needed to respond. A notification without a usable sender or service reference can leave staff unable to help.

For a CRM connection, verify the actual record and assignment. An integration can accept a submission yet fail to assign it to the current owner. For an external scheduler, inspect the confirmed appointment in the scheduling system. Treat mail delivery, integration delivery, and notification delivery as separate checks whenever they are separate systems.

If something fails, preserve the test reference and the available error evidence. The next fix might belong to the website, mail service, form provider, or CRM administrator. Repeatedly changing SEO metadata will not repair a broken delivery connection.

## Check what analytics actually records

Observe the test in your analytics debugging tools and compare it with the business record. Document what triggers the event: a click, a browser callback, an accepted response, or a confirmation view. Pick one primary success definition for the route and check that a single submission does not count several times through overlapping tags.

Repeat under the consent choices your site offers. A customer may successfully contact you while analytics remains unavailable. Keep consent behavior intact and explain the resulting measurement limit. Do not force a match between inbox totals and recorded analytics events by ignoring visitors' choices.

Keep names, email addresses, message text, and other identifying details out of analytics events and URLs sent to analytics. Google's [guidance on avoiding personally identifiable information](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/6366371) describes this requirement. Use a nonpersonal form label or service category when appropriate, and inspect the payload rather than assuming a plugin is configured correctly.

## Keep a small evidence sheet

For each tested route, record the starting URL, destination, device, time, consent state, expected recipient, observed confirmation, actual receipt, and analytics behavior. Add a status such as passed, failed, or unverified. Use unverified when you lack access to a system; a missing permission is not proof that the system failed.

Retest the failed route after its repair with another labeled submission. Include at least one unsuccessful attempt to confirm that validation no longer produces a false success. Save the outcome and tell the receiving team which test records can be removed. Repeat the essential checks after a redesign, form replacement, or change of destination.

## Decide whether the next problem is visibility or follow-up

Once delivery works, review a suitable period of actual inquiries with the business owner. Separate spam, duplicate contacts, unsupported requests, and suitable prospects. If suitable inquiries arrive but remain unanswered, the bottleneck is follow-up. If the route works but relevant visitors rarely reach it, investigate the landing pages and search visibility. The diagnosis should determine the work.

I offer a [website inquiry audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/inquiry-path-audit/) for this investigation, with a defined route list and written findings. If the evidence instead points toward discovery or indexing, a [technical SEO audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/) is the next useful step.

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Spam link spikes and the disavow file: when to act at all

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

Sooner or later a backlink tool shows a chart with a cliff in it: hundreds of new links in a month from domains nobody recognizes, scraped directories, foreign casino pages, and strings of nonsense. The instinct is to fight back with a disavow file. Usually the right response is to write the spike down, check one or two things, and leave it alone. Sometimes it isn't, and the difference matters.

## What Google does with junk links

Since the Penguin 4.0 update in 2016, Google has treated most manipulative links by discounting them rather than punishing the site they point to. Its people have repeated the point for years. In April 2024 John Mueller said Google ignores link spam and that links pointing at pages returning 404 count for nothing at all. In April 2025, speaking at a Search Central event, he went further: Google has no internal concept of "toxic backlinks," the disavow tool is not routine maintenance, and he would reach for it only with a manual action in hand.

Google's own help page for the tool says the same thing in drier language. Most sites don't need it. It is meant for a site with a considerable number of spammy, artificial, or low quality links that have caused a manual action or are likely to cause one. And it is labeled an advanced feature, because a careless file can hurt a site's performance in search.

## Why spikes look scarier than they are

Third party backlink tools count everything they find, and they find a lot of garbage. Scraper sites copy pages wholesale with the links intact. Automated directories list every domain they can reach. Spam networks link to well known sites to look legitimate. None of that was your doing, and Google has had about two decades of practice ignoring it. A "toxicity" score in a commercial tool is that tool's opinion, built on its own crawl, and Google doesn't share it.

Spikes also coincide with real traffic losses often enough to be framed for them. This year a client's tool showed close to nine times the usual monthly count of new referring links in the same weeks that branded searches fell. The links were real and ugly. They were also not the only thing that changed that month, so they went into the investigation as one hypothesis with a test, rather than as the answer.

## When a spike deserves attention
- **Search Console shows a manual action** for unnatural links to your site. This is the case the tool was built for.
- **Someone bought links in your name.** A previous agency, an old owner, or an overeager employee paid for placements, link exchanges, or private blog network posts. Google's spam policies treat those as link schemes whoever arranged them.
- **The pattern is targeted.** Hundreds of exact match commercial anchors pointing at one money page look like an attempt to trip a filter, which is different from random scraper noise.
- **The links point at real pages and the timing fits a loss** that survives every other test. Even then, the disavow is a contained experiment, not a cure.

If none of those apply, record the spike with its dates and sources in your SEO log, keep an eye on Search Console, and spend the hours on something that moves rankings.

## Build the file from Google's data first

Start with the Links report in Search Console, which shows the linking sites Google itself knows about, and use third party exports only to fill gaps. Review the list by domain, not by URL, and sort it into three piles: plainly manipulative, plainly fine, and unsure. Only the first pile goes in the file. The unsure pile stays out, because a wrongly disavowed link from a real publication throws away value you can't easily get back.

Before disavowing a link you arranged, try to get it removed. Google asks for that first, and if you're filing a reconsideration request after a manual action, documented removal attempts are part of a credible case.

## The file format, exactly
- A plain text file with a `.txt` extension, encoded in UTF-8 or 7-bit ASCII.
- One entry per line: a full URL, or a whole domain written as `domain:example.com`. Subfolders can't be disavowed on their own.
- Lines starting with `#` are comments and are ignored. Use them to date each batch and note why it's there.
- At most 100,000 lines, comments and blank lines included, and 2 MB. Each URL can be up to 2,048 characters.

```
# Reviewed 2026-10-24: paid placements from a former vendor, removal requests unanswered
domain:cheap-article-network.example
domain:spun-directory.example
# A single page on an otherwise legitimate site
https://news.example/sponsored/old-placement.html
```

## Uploading, replacing, and undoing

Only a property owner can upload, and the tool works with URL prefix properties, not Domain properties, so verify the right one first. A list applies to that property and its child properties, and the http and https versions need their own lists. Each upload replaces the previous file entirely, so always edit the current file rather than uploading a fresh one with only new entries; errors are flagged immediately and leave the old list in place. A button cancels every disavowal for the property. Google says changes in either direction take a few weeks, and disavowed links keep appearing in the Links report afterward, which surprises everyone the first time.

## Mistakes I clean up
- **Disavowing the whole export.** Someone uploads a tool's full "toxic" list and quietly throws away links from local news, suppliers, and universities.
- **Losing the old file.** A new upload replaces the old one, so years of careful entries vanish when someone starts over.
- **Forgetting a migration.** The old domain's file doesn't follow the site to a new domain or protocol.
- **Treating disavow as the fix for a traffic drop** while the real cause sits in templates, indexing, or redirects.

## How I handle link reviews

I don't sell link building, for reasons I explain in [why I turn down backlink work](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/buying-backlinks/), and I don't sell disavow files by the thousand lines. I review the profile against Search Console's data, keep the file conservative, and treat links as one hypothesis among several, as in [the clinic migration](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/), where I rebuilt an inherited file to keep legitimate domains. If a spike landed in the same month as a traffic loss, start with a [technical SEO audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/) that finds the cause before anyone uploads anything.

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# AI visibility: what the answer engines say about your business, and how to change it

For buying searches, the first thing a customer reads is increasingly a paragraph written by a machine. In August 2026, Google showed an AI Overview for 88% of the 400 US commercial keywords Semrush tracks, close to double its share a year earlier, according to [Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-nearly-double-commercial-keywords-498078). I find out what those paragraphs say about you, fix the sources they draw on, and report on them every month.

## Why the answer gets it wrong

An AI answer is assembled from whatever the system can find and cross-check: your website, your Google Business Profile, directory listings, reviews, and what other sites say about you. When those sources disagree on your name, address, services, or hours, the system picks whichever version it can corroborate, and that is often a competitor's. "Best," "near me," and "which should I choose" searches have shifted the most, and those are the searches where a customer makes up their mind.

## Three ways to work with me

### 1. AI Visibility Audit: $750, fixed price

I run the searches that bring you business through Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini and record every answer: correct, wrong, missing, or naming a rival. Then I compare your name, address, phone, and services across your site, your Business Profile, and the main directories. You receive a written report with each fix ranked by impact. You own it, and any developer or agency can act on it.

### 2. The Claim Sprint: $1,500, fixed price

The sprint repairs what the audit finds, in two layers.
- The technical base: a full crawl, a Search Console review, titles and meta descriptions, and broken links and redirects.
- The claim layer: entity schema with sameAs links, an llms.txt file, one canonical page that explains what the business is, and FAQ markup, so an assistant has something precise to quote.

Changes I can make directly, I make. Anything inside your developer's codebase reaches them as a ticket with the exact change and a way to check it, the same way I work on [release QA](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-release-qa/).

### 3. AI Presence, Measured: $500 a month

Answers move. A competitor publishes, a directory updates, and the assistant that recommended you in March names somebody else by June. Each month I rerun your search set across Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, and Perplexity and send a short written report: what moved, what the answers say now, and the next fix.

## Where it's already running
- A fireworks retailer with several locations: a baseline, then monthly measurement across Google Search, Maps, ChatGPT, and Perplexity.
- A therapy practice: the complete audit, with every listing checked against what the assistants read.
- A media company: the claim layer itself, with entity schema, llms.txt, an explainer page, and a baseline.

For the method behind it, see [measuring AI share of voice](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/) and my own [AI visibility baseline](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/ai-visibility-baseline/), published with the unflattering numbers.

# The Machine Answers First Now

*A field note from the SEO work*

I have done search work long enough to remember when the whole job was ten blue links and an argument about their order. That world is gone, and I do not think it is coming back. When somebody searches for a business like yours now, the first thing they meet is a paragraph, written by a machine, in a confident tone, before a single link appears.

The numbers caught up with what I was already seeing. [Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-nearly-double-commercial-keywords-498078), reporting Semrush's tracking of 400 US desktop commercial keywords, found Google's AI Overviews on 88% of them in August 2026. That is nearly double the share those answers held in September 2025. In the space of a year, the machine's answer went from an experiment to the front of the line.

## What I keep seeing in the work

The answer on top is assembled from parts. The machine gathers what it can find about a business—its website, its Google Business Profile, its directory listings, reviews, stray mentions—and it trusts whatever agrees with itself. Then it summarizes. Here is what that looks like from where I sit:

A multi-location retailer I work with needs to be the named answer in four different towns, for four different stores, and the facts for those stores have to be right town by town. A therapy practice I audited had its name, address, and phone number disagreeing with each other across the very sources the machines read first, so the machines hedged, and hedging means somebody else gets named. A media company found that its own name was being patiently explained to the world by everyone except the company itself.

Bad websites were missing from that list; the websites were mostly fine. The problem is that a business no longer speaks with one voice in one place. It speaks in fragments, scattered across a decade of listings, profiles, and pages, and the machine is the first reader who ever tried to hear all of it at once. It believes the fragments that agree. It discards the ones that don't. Sometimes the fragment it discards is your phone number.

## You do not get to opt out of being summarized

Owners tell me they want nothing to do with AI. I understand the sentiment. The AI writes about them anyway. The answer about their business exists today, in production, in front of their customers, whether or not anyone at the business has ever read it. Being summarized has become a condition of being findable at all.

The only choice on the table is whether the summary is accurate—whether it names you, describes what you actually do, and cites your pages as the source. That is a choice you make by tending the record, or one that gets made for you by whoever's record is tidier.

## Claim it, then measure it

The fix is unglamorous. First, you claim your entity: one canonical account of what the business is, stated on your own site, tied together with entity schema and sameAs links, an llms.txt file for the machines that read those, and a page that answers "what is this business" so plainly that a summarizer can quote it instead of improvising. Second, you fix the disagreements: the listings, the profile, and the site telling one story. Third—and this is the part almost nobody does—you measure. AI answers drift. A competitor publishes, a directory changes, and the answer that named you in the spring names someone else by summer. So the money questions get re-asked every month, and the changes get written down.

That is the work I sell, and I sell it in pieces so you can stop wherever it stops making sense: an AI Visibility Audit for $750 that tells you exactly what the answers say about you today, a Claim Sprint for $1,500 that fixes the layer underneath, and AI Presence, Measured at $500 a month for the receipt that keeps it true.

## Let's have a chat about it

If you have never actually read what the machine says about your business, you are flying on instruments somebody else set. Let's have a chat about it. I can help. Thirty minutes, bring your website and the searches you wish you won: [book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30).
