# Reading the new Google Business Profile performance reports

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

Google is testing a rebuilt Performance section inside Google Business Profile, with an Overview that leads with recommendations and separate sections for Engagement, Reviews, Audience, and Search trends. The test arrived about a day after Google launched its new Business Home portal, and it changes what an owner should look at first. I covered the announcement in [my weblog post on the rebuilt scoreboard](https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/google-rebuilds-the-scoreboard.html) and promised a full guide to reading the new reports. This is that guide, section by section, in the order I read them myself.

## First, check whether you have it

Open your Business Profile and choose Performance. If the page opens with recommendations and the five new section names, your account is in the test and everything below applies to the screens in front of you. If it still shows the familiar single page of totals and charts, you are on the old reports and nothing is wrong with your account.

The rollout is gradual and account by account. Search Engine Roundtable reported the test on October 23, 2026, after Jaikishan Raturi of Wisevu and Syed Amir shared screenshots and video of their accounts, and noted that Barry Schwartz did not yet have it in his own account that day. There is no setting to request and no form to submit. While you wait, capture one screenshot of your old totals as a baseline. Old and new figures may not line up neatly, and a saved baseline settles arguments that memory always loses.

## Overview: start with the recommendations

The Overview is the summary screen, and its most useful addition sits at the top: a short list of recommendations drawn from your profile's completeness and recent performance. Read that list before any chart on the page. It is Google's own prioritised worklist for this profile, and it tells you what the platform currently thinks is unfinished, stale, or worth confirming.

A new recommendation usually means one of two things: Google changed what it wants from profiles, or your details drifted out of date as hours, services, and attributes changed in the real business. A recommendation that disappears means the gap it named has closed. Work the list from the top, but verify every item against the business itself before accepting it. A recommendation is a prompt, not an order, and the owner who knows the shop floor outranks the algorithm's guess. Where a suggestion is wrong for your business, decline it and move on with a clear conscience.

## Engagement: actions, counted honestly

Engagement gathers the actions people took from your profile: the calls, messages, direction requests, website visits, and bookings your listing produced. Look first at the direction of the totals across a whole quarter rather than any single week. Local demand moves with weather, holidays, school terms, and road works, and a quarter smooths most of that noise into a line you can actually read.

A rise means more searchers reached the point of acting, which is the only point that pays. A fall means less until you have run the interpretation check two sections below, because some of those actions now happen somewhere else. Before blaming the market, compare each action against the channel that receives it. If calls fall, ring the number on your own profile and confirm it connects to the right desk. Broken plumbing hides inside report totals far more often than lost demand does, and it is cheaper to fix.

## Reviews: read below the star rating

The Reviews section breaks the detail out instead of compressing everything into one average: how many reviews arrived, how the ratings spread, and the words themselves, close enough to read in place. Look first at the distribution and the pace. Ten reviews carrying two furious outliers tell a different story than a smooth average suggests, and a steady trickle of recent reviews outweighs a proud total gathered years ago.

Then read the text as field research. A cluster of new reviews after a menu change, a hire, or a remodel is your customers writing the changelog. Phrases that repeat across reviews are the phrases the next searcher will meet, so note them exactly. Answer every review briefly and without argument, especially the unfair ones, because the reply is written for the reader who comes after. Then fix the operational thing the complaints repeat. Owners tend to read reviews as reputation. Read them as the cheapest customer research you will ever be handed.

## Audience: who is finding you

Audience gathers the people behind the views into one place, so you can see who the profile reaches instead of guessing from the totals. Look first for a match or a mismatch: whether the audience arriving looks like the customers you actually want to serve. A profile can be busy and wrong at the same time, and busy wrongness still costs you the hours spent answering it.

A widening audience after a new service, a move, or a name change usually means the profile started matching new searches, which is growth you can plan around. A narrowing one can mean a competitor opened closer to your best customers, which is a different problem entirely. Hold the audience picture next to your service list and your service area. If strangers keep arriving for something you do not sell, your categories or services are promising it on your behalf. Correct the listing before you correct the customers.

## Search trends: the customer's own words

Search trends shows the searches that led people to your profile and how those searches are moving over time. Look first at rising terms you did not plan for, and at your core money terms if they start slipping down the list. Both ends of that movement are instructions, one about what to add and one about what to defend.

Searchers rename things before businesses do. When a trade term gives way to a plain phrase, the market is rewriting your signage in its own vocabulary, and the profile that answers in that vocabulary wins the next visit. Mirror the winning words in your services, your business description, and the local pages of your website, spelled the way customers spell them. Retire the phrases nobody types anymore, however fond the founder remains of them. Sentiment is not a search strategy.

## Falling interactions are not falling demand

The old reports trained owners to treat every interaction as demand arriving at the door. That link is weakening. AI answers now resolve questions that used to end with a tap on your profile: the hours, the price range, whether you stock the thing, whether people rate you well. The customer still buys. The tap just happens inside the answer instead, or never happens at all.

An October 2026 analysis of three American florists found profile interactions down 26 percent year over year, with website clicks down 30 percent, calls down 21 percent, and direction requests down 15 percent, while the shops traded on. Three shops make a small sample, so treat those figures as a direction rather than a measurement of your market. Still, the direction matches what I see across accounts: when interactions fall while revenue holds, demand did not vanish. The answer moved upstream. Your job shifts from winning the tap to being the business the answer names, which is why I track [AI share of voice](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/) alongside these reports every month. Never judge a month by interactions alone again.

## A monthly routine that takes twenty minutes

Pick one morning a month and give the reports twenty honest minutes, in this order. First, the Overview, clearing or consciously declining each recommendation. Second, Engagement, comparing the month with the month before and with the same month last year. Third, Reviews: the count, the average, the pace, and the three phrases customers repeated most. Fourth, Audience, in a single line about whether the people arriving are the people you want. Fifth, Search trends, choosing one rising term to adopt and one fading term to retire.

Write those five lines down in the same place every month. Reports reward memory, and a profile read monthly for a year teaches more than any single deep dive performed in a panic. End the routine by choosing exactly one action for the month ahead. A reading that produces nine worries produces none of the fixes, and the reports will be there next month to grade the one you picked.

## Mistakes owners make with the old reports

Most of these will survive the redesign, so retire them now. Judging by days, and reading one rainy Tuesday as a trend. Comparing December with January and calling the difference decline. Chasing views, and celebrating impressions while calls and bookings quietly thin out. Treating a drop in calls as lost customers before checking the AI answers, the phone number, and the calendar for an explanation. Never capturing a baseline, so every redesign leaves the owner arguing with a memory. And reading the reports only when something already feels wrong, which guarantees the numbers arrive attached to a bad mood and get believed for the wrong reasons.

## Where I fit

Reading these reports well is judgement work, and it sits inside the [local search work](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/) I do for clients: profile upkeep, a steady review rhythm, and a monthly read of what Google and the AI answers are telling the market about a business. If the new layout has reached your account and you want the first read done properly, [book a thirty minute call on my calendar](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) and bring your Performance screen with you. I will read it with you from the top, and you will leave knowing which numbers deserve action and which deserve a shrug. If you would rather start in writing, [write to me through the contact page](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/) and tell me what your reports have been doing.

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Google Business Profile video verification: plan the take before you press record

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

For a lot of businesses, the only verification option Google offers now is a video recorded on a phone. It looks easy, and it fails for reasons that are easy to avoid: the street wasn't clear, the sign didn't match the profile, or nothing on screen proved the person filming runs the place. Google judges one continuous take, so every one of those mistakes means starting over. This is the checklist I work from, built on what Google's help pages say as of October 2026.

## You don't pick the method

Google decides which verification methods a profile gets, and its help page says plainly that they "can't be changed." Depending on the business type and region, the menu can include phone or text, email, a postcard, a live video call with a Google representative, or a recorded video. If the recorded video is the only choice on your screen, that's the one to prepare for.

## The rules for the recording itself
- **One continuous take of at least 30 seconds.** Google wants it unedited, unique, and complete, with no breaks.
- **Recorded live on a phone, through the Business Profile.** Footage shot earlier and uploaded later doesn't count, and neither does anything from a desktop.
- **Nothing sensitive.** Keep bank, tax, and ID numbers, other private details, and other people's faces out of the frame. Film before opening or when the shop is empty.

In the app, the path is Get verified, then Business video. Google reviews the upload in up to five business days.

## What a storefront or hybrid business has to show

Google treats a storefront as a business that serves customers in person at an address with permanent signage. A hybrid business does that and also travels or delivers. The video needs three things, in this order.
1. **Where you are.** Start outside with a street sign, the building number, a neighboring business, or a landmark, so a reviewer can match the spot on Google Maps.
2. **That the business exists there.** Pan to the storefront and the sign. Google requires the business name printed on a permanent fixture, a signboard, wall, or window, and it must match the name on the profile. A banner zip-tied to a fence doesn't qualify, and neither does a sign still carrying an old trade name.
3. **That you manage it.** Unlock the door, walk in, and show something only staff can reach: the register or point-of-sale screen, the kitchen, the stockroom.

Google's own advice is that a business without permanent signage should be set up as a service-area business instead.

## What a service-area business has to show

Plumbers, cleaners, mobile groomers, and every other business that goes to its customers verify differently, and Google says a service-area business shouldn't show its address on the profile at all.
1. **Where you operate from.** Street signs or landmarks at the business address. If you work from home, Google says the signs and landmarks in your immediate neighborhood are acceptable. It specifically warns against filming empty land or places with no clear markers.
2. **That the business exists.** Professional tools, equipment, stock, a branded vehicle, business cards, or branded uniforms.
3. **That you run it.** Perform a piece of the service, or unlock the branded van and show what's inside. Google also accepts a business permit, invoice, or utility bill in the business name, held to the camera with the account numbers covered.

## Rehearse it, then record it once

Walk the route before you record, with the phone in hand and the app closed. Decide where you'll start, which sign you'll hold on for a few seconds, which door you'll unlock, and which document you'll show. Do it in daylight. Hold each proof steady long enough to read; a quick swipe past the sign is as good as no sign. Narrating as you go ("this is the corner of Main and Fifth, here is the sign, here is the register") costs nothing and leaves the reviewer less to guess.

Before you start, open the profile and compare it against what the camera will see. The business name, the address, and the category on the profile should match the sign, the building, and the work. A profile name stuffed with keywords that appear on no sign is a mismatch the video will expose.

## If the video fails

Google tells you why it rejected the video and offers a Review issues button. The replacement has to include everything from the first recording plus whatever was missing, so record the whole sequence again, start to finish, with the gap fixed. Read the reason closely before trying again; a second video with the same flaw will fail the same way. Google's help page also suggests trying another verification method, if one is offered, before contacting support.

When the reason makes no sense, or the profile fails again and again, the trouble usually sits in the profile itself: a name that doesn't match any document, an address Google associates with another business, a category that doesn't fit what's on camera, or a history of edits that made the listing look unstable. Those need fixing before the next video, or every recording will hit the same wall.

## Don't edit the profile mid-verification

Google's help page warns that changing the business name, address, or category while a postcard is on its way makes the code stop working. The same logic applies to every method: an edit hands Google a new set of facts to check. Settle the details first, verify, and make any planned changes afterward, one at a time.

## How I help with stuck verifications

I take on profiles that keep failing verification, along with suspensions, duplicates, and listings stranded with a former agency. I start by reconciling the profile against the real business and its paperwork, then script the video with the owner so the single take shows everything Google asks for. Google makes the decision, and no one can promise its outcome, but a prepared take removes the avoidable reasons to fail. See [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/), the [reinstated profile case](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/), or [send me the listing](https://christopherabraham.com/contact/).

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# XML sitemaps that tell the truth

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

An XML sitemap is a list you hand to search engines that says, in effect, "these are the pages I want found, and this is when each one last changed." Search engines treat it as a hint, never an order, and they decide how much to trust it by checking it against what they actually find. A sitemap that lists redirects, duplicates, and dates that change every night teaches them to ignore it. A sitemap that matches the site exactly earns the opposite. Most of the sitemaps I audit fall somewhere in between, and the fixes are almost always about honesty rather than tags.

## What a sitemap is for, and what it can't do

A sitemap helps discovery. It's most useful on large sites, new sites with few links pointing in, sites with pages that sit deep in the navigation, and sites that publish or change often. On a twenty page site where every page is linked from the menu, Google will find everything without one, though a sitemap still costs nothing and gives you a tidy report in Search Console.

What a sitemap can't do is make a page indexable. If a page is thin, duplicated, blocked, or canonicalized somewhere else, listing it in the sitemap doesn't overrule any of that. It just adds a line to the Page indexing report explaining why the URL you submitted wasn't indexed. If your real problem is pages that are discovered and then left out, that's a quality and duplication question, and my guide to [reading the Page indexing report](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/page-indexing-report/) is the better starting point.

## The one rule: list only the URLs you want in search

Every URL in the file should pass four tests at once:
1. **It answers 200.** Not a 301, not a 404, not a soft 404 that says "no results" with a 200 status.
2. **It's the canonical.** The page's own canonical tag points to itself, exactly as written in the sitemap: same protocol, same host, same trailing slash.
3. **It's indexable.** No noindex in the robots meta tag or the X-Robots-Tag header.
4. **It's crawlable.** robots.txt doesn't block it.

That rules out a lot of what plugins and platforms put in by default: tag archives you've set to noindex, paginated listings, internal search results, attachment pages, staging hostnames, and the http or non-www versions of URLs. The sitemap and the canonical tags have to agree. When they contradict each other, you've sent two signals and asked Google to pick one.

## Honest lastmod dates

Of the optional tags, `lastmod` is the only one that still matters. Google has said it uses lastmod when the dates are consistently and verifiably accurate, and Bing has written publicly that it leans on lastmod to decide what to recrawl. The key word is accurate. A lastmod should change when the main content of the page changes: a rewritten section, a corrected fact, new prices. It shouldn't change because the footer copyright year rolled over, a sidebar widget updated, or the site was rebuilt.

The common failure is a generator that stamps every URL with the build time. Every page claims it changed today, every day, and the search engine learns that this site's dates mean nothing. On this site, each page's source carries an `updated` date that I change by hand when the content changes, and the build writes that date into the sitemap, the visible "Updated" line, and the structured data. One date, set on purpose, appearing in three places that agree.

## The tags to leave out

`priority` and `changefreq` are in the original protocol, and Google ignores both. You can leave them in without harm, but I take them out, because every field in a file should mean something, and these give people the false comfort of having "prioritized" pages that no crawler is listening to.

The same goes for most of the image sitemap extension. Google retired the image caption, title, geographic location, and license tags in 2022. Only the image location is still read. Image entries are worth including for images that matter in search, such as products, diagrams, and original photography, and not worth bloating the file with every icon and spacer.

## Size limits and sitemap index files

One sitemap file can hold up to 50,000 URLs and be up to 50 MB uncompressed. Past either limit, split it into several files and list them in a sitemap index file, then submit the index. You can gzip the files to save bandwidth; the size limit applies to the uncompressed version.

Splitting is useful well below the limit. On a programmatic site of more than 20,000 pages, I gave each content type its own sitemap, so Search Console reported indexing for each group separately, and a problem in one template stood out instead of hiding in a site-wide average. The [price index case study](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/card-price-index/) shows how that played out. Split by template or section, not alphabetically or at random, because the point is to make the reports readable.

## Telling search engines where it lives
- **robots.txt.** Add a line such as `Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml`. It must be an absolute URL, and it can sit anywhere in the file. Every crawler that reads robots.txt finds it there, including ones you'll never submit to by hand.
- **Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.** Submit it once in each. You don't need to resubmit after every change; they fetch it again on their own.
- **No more pings.** Google retired its old sitemap ping address in 2023, so scripts that still call it are doing nothing. For Bing and the other engines that support it, IndexNow is the way to announce changed URLs quickly.

One ordering detail I care about: if you announce new URLs with IndexNow, do it after the new sitemap is actually live, not the moment you push. On this site, the IndexNow job waits until the public sitemap matches what the release meant to publish, because an announcement about a page that's still deploying wastes the crawl.

## How I audit a sitemap

I compare three lists: what the sitemap says, what a crawl finds, and what Search Console reports. In Screaming Frog, I run a normal crawl with the option to crawl linked XML sitemaps switched on, then look at the Sitemaps tab. Three filters do most of the work:
- **Non-indexable URLs in sitemap.** Redirects, errors, noindexed pages, and canonicalized pages that shouldn't be listed. Each one is a broken promise.
- **URLs not in sitemap.** Indexable pages the crawl found that the sitemap forgot. Often a whole post type or a newer section the generator wasn't told about.
- **Orphan URLs.** Pages in the sitemap that nothing on the site links to. Search engines can find them, but an orphan with no internal links rarely ranks. Usually the fix is [a few good internal links](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/internal-linking/), sometimes it's deleting a page nobody meant to keep.

Then I open Search Console's Sitemaps report to confirm the file was read without errors, and filter the Page indexing report to submitted URLs only. The gap between "submitted" and "indexed" for each sitemap is the clearest single measure of how much of your intended site Google has accepted.

I also open the file in a browser and read it. A sitemap with a stylesheet attached shows as a readable table instead of raw XML, which makes it easy to spot a staging hostname, a duplicated section, or a run of identical dates at a glance. The [sitemap for this site](https://christopherabraham.com/sitemap.xml) works that way.

## Common mistakes I find
- Two sitemaps from two plugins, both submitted, listing different versions of the same URLs.
- An old sitemap still submitted in Search Console from a previous platform, full of URLs that now redirect.
- Development or staging hostnames inside the production file.
- The sitemap itself blocked in robots.txt, or served with a noindex header that some crawlers read as a reason to drop it.
- Trailing slash or capitalization mismatches between the sitemap and the canonical tags.
- A cache layer serving a sitemap that's weeks old, so new pages never appear in it.

None of these is dramatic on its own. Together they make a sitemap that search engines treat as noise.

## Questions people ask about sitemaps

### Does a sitemap help me rank?

Not directly. It helps search engines find and recrawl pages. Ranking comes from what's on the pages and who links to them.

### Do AI search tools read XML sitemaps?

Many of the crawlers that feed AI answers read robots.txt and follow its sitemap line, and Bing's index, which several AI tools draw on, uses sitemaps and IndexNow. An accurate sitemap is part of being easy to read for every kind of machine, alongside an [llms.txt file](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/llms-txt/).

### Should I list PDFs in my sitemap?

Yes, if they're useful documents you want found in search and they answer 200 at a stable address. Leave out drafts and duplicates of HTML pages.

### How often should the sitemap update?

Whenever a page is added, removed, or meaningfully changed. Generate it from the same source as the site, so it can't fall behind.

If your sitemap and Search Console disagree and you can't tell why, that's the kind of thing I sort out in a [crawling and indexing engagement](https://christopherabraham.com/services/indexing/). The bigger picture of crawl health is in my [site-wide technical SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/sitewide-technical-seo/) work.

# How to choose the next SEO fix when developer time is scarce

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

An audit can produce a hundred findings while the development team has room for two changes. The useful question is which two deserve the available time. Counting warnings will not answer it.

I organize that decision around the pages the business depends on, the strength of the diagnosis, and the work required to deliver a change. A priority list is a set of choices under constraints. It should explain why something moves first and what evidence would change that choice.

## Identify the pages that matter to the business

Begin with a short inventory of useful destinations: the services people inquire about, products currently available to buy, location pages for operating branches, and articles that support a real customer decision. Ask the owner which actions make those pages valuable.

Traffic alone can mislead. An old article may bring many visits without producing relevant inquiries, while a specialist service page attracts a small audience with a strong reason to call. Avoid inventing a monetary value for either. If conversion evidence is absent, record the owner's explanation and label it as a business judgment.

Use Search Console to examine search visibility alongside that inventory. Google's [introduction to Search Console](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/search-console-start) describes its crawl, indexing, and performance reports. Those reports supply observations about search; they do not establish the value of a lead or identify every cause of a change.

## Separate active failures from improvement opportunities

A broken inquiry form on an important service page needs a different conversation from a title that could be clearer. Likewise, an accidental exclusion affecting a whole product category deserves investigation before a cosmetic improvement to an infrequently used archive.

Use three practical queues:
- **Restore:** an important customer action or access path has failed.
- **Investigate:** evidence suggests a material problem, but the cause or scope remains uncertain.
- **Improve:** the current experience works, and a bounded change could make it more useful.

These queues prevent an attractive improvement from displacing an unresolved failure. They also avoid treating every suspicion as an emergency. A sudden graph change may justify checking the data before changing the website.

## Compare candidates without false precision

For each candidate, record five fields: business relevance, affected population, confidence in the diagnosis, implementation effort, and dependencies. Use plain descriptions. “Shared template serving the current product catalog” is more informative than an unexplained impact score of nine.

Confidence concerns the explanation, not the confidence of the person presenting it. A reproducible failure with a known template cause is different from a correlation between a release and falling visits. Give the second case an investigation task that could confirm or reject the theory.

Effort includes review, release coordination, content preparation, and verification. A ten minute code edit that needs a vendor's approval and an overnight maintenance window is not a ten minute delivery. Ask the developer for an estimate before ranking the task as an easy win.

A simple high, medium, or low label can help sort a discussion, provided its meaning is written down. Avoid multiplying arbitrary scores into a precise looking return forecast. The ordering is a decision aid, not a prediction of future rankings.

## Work through a small hypothetical backlog

Imagine a supplier with one developer afternoon available. Three findings arrive: the quote form fails on mobile, twenty product pages have similar descriptions, and an old archive has short meta descriptions. These are invented examples, not reported client results.

The quote form belongs in Restore if testing reproduces the failure. Fixing it protects the customer action that existing visits are supposed to support. The product descriptions need more context: do the products serve different needs, and is important specification information absent? That may become an editorial assignment before any code work is required.

The archive descriptions can wait unless someone establishes a stronger business reason. A crawler highlighting them in red does not change that. The outcome of the afternoon should be a repaired and verified quote path, plus a clearly assigned investigation of the product pages.

If the form failure turns out to be a test configuration problem, revise the queue immediately. Good prioritization leaves room for new evidence rather than defending yesterday's order.

## Make each selected task small enough to finish

Turn “improve product SEO” into a bounded assignment: inspect one product family, identify missing information, decide which template fields are needed, and verify the revised output on named examples. The next task depends on that result.

Assign one owner and specify the closing evidence. A title change needs the expected title on the relevant production URLs. A redirect repair needs the intended destination and response behavior for the agreed source set. A form repair needs a successful submission and confirmed receipt, following the [page to inbox inquiry test](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/test-website-inquiries/).

Do not require a ranking increase to close a development ticket. That would leave a technically complete change permanently open while search performance moves for many reasons. Track implementation and business measurement in separate fields.

## Review the queue after each release

Keep a compact change log: what changed, where, when, who checked it, and what remains unknown. If the evidence reveals a wider issue, expand the next task with that evidence. If a hypothesis fails, remove it from the implementation queue.

Review outcomes over a period appropriate to the question, acknowledging seasonality and other releases. A clean before and after crawl establishes changed technical behavior. It does not isolate the cause of every later traffic movement. The guide to [verifying SEO repairs](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prove-seo-fixes/) covers that distinction.

The deliverable is a short list somebody can act on: an owner, a reason, a prerequisite, and a test for each item. That is what I expect from [a technical SEO audit](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/) and from [ongoing SEO support](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-retainer/). Progress becomes easier to assess when the queue records decisions instead of accumulating warnings.

Drafted with OpenAI Codex at the publisher's request. The backlog example is hypothetical; no traffic or revenue outcome is claimed.

# Service-area businesses on Google Business Profile

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

A plumber, a roofer, a mobile dog groomer, or a pest control company does its work at the customer's door. Google calls these service-area businesses, and it treats them differently from shops: no public street address, a list of areas served instead, and a stricter eye on the details that remain. Most of the trouble I see with these profiles comes from three fields, the address, the areas, and the phone number, so this guide works through each one.

## Which kind of business you are

Google recognizes three setups. A storefront serves customers at its address. A service-area business goes to its customers and has no premises where customers are received. A hybrid does both: a showroom or office that customers visit during posted hours, plus crews that travel. A tile company with a showroom is a hybrid; an electrician working from a home office is a service-area business.

Pick the one that matches how customers meet you, because the rest of the profile follows from it. A home-based business that lists its house as a storefront invites strangers to the door and tells Google something it can check and will eventually doubt.

## Remove the address when customers don't come to you

Google's service-area help page is direct about it: if you don't serve customers at your business address, remove the address from the profile and enter only your service area. The address still exists in Google's records for verification and for placing you on its internal map. It just stops showing to the public.

Two addresses never qualify. Google's guidelines rule out a rented mailing address where the business doesn't operate, and they rule out P.O. boxes and remote mailboxes. A service-area business can list a so-called virtual office only if staff are actually there during business hours. A coworking desk you visit once a month fails that test.

## Choose service areas you can serve

A profile can hold up to 20 service areas, set as cities, postal codes, or other named areas. Google's own tip is that the whole area shouldn't stretch beyond about two hours of driving time from where the business is based. Treat that as an outer limit.

Service areas describe where you work, and they carry little weight in where the profile ranks. Map results still weigh the distance between the searcher and the business location Google holds on file, so a company based in one suburb won't start ranking across a whole metro by listing twenty towns. What wins the farther towns is the website: a useful page for each area where you have real jobs, real photos, and real reviews to show.

## Use a phone number that belongs to this business

The guidelines ask for a number that connects to the individual business location, a local number in place of a central call-center line whenever possible, and a number under the business's direct control. Premium-rate numbers aren't allowed at all.

This is where I find the quietest damage. A business with one number on its profile and another on its website may have two perfectly legitimate lines, and it still gives Google, directories, and AI tools two answers to the simplest question about the business. Pick one primary number, put it on the profile, the website header, and the contact page, and keep tracking numbers out of the primary slot.

## Keep the name clean

Service-area businesses are tempted to add the city or the service to their name: "Smith Plumbing Denver Emergency Drain Cleaning." Google's guidelines say plainly that unnecessary information in the business name isn't permitted and can lead to suspension. The name on the profile should match the name on the truck, the invoice, and the state registration.

## Verification is the gate

Until a profile is verified, nobody can change it, owner or manager. A profile that has never been verified can show in public with outdated details that nobody is able to correct. If your profile is in that state, verification comes before every other fix. For service-area businesses that usually means a video showing the vehicle, tools, and proof of management; my [video verification guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-video-verification/) covers what to film.

## What competitors' listings tell you

Look up the businesses that outrank you and note what they show. Competitors set up as storefronts or hybrids display a street address, and a true service-area business shouldn't add one to match, because it has no premises for customers to visit. A true service-area business competes on what it can prove: reviews that mention the towns and jobs, photos from real sites, prompt answers to questions, and location pages that read like the work of someone who has been there.

## A short checklist
- Business type matches how customers meet you: storefront, service area, or hybrid.
- Address removed from public view if customers never come to it; no mailboxes or unstaffed offices.
- Service areas limited to places you serve, within about two hours of your base.
- One primary local number, the same on the profile and the website.
- Business name exactly as it appears on signage and paperwork.
- Profile verified, with at least two people holding access.

## Questions service businesses ask

### Will removing my address hurt my rankings?

Google still knows where the business is based and uses that location. Removing the address from public view follows Google's guidance for businesses that don't receive customers, and it protects the privacy of a home address.

### Can I have a profile in every town I serve?

No. One business gets one profile per real location where it operates. Extra profiles at virtual addresses are a common cause of suspensions.

### Should my website list my address?

If you work from home, list the areas you serve and your phone number instead. Your legal notices and invoices can carry the mailing address.

If your profile is stuck, mismatched, or unverified, that's work I take on through [local SEO consulting](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/) and, for profiles nobody can edit, [Business Profile verification help](https://christopherabraham.com/services/gbp-verification/).

# Black Friday sale pages that keep their rankings

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Every November I find shops publishing a brand-new Black Friday page at an address like /black-friday-2026, while last year's page sits forgotten at /black-friday-2025 with all the links people gave it. The new page starts with nothing, and Google has to find it, crawl it, and decide what it's worth in the few weeks that matter. One permanent address fixes that, and it's the advice Google itself has given.

## What Google has said

In July 2021, Alan Kent of Google's Search Relations team published a post on deal pages that restated the earlier Black Friday advice in a short list: create dedicated pages for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, reuse the same URL each year, create the pages early so Google can index them, link to the sale page from the home page, and include a high-quality image. The same post added that the page title should carry the event description, the page should have text that describes the event, and if the deals are revealed on the day, the page should go up early with general information and be recrawled after the update.

That post is five years old, and it's still the most specific official statement on sale pages I can find. The reasoning hasn't aged: a page that has existed for years has links, history, and a place in the index that a new page has to earn from scratch.

## One URL, updated every year

Choose an address with no year in it, such as /black-friday/ or /sale/black-friday/. Put the year in the title and the heading, where shoppers want to see it, and change it each autumn. The address stays put. If you have old yearly pages, redirect each one to the permanent address with a 301 so the links pointing at them still count.

Cyber Monday is a separate search with its own audience, so it can earn its own permanent page. A single combined page works too when the offers are identical. What fails is a new page per year per event, which turns one strong page into eight weak ones over four years.

## When to publish

Google Trends shows searches for Black Friday building for weeks before the day, every year. Publish the page, or refresh last year's, by early November. If you can't reveal the deals yet, say what's coming: which departments, when the sale opens, how to get notified. That gives Google something real to index. On the day the deals go live, update the page and request recrawling of that URL in Search Console's URL Inspection tool.

Link to the page from the home page and the main navigation while the sale runs. That link is the strongest signal you can send about which page matters this month.

## What goes on the page

Write a few paragraphs a shopper would read: what's on sale, the dates, shipping cutoffs for delivery before the holidays, the return window for gifts, and how the discount is applied. Then link to the actual sale products and categories. A page that's only a banner and a countdown clock has nothing for a search engine or an AI assistant to quote.

Prices belong on the product pages. If those pages carry merchant listing structured data, the sale price can appear in Google's shopping results. Check that the price in the markup matches the visible price on the day the sale starts; when they disagree, Google has two prices and no reason to trust either.

## After the sale

Don't delete the page in December, and don't redirect it to the home page. Keep it live with a short note that the sale has ended, a sentence about when it returns, an email signup if you have one, and links to current offers. Take it out of the main navigation, but leave it linked from somewhere on the site, such as a sales or offers hub, so it stays crawlable.

The page will rank for little in March. What matters is that in November it wakes up with years of history behind it instead of none.

## Measure it the same way each year

In Search Console, filter the Performance report to the page's URL and compare the same date window around Black Friday each year. Because the address never changes, the comparison is simple. That's another quiet benefit of one permanent URL: yearly pages make the history impossible to read. Keep a note of the dates the page was refreshed and the deals went live, so a jump or a dip can be traced to something that happened.

## Questions about holiday sale pages

### Should the year be in the title?

Yes. Shoppers search for "Black Friday 2026" and expect current deals. Put the year in the title and heading, and keep it out of the URL.

### What about other seasonal sales?

The same rule fits any sale that returns: a back-to-school page, a spring sale, an anniversary event. One permanent address per recurring event.

### My platform made a new page every year. What now?

Pick the strongest one, usually the oldest or the one with the most links, move it to a year-free address, and redirect the rest to it.

For a store with more than a handful of seasonal pages, I map them, merge them, and set the redirects as part of [ecommerce SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ecommerce-seo/) work. For the store-hours side of the holidays, see the [holiday hours checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/holiday-hours/).

- [Google Search Central: Merchant listing (Product, Offer) structured data](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/merchant-listing)

# Google Merchant Center free listings for small shops

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Plenty of small store owners assume Google Shopping is only an ad product. Free listings, the unpaid half, shows products from any eligible store at no cost, and many of the shops I audit have never switched it on or have a feed full of errors nobody has read. For a shop with a few dozen to a few thousand products, it's some of the cheapest visibility left in search.

## Where free listings appear

Google's Merchant Center help page lists the places: the Shopping tab, product rich results in Search with price, availability, and reviews, Google Images and Lens (including Lens results for similar products), YouTube in some countries, Maps, the products section of a Business Profile, and Gemini. The page is careful to say eligibility doesn't guarantee your products will show. Free listings compete on relevance and data quality, and incomplete data loses.

## Setting it up

You need a Merchant Center account, a verified and claimed website, and a product source. On Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce, and most hosted platforms, the Google sales channel or an official app builds the feed from your catalog and keeps it current. New Merchant Center accounts are opted in to free listings by default; on an older account, look for the free listings card under Marketing methods and confirm it's on.

A store without a platform integration can upload a spreadsheet feed, but a manual spreadsheet goes stale the first time a price changes. I prefer an automated feed, or, for a small static catalog, letting Merchant Center read the structured data already on the product pages.

## The attributes that decide eligibility

Google requires an ID, title, link, image link, price, description, and availability for every product. Depending on the product, it also wants the condition, the brand, a GTIN or manufacturer part number, and whether the item is a multipack or bundle. Clothing needs color, size, age group, and gender.

The GTIN, the barcode number, causes the most confusion. If you resell branded goods, the manufacturer's GTIN belongs in the feed and helps Google match your offer to the product. If you make the products yourself, there's no GTIN to supply, and you mark that the identifier doesn't exist instead of inventing one.

## Shipping and returns

In the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Germany, and several other countries, shipping settings are required. Google also asks for a return policy, ideally set in Merchant Center. These details appear on the listings, and a shopper comparing two stores at the same price will pick the one with free returns shown. Set them once at the account level and they apply to every product.

## Fix the Needs attention tab first

The Products page in Merchant Center has a Needs attention tab. That tab is the whole job for the first week. The usual problems I find:
- **Price mismatch.** The feed says one price and the page shows another, often because a sale ran on the site and the feed didn't update.
- **Availability mismatch.** Products listed in stock that the site says are sold out.
- **Image problems.** Promotional overlays, watermarks, or placeholder images.
- **Missing identifiers.** Branded products with no GTIN.
- **Policy issues.** Restricted products, or a website missing contact details and a return policy.

Each of these has a cause in the store setup. Fixing the cause once beats fixing products one at a time every week.

## Write titles for shoppers

The product title in the feed is the line a shopper reads in the results. Lead with what the product is, then the attributes people search by: brand, material, size, color, model. "Walnut cutting board, 18 x 12 inch, end grain" will match more searches than "The Hearthside." Your on-site title can keep the brand flourish while the feed title does the describing.

## Connect the pieces

Google's help page recommends linking your Business Profile and any third-party platforms you sell through, and keeping Merchant Center data consistent with your store. Consistency runs in both directions: the product page's structured data, the feed, and the visible page should all carry the same price and availability. When they agree, Google has one answer. When they don't, it has to choose.

## How to tell it's working

Merchant Center's performance reports show clicks and impressions from free listings separately from ads. In Search Console, the Performance report's search appearance filter separates merchant listings and product snippets. Give it a few weeks after the errors clear, then compare clicks by product category to see which parts of the catalog Google is showing and which it isn't.

## Questions about free listings

### Do I need to run Shopping ads?

No. Free listings work on their own. Ads are a separate, paid choice in the same account.

### How long until products show?

Google reviews products after the feed is submitted, which can take a few business days. Errors you fix are rechecked on the next feed update.

### Do free listings help in AI answers?

Google's help page lists Gemini among the surfaces, and accurate product data is what any shopping assistant needs. Clean feed data is the price of entry.

Feeds and product page structured data are part of my [ecommerce SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/services/ecommerce-seo/) work. For the markup itself, see the [small business schema guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/small-business-schema/).

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Apple Maps and Bing Places: local listings past Google

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Local SEO conversations start and end with the Google Business Profile, and for good reason. But every iPhone owner who asks Siri for a nearby locksmith, taps a business in Apple Maps, or opens directions from a text message is reading Apple's data. Every search in Bing, and the local results that Microsoft's products draw from it, reads Bing's. Both listings are free, both take an afternoon, and most of the small businesses I check have claimed neither.

## Apple: the place card

Apple's listing for a business is called a place card. It shows the name, hours, phone, website, photos, and actions such as booking or ordering. Apple describes Business Connect as a free platform for controlling how a business shows up across Apple Maps, Wallet, and other Apple apps. The old businessconnect.apple.com address now forwards to business.apple.com, where Apple has folded the tool into a wider product called Apple Business that also covers devices and email for small companies. The Maps part works the same way: claim the location, prove you run it, and edit the card.

What you can manage on the card:
- Logo, header image, and photos.
- Hours, including special hours for holidays.
- Actions that let people order, reserve, or book from the card.
- Showcases, Apple's term for short promotions and seasonal offers.
- Insights on how people found and used the card.

## Claiming on Apple

Sign in at business.apple.com with an Apple Account, ideally one tied to the business email instead of someone's personal ID. Add the company, search for the location, and claim it. Apple verifies the business before you can edit. For a business with many locations, Apple offers bulk tools and works with listing-management services that push data to it.

Apple Maps has long shown ratings and reviews from partner services such as Yelp alongside its own, so a business with a poor profile on a partner site may see that reflected in Maps. Check what your card shows before assuming it matches Google.

## Bing: Places for Business

Microsoft relaunched Bing Places for Business in October 2025. Management moved to bing.com/forbusiness, existing accounts were moved over automatically, and a recommendation tool now flags missing fields such as photos, hours, and category details. Listings are free and appear in Bing Search and Bing Maps. Search Engine Journal's report on the launch noted that Microsoft plans deeper links to Copilot; I treat that as a plan until Microsoft documents it.

The fastest route is the import from Google. Bing can read an existing Google Business Profile and copy the name, address, hours, and phone. That's a good start only when the Google profile is already correct, because the import copies mistakes as faithfully as facts. Check the category afterward, since Google and Bing don't use the same category lists.

## Why these two matter for AI answers

AI assistants answer local questions from whatever business data their systems can reach. Bing's index feeds a number of them, and Apple's data feeds Siri and Apple Maps on every iPhone. If Google says you close at 6 and Apple says 5, an assistant has two answers to pick between, and a customer may drive across town to a locked door. Consistent data across the three big map providers removes the conflict before any AI system has to resolve it.

## Keep one master record

Keep a single document with the business name exactly as registered, the address or service area, the primary phone number, the website, the hours, and the categories. Every listing gets copied from that record, never from another listing. When something changes, update the record first and then each listing on the same day: Google, Apple, Bing, and then the directories and review sites that matter in your trade.

That same record pays off when a business changes its name or moves, which is when listings drift most. My guide to [changing a business name without losing search](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/business-name-change/) covers that case in detail.

## A quick audit you can do today
- Search for your business in Apple Maps on a phone. Note the hours, phone, website, and category.
- Search for it on bing.com and in Bing Maps. Note the same details.
- Compare both with your Google profile and your website's contact page.
- Claim whichever listing you haven't, and correct every difference.
- Put a reminder in your calendar to recheck all three before each holiday season.

## Questions about Apple and Bing listings

### Does claiming these help my Google rankings?

Not directly. They get you found by people who don't use Google, and they make your business data agree everywhere, which helps every system that compares sources.

### Do I need a paid listing service?

Not for one or a few locations. Both platforms are free to use directly. Services earn their fee when you manage dozens of locations.

### What if someone else already claimed my listing?

Both platforms have a dispute or ownership-request process. Start it from the listing itself and keep proof of the business, such as a utility bill or registration, ready.

Listing cleanup across Google, Apple, and Bing is part of my [local SEO work](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/), and the [AI search checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-search-checklist/) shows where these listings fit in a broader visibility plan.

# The FTC fake review rule for small businesses

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Reviews drive local search, and for years the rules around them were scattered across platform policies and general consumer protection law. Since October 21, 2024, the United States has had a specific federal rule: the Federal Trade Commission's Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 465. It lets courts impose civil penalties for knowing violations. Most honest businesses already comply, but a few common habits sit close to the lines, and those are what this guide covers.

This is a practitioner's summary, not legal advice. If you've received a letter from the FTC or a state attorney general, talk to a lawyer.

## What the rule prohibits

The FTC's own question-and-answer page groups the rule into a handful of sections:
- **Fake or false reviews and testimonials** (section 465.2), including reviews from people who never used the product and reviews that misrepresent the reviewer's experience.
- **Paying for reviews of a particular sentiment** (465.4). Incentives become a problem when there's an express or implied requirement that the review be positive, or negative about a competitor.
- **Undisclosed insider reviews** (465.5). Reviews by officers, managers, employees, or agents, and in some cases their relatives, need a clear disclosure of the relationship.
- **Company-controlled review sites** (465.6) presented as independent.
- **Review suppression** (465.7), such as legal threats, intimidation, or false accusations used to get reviews removed.
- **Fake social media indicators** (465.8), like bought followers or views, when the business knew or should have known they were fake.

## What you can still do

You can ask every customer for a review. The FTC says the rule exempts generalized requests to purchasers to post reviews about their experiences, and offering an incentive to everyone who responds doesn't change that, as long as the incentive doesn't depend on what the review says.

The incentive question has a second layer. Google's own guidelines for Business Profiles go further than the FTC and prohibit offering incentives for reviews on Google at all. A gift card for every reviewer may be legal under the rule and still get reviews removed or a profile penalized on Google. When the platform's rule is stricter, the platform's rule is the one that governs your listing.

## Review gating

Review gating means asking customers how their experience was and sending only the happy ones to Google or Yelp, while routing unhappy ones to a private feedback form. The FTC's guidance says the rule doesn't contain a specific prohibition against asking only customers you expect to be satisfied, and in the same answer it warns that the practice can still violate the FTC Act if it misleads people about how the business is rated. Google's review policy forbids selectively soliciting positive reviews.

My advice is simpler than either text: send the same request to every customer, with one link, and handle complaints in your reply to the review. Many reputation tools still ship with gating switched on by default, so check yours.

## Employees and family

Staff and relatives are the easiest source of early reviews and the most common source of trouble. Under the rule, a review by an officer or manager that doesn't disclose the relationship is a problem, and a business that asks employees to write reviews has duties to keep those reviews disclosed. Google, for its part, removes reviews that come from conflicts of interest. The cleanest policy is that employees don't review the business they work for.

## Responding to bad reviews

The suppression section targets threats and false accusations meant to get a review taken down. Replying publicly, offering to make things right, and reporting a review to the platform when it breaks the platform's rules are all ordinary practice. Threatening a customer with a lawsuit over an honest negative review, or claiming a review is fake when you know it's real, is where the rule bites.

## Testimonials on your own website

The rule covers testimonials too. Quotes on your site should come from real customers, reflect what they said, and not be edited to change the meaning. If you show only your best reviews, don't present the page as a complete or independent rating. When you pay or comp someone for a testimonial, disclose it next to the quote. And never add review star markup for reviews of your own business that you collected and display yourself; Google treats those as self-serving and won't show them.

## A compliance checklist
- One review request, sent to every customer, with no screening question in front of the link.
- No incentives for Google reviews; any incentive elsewhere offered to everyone and not tied to sentiment.
- No reviews from owners, staff, or relatives, or a clear disclosure where the platform allows them.
- No bought followers, likes, or views.
- Bad reviews answered in public, reported only for real policy violations.
- Website testimonials sourced, unedited in meaning, and disclosed when compensated.

## Questions about reviews and the rule

### Does the rule apply to a small local business?

Yes. It applies to businesses of any size that sell to consumers in the United States.

### Can I ask a happy customer in person to leave a review?

Yes. Asking is fine. The risk comes from a system that asks only the happy ones and steers everyone else away.

### Can I buy reviews from a service that promises they're real?

No. A review written to order by someone who wasn't your customer is a fake review under the rule, whatever the seller calls it.

For honest ways to earn mentions that AI tools and search engines trust, see my guide to [earned mentions](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/). Review strategy for local businesses is part of my [local SEO work](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Launch websites for a book, an album, or a new service

A launch has a date, and the website has to be right on that date: the pre-order link works, the share preview shows the cover, the press kit downloads, and a search for the title finds your page ahead of the retailers. I build small, fast launch sites on a domain you own, with the search and AI groundwork already done, so the page that announces the launch keeps working long after it.

## Who it's for
- **Authors** with a book coming out who want a home that outlasts the publisher's catalog page.
- **Musicians and labels** releasing an album or a single who need one address for streaming links, tour dates, and press.
- **Filmmakers and documentary teams** with screenings, festival laurels, and a trailer to share.
- **Consultants and small firms** opening a new practice or launching a new service who need a credible site in days.

## What gets built
- **A home page about the launch**, with the cover or key art, the date, and every place to buy, stream, or book.
- **An about page for you**, written to answer the questions a journalist or an AI assistant asks first: who you are, what you've made before, and where to find you elsewhere.
- **A press or media page** with downloadable images, a short and a long description, and contact details.
- **Structured data** for the work itself, as a Book, MusicAlbum, Movie, or Service, connected to Person or Organization markup for you, so search engines tie the title to its creator.
- **Share cards** at the right size for every page, so a link posted on Facebook, LinkedIn, or X shows the full cover and the right words.
- **A sitemap, robots.txt, and an llms.txt file**, with the site registered in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools before launch day.

## Live weeks before the date

A new domain needs time to be crawled. I aim to have the site live and submitted weeks before the launch, even if the first version only announces the date and collects email addresses. When the launch arrives, the page that already exists gets the buy links and the reviews, and search engines already know where it is. Recurring events get the same treatment: one permanent address that is updated each year, the method in my guide to [sale pages that keep their rankings](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/black-friday-pages/).

## Proof you can check

This site is static, hand-checked, and built by the same method; the [colophon](https://christopherabraham.com/about/colophon/) describes how. ## After launch

A launch site should keep earning. Reviews, interviews, and awards get added as they arrive, and the about page gets updated as the work grows. You can edit the plain files yourself, ask an AI coding assistant to make a change and review it, or have me do it, with each round of changes quoted as a fixed fee first. Every change is recorded, so any mistake can be undone.

## What I'll need from you

The domain, or the name you'd like; the cover or key art at full resolution; the launch date; the links to retailers or platforms; and a short call to agree on the words. If you have reviews, press quotes, or a bio already, send those too, with their sources, because everything on the site gets checked before it goes up.

# SEO report review

Every month a report arrives with charts that go up and a list of tasks marked done. You pay the invoice and can't tell whether the work is helping. I read the report the way an auditor reads a set of books: every claim checked against your own Search Console, analytics, and the live site, and a written answer about which parts hold up, which don't, and what's missing.

## When owners ask for this
- Traffic or leads have been flat for months while the reports say things are improving.
- A new agency delivered a long audit and you can't tell which items matter.
- You're about to renew a contract, raise a budget, or switch providers.
- A board member or investor asked how search is going and you'd like an outside answer.

## What I check
- **The numbers.** Do the clicks, impressions, and rankings in the report match what your own Search Console and analytics show for the same dates and the same pages? Are year-over-year comparisons using matching windows?
- **The metrics chosen.** Reports full of vanity numbers, such as total keywords ranked or a domain score from a third-party tool, can rise while revenue-earning pages decline. I look at the pages and queries that bring your customers.
- **The work claimed.** If the report says titles were rewritten, redirects fixed, or schema added, I check the live pages to see it.
- **The audit findings.** For a long technical audit, I sort the findings into the few that change outcomes, the many that are housekeeping, and any that are wrong.
- **What's missing.** Problems the report doesn't mention: indexing issues, a broken inquiry form, AI answers getting your business wrong.
- **Links and risk.** If the report counts new backlinks, I look at where they came from, because bought links are a risk for you, not the agency.

## What you get

A written review in plain English: each major claim in the report, what your data shows, and my verdict. A short list of the questions to put to your agency. And, where the work is sound, I say so, because a good agency deserves the renewal. My guide to [proving an SEO fix worked](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prove-seo-fixes/) shows the standard of evidence I hold reports to, and [what an SEO audit should deliver](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-audit-deliverables/) covers what a good audit looks like.

## What I need from you

The report or audit itself, read access to Search Console and your analytics, and the contract or statement of work so I know what was promised. Read-only access is enough; I don't change anything on your site during a review.

## Independent findings

The review stands on its own. You get the findings whether you keep your agency, change its brief, or move on. If you then want help with the fixes, that's a separate conversation; my [guide to hiring an SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/hiring-an-seo/) is useful either way.

## How it's delivered

A fixed-scope review, quoted as one fixed fee from the size of the report and the site. Payment terms are settled in conversation before the review starts. Terms are on [Hire Me](https://christopherabraham.com/hire-me/).

# Google Business Profile verification help

A Business Profile can be visible on Google Maps and still be locked. Until it's verified, nobody can correct the phone number, the hours, or the category, whether they're the owner or a manager. I work on the profiles stuck at that gate: video verifications that keep failing, listings with no reachable owner, and service-area businesses Google keeps asking to prove themselves.

## The cases I take
- **Failed video verification.** The video was rejected, sometimes more than once, and the dashboard offers no explanation.
- **Visible but unverified.** The listing shows in public with wrong or outdated details, and every edit is blocked until verification succeeds.
- **Owner unknown or gone.** A former employee, an old agency, or a founder's personal account owns the profile, and nobody current has owner access.
- **Service-area doubts.** A business that travels to customers, with a hidden address, a home office, or a vehicle as its main proof of existence.
- **Re-verification after changes.** A name change, a move, or a category change triggered a new verification request.

## How I work a case

First I find out who holds which access, what the profile shows in public, what the dashboard asks for, and what has already been tried. Then I check the profile against Google's guidelines, because a verification attempt on a profile that breaks a rule, such as keywords in the name or a mailbox for an address, tends to fail no matter how good the video is. Those get fixed first.

For video verification, I plan the recording with you: what to show, in what order, and what proof of management to have in hand, such as keys to the premises, equipment with the business name, or business documents. My [video verification guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-video-verification/) lays out the method. If the business serves customers away from its base, the [service-area business guide](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/service-area-business/) covers the address and service-area setup that should be in place first.

## Ownership problems

When the owner is unreachable, Google has a process for requesting ownership. It works best with documents that tie the requester to the business and a clear, honest account of what happened. I help put that request together and keep a record of each step, because these requests can take weeks and the details get lost.

## Who decides

Google makes the verification decision, on its own schedule, and its support team can't be hurried. I sell the diagnosis, the preparation, and the persistence, and the fee covers that work whatever Google decides. A related case, a suspended profile restored on appeal, is in the [profile reinstatement case study](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/).

## What I'll need from you

Manager or owner access if anyone has it, the business registration and a recent utility bill or lease, photos of signage or vehicles, the history of earlier attempts, and an hour on a call to plan the next one.

# Local competitor recon

Owners usually know their competitors by name and by reputation. What they rarely have is a side-by-side record of what Google actually shows for each one: the primary category, the rating and review count, whether an address appears, the hours, the phone number, and the website. I build that record from Google's own data, put your profile in the same table, and point out where the differences are worth acting on.

## Who it's for
- Local businesses that slipped in the map results and want to see who moved past them.
- Service-area businesses deciding how to present a hidden address, a set of service areas, and their reviews.
- Multi-location businesses comparing each branch with the competitors around it.
- Agencies that need a clean evidence table before they advise a local client.

## How it works

First you and I settle on the searches that matter, such as "roof repair" plus the towns you serve, and the businesses you consider rivals. I query Google's Places data for those searches and record what comes back for every listing: name, primary and secondary types, rating, number of reviews, whether a street address is shown, opening hours, phone, website, and the business status Google reports. The raw responses are kept with the date they were pulled, so anyone can check the table against its source.

Your own profile goes through the same pull. That is often where the most useful findings are: a phone number on the listing that differs from the website, a category that undersells what you do, hours that stopped matching reality, or a profile that shows in public but has never been verified.

## What you get
- An evidence table of every listing in the comparison, with the date of the pull.
- A short written read of what the table shows: where you lead, where you trail, and which gaps you can close.
- A checklist of changes to your profile and website, in order, with the ones Google's guidelines require marked separately from the ones that are only good practice.
- The method written down, so the same pull can be repeated later and compared like for like.

## Ground rules

Recon reads public listing data. It doesn't create profiles, contact competitors, or post reviews, and it never adds anything to a listing that isn't true of the business. Any changes to your own profile come after the read, with your approval. If the profile turns out to be unverified, verification comes first; see [Business Profile verification help](https://christopherabraham.com/services/gbp-verification/).

## Related reading

The setup questions behind most findings are covered in my guides to [service-area businesses](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/service-area-business/), [Apple Maps and Bing Places](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/apple-and-bing-listings/), and [Business Profile performance reports](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-performance-reports/). Broader local work sits under [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).

# Peak season readiness

Some businesses earn most of their year in a few weeks: fireworks before the Fourth, costumes before Halloween, garden centers in spring, ski shops at the first snow. For them, a search problem found during the rush is a problem found too late. I prepare the listings, pages, and measurement months ahead, so the busy weeks run on work that was finished and checked in the quiet ones.

## Who it's for
- Seasonal retailers with one or several locations and a selling window measured in weeks.
- Pop-up and temporary locations that open and close on a calendar.
- Year-round businesses with one dominant season, such as tax preparers or HVAC companies at the first heat wave.

## What gets prepared
- **Listings for every location** on Google, Apple Maps, and Bing, with seasonal hours set as special hours so the profiles never read as closed for good.
- **Location pages** that answer what shoppers ask before they drive: what's in stock, the season's dates and hours, directions, parking, and local rules where they apply.
- **Permanent seasonal pages** that come back at the same address every year, so their history and links carry forward instead of starting over.
- **AI answers** checked for each location: what ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI features say about hours, products, and directions, with errors traced to their sources.
- **The online store**, where there is one: product data, feeds, and structured data consistent with what the stores sell.
- **Measurement** set up before the season, with comparable date windows, so the results can be read honestly afterward.

## How it works

I start from the selling calendar: when customers start researching, when they buy, and when each location opens and closes. Work is scheduled backward from those dates, with substantial changes finished during the quiet months and a cutoff agreed before the rush. During the season the job narrows to watching for errors that cost sales, such as wrong hours, a broken store locator, or a listing marked closed, and fixing them as they appear.

After the season I set what happened beside the baseline and write down what to keep, what to change, and what to start earlier next year.

## What I'll need from you

The selling calendar for each location, including opening and closing dates; access to your Business Profiles, Search Console, and analytics; the list of products or services that sell in the season; and last season's numbers if you kept them. A list of what went wrong last year is just as useful, because the worst surprises tend to repeat.

## Related reading

The measurement side is laid out in [measuring seasonal local SEO](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seasonal-local-seo/), store hours in the [holiday hours checklist](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/holiday-hours/), and recurring sale pages in [Black Friday pages that keep their rankings](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/black-friday-pages/). For year-round local work, see [local SEO and Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/services/local-seo/).
