# Website archive recovery

Websites disappear. A host shuts down, a hosting bill lapses, an old content system stops running on a new server, or a database gets corrupted and the last backup is years old. The writing, the photos, and the links other sites made to it seem gone. Often they aren't. Between the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, scattered backups, and old exports, most of a lost site can be found again. I find it, rebuild it as a fast static site, and put it back at the addresses the world still links to.

## Who it's for
- Writers and artists whose blog, serial, or portfolio went dark with an old host.
- Organizations that lost a historic site, an event archive, or a past campaign.
- Businesses whose old site still draws links and searches to pages that now return errors.
- Anyone holding a site on a dead platform, such as an old Movable Type, PHP-Nuke, or abandoned CMS install, who wants it preserved before it fails completely.

## How the recovery works

First I count what existed. The Wayback Machine keeps an index of every address it captured for a domain, often thousands, including archive pages, feeds, images, and files. Combined with any backups, database dumps, or exports you still have, that list becomes the inventory: every URL the site ever published, and the best surviving copy of each.

Then I rebuild. Content is pulled from the best source for each page, stripped of the archive's toolbar and rewritten links, and placed into clean, readable templates. Images and downloads come back where copies survive. Where a page is truly gone, I mark it plainly instead of inventing it.

Then I put it back where people expect it. The rebuilt site keeps the original addresses wherever possible, with permanent redirects for the rest, so old links from other sites, bookmarks, and search results land on the right page again. It goes live as static HTML on modern hosting, with HTTPS, a sitemap, and Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools set up for the domain.

## What you get
- The restored site, live on a domain you control, in a repository you own.
- An inventory of every URL found, with what happened to each: restored, redirected, or marked as lost.
- A log of the sources used for each page, so the recovery can be checked.
- A site that needs no database, no plugins, and no security patches to stay online.

## My own archive

I learned this on my own work. A serialized novel I published as a blog for seventeen years outlived the software it ran on, and I moved it to static hosting with every one of its old addresses intact; the method is in the [Movable Type novel case study](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/movable-type-novel/). I've also rebuilt a redirect map by pulling every address the Wayback Machine captured for a site that had lived on three platforms, then testing each one against the live site.

## What I'll need from you

The domain name, or the domains the site lived on over the years; any backups, exports, or old files you can find, however incomplete; and access to the domain's registrar and DNS, or the help of whoever holds them. If you own the content but not the domain, tell me early, because getting the domain back is its own project; my guide to [lapsed domains](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/lapsed-domains/) covers that side.

## Related work

For sites that are alive but stuck on an old platform, see [static websites built for search](https://christopherabraham.com/services/static-sites/) and [site migrations and 301 redirects](https://christopherabraham.com/services/migrations/).

# Search Console comparisons that support better decisions

By [Christopher Abraham](https://christopherabraham.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

An upward line can conceal a weak month. A downward line can follow a useful expansion into new searches. I want a comparison that identifies which pages changed, which searches changed, and what decision the evidence supports. A percentage on its own leaves too much room for a confident explanation that the data never established.

## Write the question before choosing the dates

Decide whether you are checking a release, reviewing a month, or investigating a loss. Each calls for a different comparison. A monthly review needs a view of the whole property. A product-template change needs the affected product pages, with an unchanged group beside them where the site has a suitable comparison. Keep the release date in the notes so later readers can distinguish the work from the measurement window.

Record the property, search type, country, device, page filter, query filter, dates, and export date. Save the original exports. Another person should be able to reopen the report and understand what you selected.

## Match the calendar to the business

I start a routine comparison with two complete 28-day periods. Each contains four of every weekday. That is a reporting choice, and it removes one source of noise for businesses whose weekday and weekend traffic differ. It does not remove holidays, promotions, school schedules, or changes in demand.

For seasonal work, add the comparable period a year earlier and explain any holiday shift. Google's traffic-drop guidance recommends looking across 16 months and checking search demand in Google Trends. Trends supplies context about interest; it does not tell you how many visits your website should have received. Avoid using an unfinished day or preliminary data as the endpoint of a performance claim.

## Keep a stable group of pages

Compare pages that existed in both periods separately from newly published pages. Otherwise a larger site can appear to have improved its existing material when the extra clicks came from additions. For a migration, preserve the mapping from old addresses to new ones before grouping results. Explain which addresses you treated as the same content.

Separate brand searches from the service or product searches relevant to acquiring customers. Define the brand spellings you included. A query filter creates a particular view of the data; describe that view rather than presenting it as the whole market.

## Read the metrics together

Google defines click-through rate as clicks divided by impressions. Average position summarizes the highest result from your site across the observations in the selected view. Neither number is a permanent rank for a keyword. Device, country, page, and query groups help explain changes that the property total hides.

Consider an invented example. An established page receives 100 impressions at position 2. It then starts appearing for another 100 searches at position 20 while retaining its original visibility. The combined average becomes 11. Reporting that change as a nine-place collapse would misdescribe what happened. The page gained exposure to a second set of searches.

Calculate the click change in absolute numbers as well as percentages. A move from two clicks to four is a 100 percent increase and two additional clicks. Both statements belong in the report. Calculate a combined CTR from total clicks divided by total impressions, rather than averaging the percentages of rows with different impression counts.

## Give the reader a compact evidence record
- **Scope:** the property, filters, and page group.
- **Window:** two complete periods, with calendar differences explained.
- **Result:** clicks and impressions in each period, absolute changes, and percentage changes.
- **Explanation:** the pages and query groups responsible for most of the movement.
- **Limit:** what remains unresolved, and the next check that will resolve it.

A useful conclusion sounds like this: in this hypothetical comparison, existing service pages lost 30 clicks, new guides added 45, and the property gained 15 overall. The service-page loss still needs investigation. That gives the owner a task the headline total concealed.

## Separate a release check from a growth claim

My guide to [verifying an SEO fix](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prove-seo-fixes/) covers whether the intended change reached the pages. This comparison answers a later question about search performance. A successful deployment and a rise in clicks are separate observations. Concurrent campaigns, seasonality, competitors, and other releases can affect the second.

I bring this reporting discipline to [SEO audits](https://christopherabraham.com/services/seo-audit/): preserve the baseline, identify the affected group, and explain what the next decision rests on. An owner should be able to challenge the conclusion using the evidence delivered with it.

## Let me help you with this

If you'd rather have this done than do it yourself, it's exactly the work I do for clients. Tell me about your site and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email cja@well.com](mailto:cja@well.com)

- [Accessibility as SEO: the search, AI, and trust dividends](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/accessibility-seo-dividends/): WCAG fixes pay off more than once: alt text, headings, link text, labels, and captions lift rankings, AI answers, agent browsing, and trust, and cut legal risk.
- [The Lynx test: see your website the way crawlers and AI read it](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/lynx-test/): Lynx, a text browser, shows what search engines and AI crawlers that skip JavaScript receive. How to install it, what to check, and online alternatives.
- [How to hire an SEO on Upwork: the questions that reveal real skill](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/hiring-an-seo/): How to vet an SEO consultant on Upwork: the screening questions that expose real skill, what good answers sound like, the red flags, and a safer first step.
- [Reddit and AI answers: what a moderator wants brands to know](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/reddit-ai-answers/): Why Reddit threads now shape Google and ChatGPT answers about your business, what moderators remove on sight, and the honest ways a brand can take part.
- [SEO for websites built with AI app builders: what to check before you launch](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-built-websites/): AI app builders ship a site in an afternoon. Here is how to check that Google and AI crawlers can read it: rendering, links, titles, status codes, and sitemaps.
- [Digital PR for AI search: how to earn mentions the answer engines repeat](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/earned-mentions/): AI answers repeat what other sites say about you. How to earn honest mentions in the press, newsletters, and niche sites, plus the FTC and Google rules on pay.
- [I turn down backlink work. Here's the one agency I recommend instead](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/buying-backlinks/): Why I refuse backlink campaigns, why FatJoe is the one agency I recommend after a decade as one of its publishers, and Google's rule on paid links to know.
- [How to change a business name without losing your Google reviews](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/business-name-change/): How to rename a business without losing its Google Business Profile, reviews, or rankings: edit the existing listing, sequence the change, and update the web.
- [Holiday hours on Google: set them before you need them](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/holiday-hours/): How and when to set special hours on Google for Thanksgiving, December, and New Year, when to mark a business temporarily closed, and what searchers see.
- [Hit by a 2026 Google update? A recovery checklist that works](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/update-recovery-2026/): How to tell whether a 2026 Google core or spam update hit your site, rule out reporting quirks, find the pages that lost, and fix them in the right order.
- [Where to get reliable SEO and AI search news in 2026](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-news-sources/): The SEO and AI search news sources I read, from Google's own records to daily trade press, who owns them, and how to tell a real finding from a vendor pitch.
- [WordPress SEO 101: the settings and habits that matter most](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/wordpress-seo-101/): A beginner's WordPress SEO primer: the settings to change on day one, the plugins I recommend, alt text, descriptive links, speed, and accessibility.
- [Cloudflare for WordPress: setup, plans, and what to budget](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/cloudflare-wordpress/): How to put a WordPress site behind Cloudflare: moving DNS, what the free plan already does, APO and Polish on paid plans, HTTPS settings, and a monthly budget.
- [Will Google penalize AI-written content? What Google actually says](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-content-seo/): Does Google penalize AI-written copy? What Google's guidance says in 2026, what the data shows, the new fact checking rule, fake authors, and safe AI use.
- [Is a Screaming Frog licence worth $279 a year? Mine was](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/screaming-frog-licence/): Why I finally paid for the Screaming Frog SEO Spider, what the free 500 URL version leaves out, and everything a $279 a year licence can do in 2026.
- [Why your SEO should work in your Git repository, with AI at their side](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/seo-in-your-repository/): An SEO using OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, or GitHub Copilot can trace search problems to the files that cause them. What repository access and review should mean.
- [How to find near-duplicate pages and multiple H1s across a whole site](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/near-duplicates-and-h1s/): Find near-duplicate pages and heading problems across an entire site with Screaming Frog, then decide which pages to rewrite, merge, redirect, or canonicalize.
- [Screaming Frog custom extraction recipes for sitewide SEO audits](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/custom-extraction/): XPath and regex recipes for Screaming Frog custom extraction to audit a site: heading counts, canonicals, robots tags, schema types, alt text, and tag IDs.
- [How to prove an SEO fix actually worked](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prove-seo-fixes/): Proof that an SEO fix shipped: compare before-and-after crawls in Screaming Frog, check change detection, then confirm in Search Console with validation.
- [How to measure your share of voice in AI answers](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ai-share-of-voice/): Track how often ChatGPT, Claude, and Google's AI name you beside competitors, in what tone, and from which sources, with a fixed question set and a monthly run.
- [Topic clusters for AI search, without your pages competing with each other](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/topic-clusters/): Plan a hub page and one page per buyer question so AI fan out searches find a match for every subtopic, and keep your pages from competing for one query.
- [How to load Google Analytics 4 without hurting PageSpeed](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ga4-pagespeed/): On a fast static site, gtag.js caused most of the blocking time. Loading it after the first scroll or tap took mobile Lighthouse to 100. How, and the cost.
- [Glossary of SEO and AI search terms](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/): Plain-English definitions of SEO and AI search terms: AEO, GEO, canonical tags, crawl budget, entities, INP, IndexNow, llms.txt, soft 404s, and many more.
- [The show notes cascade: podcasting as an AI search strategy](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/show-notes-cascade/): Every podcast episode publishes its show notes into hundreds of trusted directories, and AI answers cite those copies. How to write notes that get quoted.
- [Internal linking: stitching your pages into a useful website](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/internal-linking/): Build useful paths through your existing pages with contextual links, clear anchor text, working section targets, and an internal linking worksheet.
- [Moving a website? Check its images and PDFs before closing the old host](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/media-migration/): Keep images, PDFs, and share cards working during a website move. Inventory old media URLs, test the new files, and find references to the retiring host.
- [Your website form says success. Did anyone get the inquiry?](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/test-website-inquiries/): Trace a test inquiry from landing page to form, confirmation, inbox, and reporting. Find delivery failures and false conversion counts before buying traffic.
- [Spam link spikes and the disavow file: when to act at all](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/disavow-links/): A burst of junk backlinks rarely needs a response. When Google says the disavow tool fits, how to build a careful file, and the mistakes that cost rankings.
- [Reading the new Google Business Profile performance reports](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-performance-reports/): Google is testing a rebuilt Performance section for Business Profiles. How to read each new report, Overview first, and what the numbers mean.
- [Google Business Profile video verification: plan the take before you press record](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/gbp-video-verification/): Passing Google Business Profile video verification the first time: what Google wants on camera for storefronts and service areas, and what to do if it fails.
- [XML sitemaps that tell the truth](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/xml-sitemaps/): What an XML sitemap should hold in 2026: canonical URLs that answer 200, honest lastmod dates, no priority games, and how I audit one against a crawl.
- [How to choose the next SEO fix when developer time is scarce](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/prioritize-seo-work/): Choose the next SEO task using business value, affected pages, evidence, dependencies, and effort, then keep a clear record of what shipped and what changed.
- [Service-area businesses on Google Business Profile](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/service-area-business/): How a business that travels to customers should set up its Google Business Profile: removing the address, choosing service areas, and the phone number.
- [Black Friday sale pages that keep their rankings](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/black-friday-pages/): Build one Black Friday URL and reuse it every year: what Google advises for sale pages, when to publish, what to do in January, and how to track the results.
- [Google Merchant Center free listings for small shops](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/merchant-center-free-listings/): How a small shop gets its products into Google's free listings: the Merchant Center feed, required attributes, shipping, returns, and the errors to fix first.
- [Apple Maps and Bing Places: local listings past Google](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/apple-and-bing-listings/): Why a local business should claim its Apple Maps place card and its Bing Places listing, what each one feeds, how to set them up, and keeping them consistent.
- [The FTC fake review rule for small businesses](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/ftc-review-rule/): The FTC's rule on consumer reviews took effect October 21, 2024. What it bans, what it allows, and how to ask customers for reviews without risk to you.
- [Search Console comparisons that support better decisions](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/search-console-comparisons/): Compare Search Console periods with consistent filters, matched weekdays, and page groups so seasonal demand and changing query mixes do not distort the result.

## Case studies
- [Equipment retailer: product details that loaded only on scroll](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/scroll-gated-products/): An equipment retailer on Magento and Hyvä lost organic traffic because Alpine.js loaded specs and reviews only on scroll. How the cause was isolated and proven.
- [Film review site: a consent tool that emptied every article for Google](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/consent-banner/): A bilingual film review site was indexed by Bing but nearly invisible in Google. A consent platform blocked the script that displayed every article to bots.
- [Event discovery app: 2,000 pages with no way in](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/event-app-links/): An event discovery app built with Create React App had 2,000 event pages Google never found. A 13-page spec, ranked P0 to P3, gave the developer exact fixes.
- [Junk removal company on a headless stack: SEO through the repository](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/headless-local/): A junk removal company on Sanity, Vercel, and GitHub had thin rendered HTML and duplicate metadata. Priorities set, a pull request merged, prerendering checked.
- [Medical clinic: WordPress to Next.js without losing the trail](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/clinic-migration/): SEO oversight for a clinic moving from WordPress to Next.js on Netlify: a decision for every legacy URL, an AI-assisted code review, and a careful disavow.
- [Fly fishing shop: cleaning up after Squarespace to Shopify](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/shopify-cleanup/): A family owned fly fishing shop moved from Squarespace to Shopify and left 3,400 broken URLs and duplicate product paths. An audit and safe theme schema work.
- [Trading card price site: managing 20,000 pages in Google's index](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/card-price-index/): A trading card price site of more than 20,000 programmatic pages indexed well, then lost large sections of the index. How crawling is managed at that scale.
- [Health-testing store: recovering after the SEO plugin went dark](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/plugin-outage/): A WooCommerce store selling health tests lost indexing, traffic, and AI referrals when its SEO plugin was turned off. Diagnosis, fixes, and proof of recovery.
- [Custom closet brand: separating the company from its first showroom](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/closet-locations/): A custom closet company with showrooms in several states ran one website, and search engines blurred the brand with its first showroom. Entity and schema fixes.
- [Therapy practice: a suspended Business Profile restored](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/profile-reinstated/): A Canadian hypnotherapy office disappeared from Google Maps after a profile suspension. The listing was corrected, proof organized, and the profile restored.
- [Private training gym: a brand name Google kept misreading](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/training-gym/): A members only training gym in Northern Virginia had a brand name Google read as an ordinary word. Fixing its profile and pages lifted calls and visits.
- [AI research company: accurate AI answers for job seekers](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/recruiting-answers/): An AI research company hiring Bay Area engineers wanted ChatGPT and Perplexity to answer accurately about its jobs and pay. The audit findings and the plan.
- [My own consultancy: an AI visibility baseline, with nothing redacted](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/ai-visibility-baseline/): I ran sixteen buyer questions about my own services through Claude with web search, then traced every wrong fact and every missing mention to a fixable cause.
- [My own podcast: 458 episodes, each with a page of its own](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/podcast-site/): How I turned my own podcast feed into a static site with a page, share card, and alt text for each of 458 episodes, plus transcripts, updated daily.
- [A serialized novel: 17 years of Movable Type URLs, all kept](https://christopherabraham.com/case-studies/movable-type-novel/): How I moved a serialized novel off Movable Type 3.33 to static hosting, keeping all 953 old URLs: entries, archive pages, feeds, TrackBack files, and images.

## Files for machines
- [sitemap.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/sitemap.xml): the XML sitemap for search engines.
- [llms.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms.txt): a plain summary of the site for language models, linking to Markdown versions of every page.
- [llms-full.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llms-full.txt): the full text of the site in one file.
- [feed.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/feed.xml) and [rss.xml](https://christopherabraham.com/rss.xml): Atom and RSS feeds of the guides.
- [llm.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/llm.txt): the same summary as llms.txt, at the other common address.
- [robots.txt](https://christopherabraham.com/robots.txt): crawler rules; every search engine and AI crawler is welcome.

# Index

This is an index in the old sense, the kind at the back of a good book. I read every page on this site and listed the people, tools, platforms, problems, and ideas each one covers: 600 headings across 115 pages. Each locator is the short name of a page, and a bold one marks the page devoted to that subject. Hover over a name to see the full title.

People are listed surname first. Cross-references point to related headings. For definitions, the [glossary](https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/) is the place to start; for a plain list of pages, the [site map](https://christopherabraham.com/sitemap/).
